fescennine.c: Fescennine Fes"cen*nine (?), a. [L. Fescenninus, fr. Fescennia, a city of Etruria.] Pertaining to, or resembling, the Fescennines. -- n. A style of low, scurrilous, obscene poetry originating in fescennia.

fescue.c: Fescue Fes"cue (fĕs"ku), n. [OE. festu, OF. festu, F. fétu, fr. L. festuca stalk, straw.] 1. A straw, wire, stick, etc., used chiefly to point out letters to children when learning to read. “Pedantic fescue.” Sterne.
Fescue Fes"cue (fĕs"ku), v. i. & t. [imp. & p. p. Fescued (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fescuing.] To use a fescue, or teach with a fescue. Milton.

fesels.c: Fesels Fes"els (?), n. pl. [Written also fasels.] See Phasel. [Obs.] May (Georgics).

fesse.c: Fesse Fess { Fess, Fesse } (?), n. [OF. fesse, faisse, F. fasce, fr. L. fascia band. See Fascia.] (Her.) A band drawn horizontally across the center of an escutcheon, and containing in breadth the third part of it; one of the nine honorable ordinaries.

fessitude.c: Fessitude Fes"si*tude (?), n. [L. fessus wearied, fatigued.] Weariness. [Obs.] Bailey.

fesswise.c: Fesswise Fess"wise (?), adv. In the manner of fess.

fest.c: Fest Fest (?), n. [See Fist.] The fist. [Obs.] Chaucer.

feste.c: Feste Fest { Fest, Fes"te (?), n. } A feast. [Obs.] Chaucer.

festal.c: Festal Fes"tal (?), a. [L. festum holiday, feast. See feast.] Of or pertaining to a holiday or a feast; joyous; festive.

fester.c: Fester Fes"ter (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Festered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Festering.] [OE. festern, fr. fester, n.; or fr. OF. festrir, fr. festre, n. See Fester, n.] 1. To generate pus; to become imflamed and suppurate; as, a sore or a wound festers.
Fester Fes`ter, v. t. To cause to fester or rankle.
Fester Fes"ter, n. [OF. festre, L. fistula a sort of ulcer. Cf. Fistula.] 1. A small sore which becomes inflamed and discharges corrupt matter; a pustule.

festeye.c: Festeye Fest"eye (?), v. t. [OF. festier, festeer, F. festoyer.] To feast; to entertain. [Obs.] Chaucer.

festinate.c: Festinate Fes"ti*nate (?), a. [L. festinatus, p. p. of festinare to hasten.] Hasty; hurried. [Obs.] -- Fes"ti*nate*ly, adv. [Obs.] Shak.

festination.c: Festination Fes`ti*na"tion (?), n. [L. festinatio.] Haste; hurry. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

festival.c: Festival Fes"ti*val (?), a. [OF. festival, fr. L. festivum festive jollity, fr. festivus festive, gay. See Festive.] Pertaining to a fest; festive; festal; appropriate to a festival; joyous; mirthful.
Festi-val Fes"ti-val, n. A time of feasting or celebration; an anniversary day of joy, civil or religious.

festive.c: Festive Fes"tive (?), a. [L. festivus, fr. festum holiday, feast. See feast, and cf. Festivous.] Pertaining to, or becoming, a feast; festal; joyous; gay; mirthful; sportive. -- Fes"tive*ly, adv.

festivity.c: Festivity Fes*tiv"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Festivities (#). [L. festivitas: cf. F. festivité.] 1. The condition of being festive; social joy or exhilaration of spirits at an entertaintment; joyfulness; gayety.

festivous.c: Festivous Fes"ti*vous (?), a. [See Festive.] Pertaining to a feast; festive. [R.] Sir W. Scott.

festlich.c: Festlich Fest"lich (?), a. [See Feast, n.] Festive; fond of festive occasions. [Obs.] “A festlich man.” Chaucer.

festoon.c: Festoon Fes*toon" (?), n. [F. feston (cf. Sp. feston, It. festone), prob. fr. L. festum festival. See Feast.] 1. A garland or wreath hanging in a depending curve, used in decoration for festivals, etc.; anything arranged in this way.
Festoon Fes*toon", v. t. [imp. & p. p. Festooned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Festooning.] To form in festoons, or to adorn with festoons.

festoony.c: Festoony Fes*toon"y (?), a. Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, festoons. Sir J. Herschel.

festucine.c: Festucine Fes*tu*cine (? or?), a. [L. festula stalk, straw. Cf. Fescue.] Of a straw color; greenish yellow. [Obs.]

festucous.c: Festucous Fes"tu*cous (?), a. Formed or consisting of straw. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

festue.c: Festue Fes"tue (?), n. [See Fescue.] A straw; a fescue. [Obs.] Holland.

fet.c: Fet Fet (?), n. [Cf. feat, F. fait, and It. fett? slice, G. fetzen rag, Icel. fat garment.] A piece. [Obs.] Dryton.
Fet Fet, v. t. [OE. fetten, feten, AS. fetian; akin to AS. fæt a journey, and to E. foot; cf. G. fassen to seize. √ 77. See Foot, and cf. Fetch.] To fetch. [Obs.]
Fet Fet, p. p. of Fette. Fetched. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fetal.c: Fetal Fe"tal (?), a. [From Fetus.] Pertaining to, or connected with, a fetus; as, fetal circulation; fetal membranes.

fetation.c: Fetation Fe*ta"tion (?), n. The formation of a fetus in the womb; pregnancy.

fetch.c: Fetch Fetch (fĕch; 224), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fetched 2; p. pr. & vb. n.. Fetching.] [OE. fecchen, AS. feccan, perh. the same word as fetian; or cf. facian to wish to get, OFries. faka to prepare. √77. Cf. Fet, v. t.] 1. To bear toward the person speaking, or the person or thing from whose point of view the action is contemplated; to go and bring; to get.
fetch fetch, v. i. To bring one's self; to make headway; to veer; as, to fetch about; to fetch to windward. Totten.
Fetch Fetch, n. 1. A stratagem by which a thing is indirectly brought to pass, or by which one thing seems intended and another is done; a trick; an artifice.

fetcher.c: Fetcher Fetch"er (fĕch"ẽr), n. One who fetches or brings.

fete.c: Fete Fete (fēt), n. [See feat.] A feat. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Fete Fete, n. pl. [See Foot.] Feet. [Obs.] Chaucer.
fete fête (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fêted; p. pr. & vb. n. Fêting.] [Cf. F. fêter.] To feast; to honor with a festival.

fetish.c: Fetish Fetich { Fe"tich, Fe"tish (?), n. }[F. fétiche, from Pg. feiti?o, adj., n., sorcery, charm, fr. L. facticius made by art, artifical, factitious. See Factitious.] 1. A material object supposed among certain African tribes to represent in such a way, or to be so connected with, a supernatural being, that the possession of it gives to the possessor power to control that being.

fetishism.c: Fetishism fetichism { fe"tich*ism, Fe"tish*ism (? or?); 277), n. }[Cf. F. fétichisme.] [Written also feticism.] 1. The doctrine or practice of belief in fetiches.

fetishist.c: Fetishist Fetichist { Fe"tich*ist, Fe"tish*ist, n. } A believer in fetiches.

fetishistic.c: Fetishistic Fetichistic { Fe`tich*is"tic (?), Fe`tish*is"tic, a.} Pertaining to, or involving, fetichism.
Fetishistic Fetishism Fetish Fe"tish (?), n., Fe"tish*ism (? or?; 277), n., Fe`tish*is"tic (?), a. See Fetich, n., Fetichism, n., Fetichistic, a.

feticide.c: Feticide Fe"ti*cide (? or?), n. [Written also fœticide.] [Fetus + L. caedere to kill.] (Med. & Law) The act of killing the fetus in the womb; the offense of procuring an abortion.

fetid.c: Fetid Fet"id (? or?; 277), a. [L. fetidus, foetidus, fr. fetere, foetere, to have an ill smell, to stink: cf. F. fétide.] Having an offensive smell; stinking.

fetidness.c: Fetidness Fet"id*ness, n. The quality or state of being fetid.

fetiferous.c: Fetiferous Fe*tif"er*ous (?), a. [Fetus + -ferous.] Producing young, as animals.

fetis.c: Fetis Fe"tis (?), a. [OF. fetis, faitis. Cf. Factitious.] Neat; pretty; well made; graceful. [Obs.]

fetisely.c: Fetisely Fe"tise*ly (?), adv. Neatly; gracefully; properly. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fetlock.c: Fetlock Fet"lock (?), n. [OE. fetlak, fitlock, cf. Icel. fet pace, step, fit webbed foot of water birds, akin to E. foot. √ 77. See Foot.] The cushionlike projection, bearing a tuft of long hair, on the back side of the leg above the hoof of the horse and similar animals. Also, the joint of the limb at this point (between the great pastern bone and the metacarpus), or the tuft of hair.

fetor.c: Fetor Fe"tor (?), n. [L. fetor, foetor. See Fetid.] A strong, offensive smell; stench; fetidness. Arbuthnot.

fette.c: Fette Fet"te (? or?), v. t. [imp. Fette, p. p. Fet.] [See Fet, v. t.] To fetch. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fetter.c: Fetter Fet"ter (fĕt"tẽr), n. [AS. fetor, feter; akin to OS. feterōs, pl., OD. veter, OHG. fezzera, Icel. fjöturr, L. pedica, Gr. pe`dh, and to E. foot. √ 77. See Foot.] [Chiefly used in the plural, fetters.] 1. A chain or shackle for the feet; a chain by which an animal is confined by the foot, either made fast or disabled from free and rapid motion; a bond; a shackle.
Fetter Fet"ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fettered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fettering.] 1. To put fetters upon; to shackle or confine the feet of with a chain; to bind.

fettered.c: Fettered Fet"tered (?), a. (Zool.) Seeming as if fettered, as the feet of certain animals which bend backward, and appear unfit for walking.

fetterer.c: Fetterer Fet"ter*er (?), n. One who fetters. Landor.

fetterless.c: Fetterless Fet"ter*less, a. Free from fetters. Marston.

fettle.c: Fettle Fet"tle (?), v. t. [OE. & Prov. E., to fettle (in sense 1), fettle, n., order, repair, preparation, dress; prob. akin to E. fit. See Fit, a.] 1. To repair; to prepare; to put in order. [Prov. Eng.] Carlyle.
Fettle Fet"tle, v. i. To make preparations; to put things in order; to do trifling business. [Prov. Eng.] Bp. Hall.
Fettle Fet"tle, n. The act of fettling. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

fettling.c: Fettling Fet"tling (?), n. 1. (Metal.) A mixture of ore, cinders, etc., used to line the hearth of a puddling furnace. [Eng.]

fetus.c: Fetus Fe"tus (fē"tŭs), n.; pl. Fetuses (fē"tŭs*ĕz). [L. fetus, foetus, a bringing forth, brood, offspring, young ones, cf. fetus fruitful, fructified, that is or was filled with young; akin to E. fawn a deer, fecundity, felicity, feminine, female, and prob. to do, or according to others, to be.] The young or embryo of a vertebrate animal in the womb, or in the egg; often restricted to the later stages in the development of viviparous and oviparous animals. showing the main recognizable features of the mature animal, embryo being applied to the earlier stages. [Written also fœtus.]

fetwah.c: Fetwah ‖Fet"wah (?), n. [Ar.] A written decision of a Turkish mufti some point of law; also applied to opinions by certain other Islamic religious authorities on points of Islamic law, such as in Iran. [Also spelled fatwah and fatwa.] Whitworth.

feu.c: Feu Feu (fū), n. [See 2d Feud, and Fee.] (Scots Law) A free and gratuitous right to lands made to one for service to be performed by him; a tenure where the vassal, in place of military services, makes a return in grain or in money. Burrill.
Feu de joie ‖Feu` de joie" (?). [F., lit., fire of joy.] A fire kindled in a public place in token of joy; a bonfire; a firing of guns in token of joy.

feuar.c: Feuar Feu"ar (fū"ẽr), n. [From Feu.] (Scots Law) One who holds a feu. Sir W. Scott.

feud.c: Feud Feud (fūd), n. [OE. feide, AS. fǣhð, fr. fāh hostile; akin to OHG. fēhida, G. fehde, Sw. fejd, D. feide; prob. akin to E. fiend. See Foe.] 1. A combination of kindred to avenge injuries or affronts, done or offered to any of their blood, on the offender and all his race.

Feud Feud, n. [LL. feudum, feodum prob. of same origin as E. fief. See Fief, Fee.] (Law) A stipendiary estate in land, held of a superior, by service; the right which a vassal or tenant had to the lands or other immovable thing of his lord, to use the same and take the profits thereof hereditarily, rendering to his superior such duties and services as belong to military tenure, etc., the property of the soil always remaining in the lord or superior; a fief; a fee.

feudal.c: feudal feu"dal (fū"dail), a. [F. féodal, or LL. feudalis.] 1. Of or pertaining to feuds, fiefs, or fees; as, feudal rights or services; feudal tenures.

feudalism.c: Feudalism Feu"dal*ism (fū"dail*ĭz'm), n. [Cf. F. féodalisme.] The feudal system; a system by which the holding of estates in land is made dependent upon an obligation to render military service to the king or feudal superior; feudal principles and usages.

feudalist.c: feudalist feu"dal*ist, n. An upholder of feudalism.

feudality.c: Feudality Feu*dal"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. féodalité.] The state or quality of being feudal; feudal form or constitution. Burke.

feudalization.c: Feudalization Feu`dal*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of reducing to feudal tenure.

feudalize.c: Feudalize Feu"dal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Feudalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Feudalizing (?).] To reduce to a feudal tenure; to conform to feudalism.

feudally.c: Feudally Feu"dal*ly, adv. In a feudal manner.

feudary.c: Feudary Feu"da*ry (?), a. [LL. feudarius, fr. feudum. See 2d Feud.] Held by, or pertaining to, feudal tenure.
Feudary Feu"da*ry, n. 1. A tenant who holds his lands by feudal service; a feudatory. Foxe.

feudatary.c: Feudatary Feu"da*ta*ry (?), a. & n. [LL. feudatarius: cf. F. feudataire.] See Feudatory.

feudatory.c: Feudatory Feu"da*to*ry (?), n.; pl. Feudatories (?). A tenant or vassal who held his lands of a superior on condition of feudal service; the tenant of a feud or fief.
Feudatory Feu"da*to*ry, a. Held from another on some conditional tenure; as, a feudatory title. Bacon.

feudist.c: Feudist Feud"ist (?), n. [Cf. F. feudiste.] A writer on feuds; a person versed in feudal law. Spelman.

feuillants.c: Feuillants ‖Feu`illants" (?), n. pl. A reformed branch of the Bernardines, founded in 1577 at Feuillans, near Toulouse, in France.

feuillemort.c: Feuillemort Feuille"mort` (?), a. [F. feuille morte a dead leaf.] Having the color of a faded leaf. Locke.

feuilleton.c: Feuilleton ‖Feu`ille*ton" (? or?), n. [F., from feulle leaf.] A part of a French newspaper (usually the bottom of the page), devoted to light literature, criticism, etc.; also, the article or tale itself, thus printed.

feuilltonist.c: Feuilltonist Feuill"ton*ist (?), n. [F. feuilletoniste.] A writer of feuilletons. F. Harrison.

feuter.c: feuter feu"ter (?), v. t. [OE. feutre rest for a lance, OF. feutre, fautre, feltre, felt, cushion, rest for a lance, fr. LL. filtrum, feltrum; of German origin, and akin to E. felt. See Felt, and cf. Filter.] To set close; to fix in rest, as a spear. Spenser.

feuterer.c: Feuterer Feu"ter*er (?), n. [Either fr. G. fütterer feeder, or corrupted fr. OF. vautrier, vaultrier; fr. vaultre, viautre, a kind of hound, fr. L. vertragus, vertraga, a greyhound. The last is of Celtic origin.] A dog keeper. [Obs.] Massinger.

fever.c: Fever Fe"ver (fē"vẽr), n. [OE. fever, fefer, AS. fefer, fefor, L. febris: cf. F. fièvre. Cf. Febrile.] 1. (Med.) A diseased state of the system, marked by increased heat, acceleration of the pulse, and a general derangement of the functions, including usually, thirst and loss of appetite. Many diseases, of which fever is the most prominent symptom, are denominated fevers; as, typhoid fever; yellow fever.
Fever Fe"ver, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fevered (fē"vẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Fevering.] To put into a fever; to affect with fever; as, a fevered lip. [R.]

feveret.c: Feveret Fe"ver*et (fē"vẽr*ĕt), n. A slight fever. [Obs.] Ayliffe.

feverfew.c: Feverfew Fe"ver*few (fē"vẽr*fū), n. [AS. feferfuge, fr. L. febrifugia. See fever, Fugitive, and cf. Febrifuge.] (Bot.) A perennial plant (Pyrethrum Parthenium, or Chrysanthemum Parthenium) allied to camomile, having finely divided leaves and white blossoms; -- so named from its supposed febrifugal qualities.

feverish.c: Feverish Fe"ver*ish, a. 1. Having a fever; suffering from, or affected with, a moderate degree of fever; showing increased heat and thirst; as, the patient is feverish.

feverous.c: Feverous Fe"ver*ous (?), a. [Cf.F. fiévreux.] 1. Affected with fever or ague; feverish.

feverwort.c: Feverwort Fe"ver*wort` (?), n. See Fever root, under Fever.

few.c: Few Few (fū), a. [Compar. Fewer (fū"ẽr); superl. Fewest.] [OE. fewe, feawe, AS. feá, pl. feáwe; akin to OS. fāh, OHG. fō fao, Icel. fār, Sw. få, pl., Dan. faa, pl., Goth. faus, L. paucus, cf. Gr. pay^ros. Cf. Paucity.] Not many; small, limited, or confined in number; -- indicating a small portion of units or individuals constituting a whole; often, by ellipsis of a noun, a few people. “Are not my days few?” Job x. 20.

fewmet.c: Fewmet Few"met (?), n. See Fumet. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

fewness.c: Fewness Few"ness, n. 1. The state of being few; smallness of number; paucity. Shak.

fey.c: Fey Fey (fā), a. [AS. fǣga, Icel. feigr, OHG. feigi.] Fated; doomed. [Old Eng. & Scot.]
Fey Fey (fā), n. [See Fay faith.] Faith. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Fey Fey (?), v. t. [Cf. Feague.] To cleanse; to clean out. [Obs.] Tusser.

feyne.c: Feyne Feyne (?), v. t. To feign. [Obs.] Chaucer.

feyre.c: Feyre Feyre (?), n. A fair or market. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fez.c: Fez Fez (fĕz), n. [F., fr. the town of Fez in Morocco.] A felt or cloth cap, usually red and having a tassel, -- a variety of the tarboosh. See Tarboosh. B. Taylor.

fiacre.c: Fiacre ‖Fia"cre (?), n. [F.] A kind of French hackney coach.

fiance.c: Fiance Fi"ance (?), v. t. [F. fiancer. See Affiance.] To betroth; to affiance. [Obs.] Harmar.
Fiance ‖Fi`an`cé" (?), n. [F.] A betrothed man; the man to whom one is betrothed.

fiancee.c: Fiancee ‖Fi`an`cée" (?), n. [F.] A betrothed woman; the woman to whom one is betrothed.

fiants.c: Fiants Fi"ants (?), n. [F. fiente dung.] The dung of the fox, wolf, boar, or badger.

fiar.c: Fiar Fi"ar (? or?), n. [See Feuar.] 1. (Scots Law) One in whom the property of an estate is vested, subject to the estate of a life renter.

fiasco.c: Fiasco ‖Fi*as"co (?), n.; pl. Fiascoes (#). [It.] A complete or ridiculous failure, esp. of a musical performance, or of any pretentious undertaking.

fiat.c: Fiat Fi"at (?), n. [L., let it be done, 3d pers. sing., subj. pres., fr. fieri, used as pass. of facere to make. Cf. Be.] 1. An authoritative command or order to do something; an effectual decree.

fiaunt.c: Fiaunt Fi*aunt" (?), n. Commission; fiat; order; decree. [Obs.] Spenser.

fib.c: Fib Fib (?), n. [Prob. fr. fable; cf. Prov. E. fibble-fabble nonsense.] A falsehood; a lie; -- used euphemistically.
Fib Fib, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fibbed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fibbing (?).] To speak falsely. [Colloq.]
Fib Fib, v. t. To tell a fib to. [R.] De Quincey.

fibber.c: Fibber Fib"ber (?), n. One who tells fibs.

fibre.c: Fibre Fiber { Fi"ber, Fi"bre }, (?), n. [F. fibre, L. fibra.] 1. One of the delicate, threadlike portions of which the tissues of plants and animals are in part constituted; as, the fiber of flax or of muscle.

fibred.c: Fibred Fibered { Fi"bered, Fi"bred } (?), a. Having fibers; made up of fibers.

fibrefaced.c: Fibre-faced Fiber-faced { Fi"ber-faced`, Fi"bre-faced` } (?), a. Having a visible fiber embodied in the surface of; -- applied esp. to a kind of paper for checks, drafts, etc.

fibreless.c: Fibreless Fiberless { Fi"ber*less, Fi"bre*less }, a. Having no fibers; destitute of fibers or fiber.

fibriform.c: Fibriform Fi"bri*form (? or?), a. [L. fibra a fiber + -form.] (Biol.) Having the form of a fiber or fibers; resembling a fiber.

fibril.c: Fibril Fi"bril (?), n. [F. fibrille, dim. of fibre, L. fibra.] A small fiber; the branch of a fiber; a very slender thread; a fibrilla. Cheyne.

fibrilla.c: Fibrilla ‖fi*bril"la (?), n.; pl. fibrillæ (#). [NL. See Fibril.] A minute thread or fiber, as one of the fibrous elements of a muscular fiber; a fibril.

fibrillar.c: Fibrillar Fi"bril*lar (?), a. Of or pertaining to fibrils or fibers; as, fibrillar twitchings.

fibrillary.c: Fibrillary Fi"bril*la*ry (? or?), a. Of of pertaining to fibrils.

fibrillated.c: Fibrillated Fi"bril*la`ted (? or?), a. Furnished with fibrils; fringed.

fibrillation.c: Fibrillation Fi`bril*la"tion (?), n. The state of being reduced to fibers. Carpenter.

fibrillose.c: Fibrillose Fi*bril"lose (? or?), a. Covered with hairlike appendages, as the under surface of some lichens; also, composed of little strings or fibers; as, fibrillose appendages.

fibrillous.c: Fibrillous Fi*bril"lous (? or?), a. [Cf. F. fibraleux.] Pertaining to, or composed of, fibers.

fibrin.c: Fibrin Fi"brin (?), n. [Cf. F. fibrine. See Fiber.] (Physiol. Chem.) 1. A white, albuminous, fibrous substance, formed in the coagulation of the blood either by decomposition of fibrinogen, or from the union of fibrinogen and paraglobulin which exist separately in the blood. It is insoluble in water, but is readily digestible in gastric and pancreatic juice.

fibrination.c: Fibrination Fi`bri*na"tion (?), n. (Med.) The state of acquiring or having an excess of fibrin.

fibrine.c: Fibrine Fi"brine (?), a. Belonging to the fibers of plants.

fibrinogen.c: Fibrinogen Fi*brin"o*gen (?), n. [Fibrin + -gen.] (Physiol. Chem.) An albuminous substance existing in the blood, and in other animal fluids, which either alone or with fibrinoplastin or paraglobulin forms fibrin, and thus causes coagulation.

fibrinogenous.c: Fibrinogenous Fi`bri*nog"e*nous (?), a. (Physiol. Chem.) Possessed of properties similar to fibrinogen; capable of forming fibrin.

fibrinoplastic.c: Fibrinoplastic Fi`bri*no*plas"tic (?), a. (Physiol.Chem.) Like fibrinoplastin; capable of forming fibrin when brought in contact with fibrinogen.

fibrinoplastin.c: Fibrinoplastin Fi`bri*no*plas"tin (?), n. [Fibrin + Gr.? to form, mold.] (Physiol.Chem.) An albuminous substance, existing in the blood, which in combination with fibrinogen forms fibrin; -- called also paraglobulin.

fibrinous.c: Fibrinous Fi"bri*nous (? or?; 277), a. Having, or partaking of the properties of, fibrin; as, fibrious exudation.

fibrocartilage.c: Fibrocartilage Fi`bro*car"ti*lage (?), n. [L. fibra a fiber + E. cartilage.] (Anat.) A kind of cartilage with a fibrous matrix and approaching fibrous connective tissue in structure. -- Fi`bro*car`ti*lag"i*nous (#), a.

fibrochondrosteal.c: Fibrochondrosteal Fi`bro*chon*dros"te*al (fī`bro*kŏn*drŏs"te*ail), a. [L. fibra a fiber + gr. cho`ndros cartilage + 'oste`on bone.] (Anat.) Partly fibrous, partly cartilaginous, and partly osseous. St. George Mivart.

fibroid.c: fibroid fi"broid (fī"broid), a. [L. fibra a fiber + -oid.] (Med.) Resembling or forming fibrous tissue; made up of fibers; as, fibroid tumors. -- n. A fibroid tumor; a fibroma.

fibroin.c: fibroin fi"bro*in (fī"bro*ĭn or fĭb"ro*ĭn), n. [L. fibra a fiber.] (Chem.) A variety of gelatin; the chief ingredient of raw silk, extracted as a white amorphous mass.

fibrolite.c: Fibrolite Fi"bro*lite (? or?), n. [L. fibra a fiber + -lite: cf. F. fibrolithe.] (Min.) A silicate of alumina, of fibrous or columnar structure. It is like andalusite in composition; -- called also sillimanite, and bucholzite.

fibroma.c: Fibroma ‖Fi*bro"ma (fi*brō"mȧ), n. [NL. See Fiber, and -oma.] (Med.) A tumor consisting mainly of fibrous tissue, or of same modification of such tissue.

fibrospongiae.c: Fibrospongiae ‖Fi`bro*spon"gi*æ (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., fr. L. fibra a fiber + spongia a sponge.] (Zool.) An order of sponges having a fibrous skeleton, including the commercial sponges.

fibrous.c: Fibrous Fi"brous (fī"brŭs), a. [Cf. F. fibreux.] Containing, or consisting of, fibers; as, the fibrous coat of the cocoanut; the fibrous roots of grasses. -- Fi"brous*ness, n.

fibrovascular.c: Fibrovascular Fi`bro*vas"cu*lar (?), a. [L. fibra a fiber + E. vascular.] (Bot.) Containing woody fiber and ducts, as the stems of all flowering plants and ferns; -- opposed to cellular.

fibster.c: Fibster Fib"ster (?), n. One who tells fibs. [Jocular]

fibula.c: Fibula ‖fib"u*la (fĭb"u*lȧ), n.; pl. fibulæ (#). [L., clasp, buckle.] 1. A brooch, clasp, or buckle.

fibular.c: Fibular Fib"u*lar (fĭb"u*lẽr), a. Pertaining to the fibula.

fibulare.c: Fibulare ‖Fib`u*la"re (fĭb`u*lā"re), n.; pl. Fibularia (#). [NL. See Fibula.] (Anat.) The bone or cartilage of the tarsus, which articulates with the fibula, and corresponds to the calcaneum in man and most mammals.

fice.c: Fice Fice (fīs), n. A small dog; -- written also fise, fyce, fiste, etc. [Southern U.S.]

fichtelite.c: Fichtelite Fich"tel*ite (?), n. (Min.) A white crystallized mineral resin from the Fichtelgebirge, Bavaria.

fichu.c: Fichu Fich"u (?), n. [F., neckerchief.] A light cape, usually of lace, worn by women, to cover the neck and throat, and extending to the shoulders.

fickle.c: Fickle Fic"kle (?), a. [OE. fikel untrustworthy, deceitful, AS. ficol, fr. fic, gefic, fraud, deceit; cf. fācen deceit, OS. f?kn, OHG. feichan, Icel. feikn portent. Cf. Fidget.] Not fixed or firm; liable to change; unstable; of a changeable mind; not firm in opinion or purpose; inconstant; capricious; as, Fortune's fickle wheel. Shak.

fickleness.c: Fickleness Fic"kle*ness (?), n. The quality of being fickle; instability; inconsonancy. Shak.

fickly.c: Fickly Fic"kly (?), adv. In a fickle manner. [Obs.] Pepys.

fico.c: Fico ‖Fi"co (?), n.; pl. Ficoes (#). [It., a fig, fr. L.ficus. See Fig.] A fig; an insignificant trifle, no more than the snap of one's thumb; a sign of contempt made by the fingers, expressing. A fig for you.

fictile.c: Fictile Fic"tile (?), a. [L. fictilis. See Fiction.] Molded, or capable of being molded, into form by art; relating to pottery or to molding in any soft material.

fiction.c: Fiction Fic"tion (?), n. [F. fiction, L. fictio, fr. fingere, fictum to form, shape, invent, feign. See Feign.] 1. The act of feigning, inventing, or imagining; as, by a mere fiction of the mind. Bp. Stillingfleet.

fictional.c: Fictional Fic"tion*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or characterized by, fiction; fictitious; romantic.“Fictional rather than historical.” Latham.

fictionist.c: Fictionist Fic"tion*ist, n. A writer of fiction. [R.] Lamb.

fictitious.c: Fictitious Fic*ti"tious (?), a. [L. fictitius. See Fiction.] Feigned; imaginary; not real; fabulous; counterfeit; false; not genuine; as, fictitious fame.

fictive.c: Fictive Fic"tive (?), a. [Cf. F. fictif.] Feigned; counterfeit. “The fount of fictive tears.” Tennyson.

fictor.c: Fictor Fic"tor (?), n. [L.] An artist who models or forms statues and reliefs in any plastic material. [R.] Elmes.

ficus.c: Ficus ‖Fi"cus (?), n. [L., a fig.] A genus of trees or shrubs, one species of which (F. Carica) produces the figs of commerce; the fig tree.

fid.c: Fid Fid (?), n. [Prov. E. fid a small, thick lump.] 1. (Naut.) A square bar of wood or iron, used to support the topmast, being passed through a hole or mortise at its heel, and resting on the trestle trees.

fidalgo.c: Fidalgo Fi*dal"go (?), n. [Pg. See Hidalgo.] The lowest title of nobility in Portugal, corresponding to that of Hidalgo in Spain.

fiddle.c: Fiddle Fid"dle (fĭd"d'l), n. [OE. fidele, fithele, AS. fiðele; akin to D. vedel, OHG. fidula, G. fiedel, Icel. fiðla, and perh. to E. viol. Cf. Viol.] 1. (Mus.) A stringed instrument of music played with a bow; a violin; a kit.
Fiddle Fid"dle, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fiddled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fiddling (?).] 1. To play on a fiddle.
Fiddle Fid"dle (?), v. t. To play (a tune) on a fiddle.

fiddledeedee.c: fiddledeedee fid"dle*dee*dee` (?), interj. An exclamatory word or phrase, equivalent to nonsense! [Colloq.]

fiddlefaddle.c: fiddle-faddle fid"dle-fad`dle (?), n. A trifle; trifling talk; nonsense. [Colloq.] Spectator.
fiddle-faddle fid"dle-fad`dle, v. i. To talk nonsense. [Colloq.] Ford.

fiddler.c: Fiddler Fid"dler (?), n. [AS. fiðelere.] 1. One who plays on a fiddle or violin.

fiddleshaped.c: Fiddle-shaped Fid"dle-shaped` (?), a. (Bot.) Inversely ovate, with a deep hollow on each side. Gray.

fiddlestick.c: Fiddlestick Fid"dle*stick` (?), n. The bow, strung with horsehair, used in playing the fiddle; a fiddle bow.

fiddlestring.c: Fiddlestring Fid"dle*string` (?), n. One of the catgut strings of a fiddle.

fiddlewood.c: Fiddlewood Fid"dle*wood` (?), n. [Corrupted fr. F. bois-fidèle, lit., faithful wood; -- so called from its durability.] The wood of several West Indian trees, mostly of the genus Citharexylum.

fidejussion.c: Fidejussion Fi`de*jus"sion (?), n. [L. fidejussio, from fidejubere to be surety or bail; fides faith + jubere to order: cf. F. fidéjussion.] (Civil Law) The act or state of being bound as surety for another; suretyship.

fidejussor.c: Fidejussor Fi`de*jus"sor (?), n. [L.: cf. F. fidéjusseur.] (Civil Law) A surety; one bound for another, conjointly with him; a guarantor. Blackstone.

fidelity.c: Fidelity Fi*del"i*ty (?), n. [L. fidelitas: cf. F. fidélité. See Fealty.] Faithfulness; adherence to right; careful and exact observance of duty, or discharge of obligations. Especially: (a) Adherence to a person or party to which one is bound; loyalty.

fides.c: Fides ‖Fi"des (?), n. [L., faith.] (Roman Muth.) Faith personified as a goddess; the goddess of faith.

fidge.c: Fidge Fidge (fĭj), n. & v. i. See Fidget. [R.] Swift.

fidget.c: Fidget Fidg"et (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fidgeted; p. pr. & vb. n. Fodgeting.] [From Fidge; cf. OE. fiken to fidget, to flatter, Icel. fika to hasten, Sw. fika to hunt after, AS. befician to deceive. Cf. Fickle.] To move uneasily one way and the other; to move irregularly, or by fits and starts. Moore.

fidgetiness.c: Fidgetiness Fidg"et*i*ness (?), n. Quality of being fidgety.

fidia.c: Fidia ‖Fid"i*a (?), n. [NL., prob. fr. L. fidus trusty.] (Zool.) A genus of small beetles, of which one species (the grapevine Fidia, F. longipes) is very injurious to vines in America.

fidicinal.c: Fidicinal Fi*dic"i*nal (?), a. [L. fidicinus, fr. fidicen, -inis, a lute player.] (Mus.) Of or pertaining to a stringed instrument.

fiducial.c: Fiducial Fi*du"cial (?), a. [L. fiducia trust, confidence; akin to fides faith. See Faith.] 1. Having faith or trust; confident; undoubting; firm. “Fiducial reliance on the promises of God.” Hammond.

fiduciary.c: Fiduciary Fi*du"ci*a*ry (? or?), a. [L. fiduciarus, fr. fiducia: cf. F. fiduciaire. See Fiducial.] 1. Involving confidence or trust; confident; undoubting; faithful; firm; as, in a fiduciary capacity. “Fiduciary obedience.” Howell.
Fiduciary Fi*du"ci*a*ry, n. 1. One who holds a thing in trust for another; a trustee.

fie.c: Fie Fie (?), interj. [OE. fi; cf. D. fif. G. pfui, Icel. f?, Sw. & Dan. fy, F. fi, L. fi, phy.] An exclamation denoting contempt or dislike. See Fy. Fuller.

fief.c: Fief Fief (?), n. [F. fief; of German origin, and the same word as E. fee. See Fee, and cf. Feud, a tief.] (Law) An estate held of a superior on condition of military service; a fee; a feud. See under Benefice, n., 2.

field.c: field field (fēld), n. [OE. feld, fild, AS. feld; akin to D. veld, G. feld, Sw. fält, Dan. felt, Icel. fold field of grass, AS. folde earth, land, ground, OS. folda.] 1. Cleared land; land suitable for tillage or pasture; cultivated ground; the open country.
Field Field (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fielded; p. pr. & vb. n. Fielding.] 1. To take the field. [Obs.] Spenser.
Field Field, v. t. (Ball Playing) To catch, stop, throw, etc. (the ball), as a fielder.

fielded.c: Fielded Field"ed, a. Engaged in the field; encamped. [Obs.]

fielder.c: Fielder Field"er (?), n. (Ball Playing) A ball payer who stands out in the field to catch or stop balls.

fieldfare.c: Fieldfare Field"fare` (?; 277), n. [OE. feldfare, AS. feldfare; field + faran to travel.] (Zool.) a small thrush (Turdus pilaris) which breeds in northern Europe and winters in Great Britain. The head, nape, and lower part of the back are ash-colored; the upper part of the back and wing coverts, chestnut; -- called also fellfare.

fielding.c: Fielding Field"ing, n. (Ball Playing) The act of playing as a fielder.

fieldpiece.c: Fieldpiece Field"piece` (?), n. A cannon mounted on wheels, for the use of a marching army; a piece of field artillery; -- called also field gun.

fieldwork.c: Fieldwork Field"work` (?), n. (Mil.) Any temporary fortification thrown up by an army in the field; -- commonly in the plural.

fieldy.c: Fieldy Field"y (?), a. Open, like a field. [Obs.] Wyclif.

fiend.c: fiend fiend (fēnd), n. [OE. fend, find, fiend, feond, fiend, foe, AS. feónd; akin to OS. fīond, D. vijand enemy, OHG. fīant, G. feind, Icel. fjānd, Sw. & Dan. fiende, Goth. fijands; orig. p. pr. of a verb meaning to hate, AS. feón, feógan, OHG. fī?n, Goth. fijan, Skr. pīy to scorn; prob. akin to E. feud a quarrel. √81. Cf. Foe, Friend.] An implacable or malicious foe; one who is diabolically wicked or cruel; an infernal being; -- applied specifically to the devil or a demon.

fiendful.c: Fiendful Fiend"ful (?), a. Full of fiendish spirit or arts. Marlowe.

fiendish.c: Fiendish Fiend"ish (?), a. Like a fiend; diabolically wicked or cruel; infernal; malignant; devilish; hellish. -- Fiend"ish*ly, adv. -- Fiend"ish*ness, n.

fiendly.c: Fiendly Fiend"ly, a. [AS. feóndlic.] Fiendlike; monstrous; devilish. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fierasfer.c: Fierasfer ‖Fi`e*ras"fer (?), n. [NL.] (Zool.) A genus of small, slender fishes, remarkable for their habit of living as commensals in other animals. One species inhabits the gill cavity of the pearl oyster near Panama; another lives within an East Indian holothurian.

fierce.c: Fierce Fierce (?), a. [Compar. Fiercer (?); superl. Fiercest (?).] [OE. fers, fiers, OF. fier, nom. fiers, fierce, savage, cruel, F. fier proud, from L. ferus wild, savage, cruel; perh. akin to E. bear the animal. Cf. Feral, Ferocity.] 1. Furious; violent; unrestrained; impetuous; as, a fierce wind.

fieri.c: Fieri facias ‖Fi"e*ri fa"ci*as (?). [L., cause it to be done.] (Law) A judicial writ that lies for one who has recovered in debt or damages, commanding the sheriff that he cause to be made of the goods, chattels, or real estate of the defendant, the sum claimed. Blackstone. Cowell.

fieriness.c: Fieriness Fi"er*i*ness (?), n. The quality of being fiery; heat; acrimony; irritability; as, a fieriness of temper. Addison.

fiery.c: Fiery Fi"er*y (? or?), a. [Formerly written firy, fr. fire.] 1. Consisting of, containing, or resembling, fire; as, the fiery gulf of Etna; a fiery appearance.

fiesta.c: Fiesta ‖Fies"ta (?), n. [Sp. See Feast, n.] 1. Among Spanish, a religious festival; a saint's day or holiday; also, a holiday or festivity.

fife.c: Fife Fife (fīf), n. [F. fifre, OHG. pfīfa, LL. pipa pipe, pipare to play on the pipe, fr. L. pipire, pipare, to peep, pip, chirp, as a chiken. See Pipe.] (Mus.) A small shrill pipe, resembling the piccolo flute, used chiefly to accompany the drum in military music.
Fife Fife, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fifed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. fifing.] To play on a fife.

fifer.c: Fifer Fif"er (fīf"ẽr), n. One who plays on a fife.

fifteen.c: Fifteen Fif"teen` (?), a. [OE. fiftene, AS. fīftȳne, fīftēne. See Five, and Ten, and cf. Fifty.] Five and ten; one more than fourteen.
Fifteen Fif"teen`, n. 1. The sum of five and ten; fifteen units or objects.

fifteenth.c: Fifteenth Fif"teenth` (?), a. [OE. fiftenthe; cf. fiftethe, AS. fīfteōða. See Fifteen.] 1. Next in order after the fourteenth; -- the ordinal of fifteen.
Fifteenth Fif"teenth`, n. 1. One of fifteen equal parts or divisions; the quotient of a unit divided by fifteen.

fifth.c: Fifth Fifth (?), a. [OE. fifte, fifthe, AS. fīfta. See Five.] 1. Next in order after the fourth; -- the ordinal of five.
Fifth Fifth (?), n. 1. The quotient of a unit divided by five; one of five equal parts; a fifth part.

fifthly.c: Fifthly Fifth"ly, adv. In the fifth place; as the fifth in order.

fiftieth.c: Fiftieth Fif"ti*eth (?), a. [AS. fīftigoða. See Fifty.] 1. Next in order after the forty-ninth; -- the ordinal of fifty.
Fiftieth Fif"ti*eth, n. One of fifty equal parts; the quotient of a unit divided by fifty.

fifty.c: Fifty Fif"ty (?), a. [AS. fīftig; akin to OHG. finfzug, fimfzuc, G. fünfzig, funfzig, Goth. fimftigjus. See Five, and Ten, and cf. Fifteen.] Five times ten; as, fifty men.
Fifty Fif"ty, n.; pl. Fifties (?). 1. The sum of five tens; fifty units or objects.

fig.c: Fig Fig (fĭg), n. [F. figue the fruit of the tree, Pr. figa, fr. L. ficus fig tree, fig. Cf. Fico.] 1. (Bot.) A small fruit tree (Ficus Carica) with large leaves, known from the remotest antiquity. It was probably native from Syria westward to the Canary Islands.
Fig Fig, v. t. [See Fico, Fig, n.] 1. To insult with a fico, or contemptuous motion. See Fico. [Obs.]

figaro.c: Figaro ‖Fi`ga`ro" (?), n. [From the name of the barber in Beaumarchais' “Barber of Seville.”] An adroit and unscrupulous intriguer.

figary.c: Figary Fig"a*ry (?), n. [Corrupted fr. vagary.] A frolic; a vagary; a whim. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

figeater.c: Figeater Fig"eat`er (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A large beetle (Allorhina nitida) which in the Southern United States destroys figs. The elytra are velvety green with pale borders. (b) A bird. See Figpecker.

figgum.c: Figgum Fig"gum (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] A juggler's trick; conjuring. [Obs.]

fight.c: Fight Fight (fīt), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fought (fät); p. pr. & vb. n. Fighting.] [OE. fihten, fehten, AS. feohtan; akin to D. vechten, OHG. fehtan, G. fechten, Sw. fäkta, Dan. fegte, and perh. to E. fist; cf. L. pugnare to fight, pugnus fist.] 1. To strive or contened for victory, with armies or in single combat; to attempt to defeat, subdue, or destroy an enemy, either by blows or weapons; to contend in arms; -- followed by with or against.
Fight Fight, v. t. 1. To carry on, or wage, as a conflict, or battle; to win or gain by struggle, as one's way; to sustain by fighting, as a cause.

Fight Fight, n. [OE. fight, feht, AS. feoht. See Fight, v. i.] 1. A battle; an engagement; a contest in arms; a combat; a violent conflict or struggle for victory, between individuals or between armies, ships, or navies, etc.

fighter.c: Fighter Fight"er (fīt"ẽr), n. [AS. feohtere.] 1. One who fights; a combatant; a warrior. Shak.

fighting.c: Fighting Fight"ing, a. 1. Qualified for war; fit for battle.

fightwite.c: Fightwite Fight"wite` (?), n. [Fight + wite.] (O.Eng. Law) A mulct or fine imposed on a person for making a fight or quarrel to the disturbance of the peace.

figment.c: Figment Fig"ment (?), n. [L. figmentum, fr. fingere to form, shape, invent, feign. See Feign.] An invention; a fiction; something feigned or imagined.

figpecker.c: Figpecker Fig"peck`er (fĭg"pĕk`ẽr), n. (Zool.) The European garden warbler (Sylvia hortensis or Currica, hortensis); -- called also beccafico and greater pettychaps.

figshell.c: Fig-shell Fig"-shell` (?), n. (Zool.) A marine univalve shell of the genus Pyrula, or Ficula, resembling a fig in form.

figulated.c: Figulated Figulate { Fig"u*late (?), Fig"u*la`ted (?) }, a. [L. figulatus, p. p. of figulare to shape, fr. figulus potter, fr. fingere to shape.] Made of potter's clay; molded; shaped. [R.] Johnson.

figuline.c: Figuline Fig"u*line (? or?), n. [F., fr. L. figulina pottery, fr. figulus. See Figulate.] A piece of pottery ornamented with representations of natural objects.
Figuline Fig"u*line (?), a. [L. figulinus. See Figulate.] 1. Suitable for the making of pottery; fictile; -- said of clay.

figurability.c: Figurability Fig`ur*a*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. figurabilité.] The quality of being figurable. Johnson.

figurable.c: Figurable Fig`ur*a*ble (?), a. [L. figurare to form, shape, fr. figura figure: cf. F. figurable. See Figure.] Capable of being brought to a fixed form or shape.

figural.c: Figural Fig"ur*al (?), a. [From Figure.] 1. Represented by figure or delineation; consisting of figures; as, figural ornaments. Sir T. Browne.

figurant.c: Figurant Fig"u*rant` (? or?), n. masc. [F., prop. p. pr. of figurer figure, represent, make a figure.] One who dances at the opera, not singly, but in groups or figures; an accessory character on the stage, who figures in its scenes, but has nothing to say; hence, one who figures in any scene, without taking a prominent part.

figurante.c: Figurante Fig"u*rante` (? or?), n. fem. [F.] A female figurant; esp., a ballet girl.

figurate.c: Figurate Fig"ur*ate (?), a. [L. figuratus, p. p. of figurare. See Figure.] 1. Of a definite form or figure.

figurated.c: Figurated Fig"ur*a`ted (?), a. Having a determinate form.

figurately.c: Figurately Fig"ur*ate*ly (?), adv. In a figurate manner.

figuration.c: Figuration Fig`u*ra"tion (?), n. [L. figuratio.] 1. The act of giving figure or determinate form; determination to a certain form. Bacon.

figurative.c: Figurative Fig"ur*a*tive (?), a. [L. figurativus: cf. F. figuratif. See Figurative.] 1. Representing by a figure, or by resemblance; typical; representative.

figure.c: Figure Fig"ure (fĭg"ur; 135), n. [F., figure, L. figura; akin to fingere to form, shape, feign. See Feign.] 1. The form of anything; shape; outline; appearance.

Figure Fig"ure, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Figured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Figuring.] [F. figurer, L. figurare, fr. figura. See Figure, n.] 1. To represent by a figure, as to form or mold; to make an image of, either palpable or ideal; also, to fashion into a determinate form; to shape.
Figure Fig"ure, v. i. 1. To make a figure; to be distinguished or conspicious; as, the envoy figured at court.

figured.c: Figured Fig"ured (?), a. 1. Adorned with figures; marked with figures; as, figured muslin.

figurehead.c: Figurehead Fig"ure*head` (?), n. 1. (Naut.) The figure, statue, or bust, on the prow of a ship.

figurial.c: Figurial Fi*gu"ri*al (?), a. Represented by figure or delineation. [R.] Craig.

figurine.c: Figurine ‖Fi`gu`rine" (? or?), n. [F., dim. of figure.] A very small figure, whether human or of an animal; especially, one in terra cotta or the like; -- distinguished from statuette, which is applied to small figures in bronze, marble, etc.

figurist.c: Figurist Fig"ur*ist (?), n. One who uses or interprets figurative expressions. Waterland.

figwort.c: Figwort Fig"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) A genus of herbaceous plants (Scrophularia), mostly found in the north temperate zones. See Brownwort.

fijian.c: Fijian Fi"ji*an (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Fiji islands or their inhabitants. -- n. A native of the Fiji islands. [Written also Feejeean, Feejee.]

fil.c: Fil Fil (?), obs. imp. of Fall, v. i. Fell. Chaucer.

filaceous.c: Filaceous Fi*la"ceous (? or?), a. [L. filum thread.] Composed of threads. Bacon.

filacer.c: Filacer Fil"a*cer (?), n. [OE. filace a file, or thread, on which the records of the courts of justice were strung, F. filasse tow of flax or hemp, fr. L. filum thread.] (Eng. Law) A former officer in the English Court of Common Pleas; -- so called because he filed the writs on which he made out process. [Obs.] Burrill.

filament.c: Filament Fil"a*ment (?), n. [F. filament, fr. L. filum thread. See File a row.] A thread or threadlike object or appendage; a fiber; esp. (Bot.), the threadlike part of the stamen supporting the anther.

filamentary.c: Filamentary Fil`a*men"ta*ry (?), a. Having the character of, or formed by, a filament.

filamentous.c: Filamentous Fil`a*men"tous (?), a. [Cf. F. filamenteux.] Like a thread; consisting of threads or filaments. Gray.

filander.c: Filander Fil"an*der (?), n. (Zool.) A species of kangaroo (Macropus Brunii), inhabiting New Guinea.

filanders.c: Filanders Fil"an*ders (?), n. pl. [F. filandres, fr. L. filum thread.] (Falconry) A disease in hawks, characterized by the presence of small threadlike worms, also of filaments of coagulated blood, from the rupture of a vein; -- called also backworm. Sir T. Browne.

filar.c: Filar Fi"lar (?), a. [L. filum a thread.] Of or pertaining to a thread or line; characterized by threads stretched across the field of view; as, a filar microscope; a filar micrometer.

filaria.c: Filaria Fi*la"ri*a (?), n.; pl. filariae. [NL., fr. L. filum a thread.] (Zool.) a small, slender nematode worm of the family Onchocercidae (Filariidae) of many species, parasitic when adult in various animals, including man. They may live within the blood, or in other bodily fluids, or within tissues or cavities of the body. Infection with such organisms may be transmitted by blood-sucking arthropods.

Filaria ‖Fi*la"ri*a (?), n. [NL., fr. L. filum a thread.] (Zool.) a former genus comprised of certain nematodes, now classed as belonging to several genera within the family Onchocercidae. See Onchocerca and Guinea worm.

filarial.c: Filarial Fi*la"ri*al (?), a. 1. (Zool. & Med.) Of, pertaining to, or caused by, filariæ and allied parasitic worms.

filariasis.c: Filariasis Fil`a*ri"a*sis (?), n. [NL.] 1. (Zool., Med.) the presence of filariae within the body of an organism; infection with filariae. It is mostly found in tropical and subtropical regions.

filasse.c: Filasse Fi*lasse" (?), n. [F., fr. fil thread, L. filum.] Vegetable fiber, as jute or ramie, prepared for manufacture.

filatory.c: Filatory Fil"a*to*ry (?), n. [LL. filatorium place for spinning, fr. filare to spin, fr. L. filum a thread.] A machine for forming threads. [Obs.] W. Tooke.

filature.c: Filature Fil"a*ture (?; 135), n. [LL. filatura, fr. filare to spin: cf. F. filature. See Filatory.] 1. A drawing out into threads; hence, the reeling of silk from cocoons. Ure.

filbert.c: filbert fil"bert (?), n. [Perh. fr. fill + bread, as filling the bread or husk; cf. G. bartnuss (lit., bread nut) filbert; or perh. named from a St.Philibert, whose day, Aug. 22, fell in the nutting season.] 1. (Bot.) The fruit of the Corylus Avellana or Corylus maxima, also called the hazel; the hazelnut. It is an oval nut, containing a kernel that has a mild, farinaceous, oily taste, agreeable to the palate.

filch.c: Filch Filch (fĭlch), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filched (fĭlcht); p. pr. & vb. n. Filching.] [Cf. AS. feolan to stick to, OHG. felhan, felahan, to hide, Icel. fela, Goth. filhan to hide, bury, Prov. E. feal to hide slyly, OE. felen.] To steal or take privily (commonly, that which is of little value); to pilfer.

filcher.c: Filcher Filch"er (fĭlch"ẽr), n. One who filches; a thief.

filchingly.c: Filchingly Filch"ing*ly, adv. By pilfering or petty stealing.

file.c: File File (fīl), n. [F. file row (cf. Pr., Sp., Pg., & It. fila), LL. fila, fr. L. filum a thread. Cf. Enfilade, Filament, Fillet.] 1. An orderly succession; a line; a row; as: (a) (Mil.) A row of soldiers ranged one behind another; -- in contradistinction to rank, which designates a row of soldiers standing abreast; a number consisting the depth of a body of troops, which, in the ordinary modern formation, consists of two men, the battalion standing two deep, or in two ranks.

File File (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Filing.] 1. To set in order; to arrange, or lay away, esp. as papers in a methodical manner for preservation and reverence; to place on file; to insert in its proper place in an arranged body of papers.
File File, v. i. [Cf. F. filer.] (Mil.) To march in a file or line, as soldiers, not abreast, but one after another; -- generally with off.

File File (fīl), n. [AS. feól; akin to D. viji, OHG. fīla, fīhala, G. feile, Sw. fil, Dan. fiil, cf. Icel. þēl, Russ. pila, and Skr. piç to cut out, adorn; perh. akin to E. paint.] 1. A steel instrument, having cutting ridges or teeth, made by indentation with a chisel, used for abrading or smoothing other substances, as metals, wood, etc.
File File, v. t. 1. To rub, smooth, or cut away, with a file; to sharpen with a file; as, to file a saw or a tooth.
File File, v. t. [OE. fulen, filen, foulen, AS. f?lan, fr. f?l foul. See Foul, and cf. Defile, v. t.] To make foul; to defile. [Obs.]

File closer File" clos`er. (Mil.) A commissioned or noncommissioned officer posted in the rear of a line, or on the flank of a column, of soldiers, to rectify mistakes and insure steadiness and promptness in the ranks.

filefish.c: Filefish File"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) Any plectognath fish of the genera Monacanthus, Alutera, balistes, and allied genera; -- so called on account of the roughly granulated skin, which is sometimes used in place of sandpaper.

filer.c: Filer Fil"er (?), n. One who works with a file.

filial.c: Filial Fil"ial (?), a. [L. filialis, fr. filius son, filia daughter; akin to e. female, feminine. Cf. Fitz.] 1. Of or pertaining to a son or daughter; becoming to a child in relation to his parents; as, filial obedience.

filially.c: Filially Fil"ial*ly (?), adv. In a filial manner.

filiate.c: Filiate Fil"i*ate (?), v. t. To adopt as son or daughter; to establish filiation between. [R.] Southey.

filiation.c: Filiation Fil`i*a"tion (?), n. [LL. filiatio, fr. L. filius son: cf. F. filiation. See Filial.] 1. The relationship of a son or child to a parent, esp. to a father.

filibeg.c: Filibeg Fil"i*beg (?), n. [Gael. feileadhbeag, i. e., little kilt; feileadh kilt + beag little, small; cf. filleadh a plait, fold.] Same as Kilt. [Written also philibeg.]

filibuster.c: Filibuster Fil"i*bus`ter (?), n. [Sp. flibuster, flibustero, corrupted fr. E. freebooter. See Freebooter.] A lawless military adventurer, especially one in quest of plunder; a freebooter; -- originally applied to buccaneers infesting the Spanish American coasts, but introduced into common English to designate the followers of Lopez in his expedition to Cuba in 1851, and those of Walker in his expedition to Nicaragua, in 1855.
Filibuster Fil"i*bus*ter, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fillibustered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Filibustering.] 1. To act as a filibuster, or military freebooter. Bartlett.

filibusterism.c: Filibusterism Fil"i*bus`ter*ism (?), n. The characteristics or practices of a filibuster. Bartlett.

filical.c: Filical Fil"i*cal (?), a. Belonging to the Filices, r ferns.

filicic.c: Filicic Fi*lic"ic (?), a. [L. filix, -icis, a fern.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, ferns; as, filicic acid.

filicide.c: Filicide Fil"i*cide (?), n. [L. filius son, filia daughter + caedere to kill.] The act of murdering a son or a daughter; also, parent who commits such a murder.

filiciform.c: Filiciform Fi*lic"i*form (?), a. [L. filix, -icis, fern + -form: cf. F. filiciforme] Shaped like a fern or like the parts of a fern leaf. Smart.

filicoid.c: Filicoid Fil"i*coid (?), a. [L. filix, -icis, fern + -oid: cf. F. filicoiïde.] (Bot.) Fernlike, either in form or in the nature of the method of reproduction.
Filicoid Fil"i*coid, n. (Bot.) A fernlike plant. Lindley.

filiety.c: Filiety Fi*li"e*ty (?), n. [L. filietas.] The relation of a son to a father; sonship; -- the correlative of paternity. J. S. Mill.

filiferous.c: Filiferous Fi*lif"er*ous (?), a. [L. filum a thread + -ferous.] Producing threads. Carpenter.

filiform.c: filiform fil"i*form (?), a. [L. filum thread + -form: cf. F. filiforme.] Having the shape of a thread or filament; as, the filiform papillæ of the tongue; a filiform style or peduncle. See Illust. of Antennæ.

filigrane.c: Filigrane Filigrain { Fil"i*grain, Fil"i*grane } (?), n. [Sp. filigrana (cf. It. filigrana, E. filigrane), fr. L. filuma thread + granum grain. See File a row, and Grain, and cf. Filigree.] Filigree. [Archaic]

filigree.c: Filigree Fil"i*gree (?), n. [Corrupted fr. filigrane.] Ornamental work, formerly with grains or breads, but now composed of fine wire and used chiefly in decorating gold and silver to which the wire is soldered, being arranged in designs frequently of a delicate and intricate arabesque pattern.
Filigree Fil"i*gree, a. Relating to, composed of, or resembling, work in filigree; as, a filigree basket. Hence: Fanciful; unsubstantial; merely decorative.

filigreed.c: Filigreed Fil"i*greed (?), a. Adorned with filigree. Tatler.

filing.c: Filing Fil"ing (?), n. A fragment or particle rubbed off by the act of filing; as, iron filings.

filioque.c: Filioque ‖Fil`i*o"que (?), n. (Eccl. Hist.) The Latin for, “and from the Son,” equivalent to et filio, inserted by the third council of Toledo (a. d. 589) in the clause qui ex Patre procedit (who proceedeth from the Father) of the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (a. d. 381), which makes a creed state that the Holy Ghost proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father. Hence, the doctrine itself (not admitted by the Eastern Church).

filipendulous.c: Filipendulous Fil`i*pen"du*lous (?; 135), a. [L. filum a thread + pendulus hanging, fr. pendēre to hang.] (Bot.) Suspended by, or strung upon, a thread; -- said of tuberous swellings in the middle or at the extremities of slender, threadlike rootlets.

filipino.c: Filipino Fil`i*pi"no (?), n.; pl. Filipinos (#). [Sp.] A native or inhabitant of the Philippine Islands, specif. one of Spanish descent or of mixed blood. [wns=1]

fill.c: Fill Fill (?), n. [See Thill.] One of the thills or shafts of a carriage. Mortimer.

Fill Fill, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Filling.] [OE. fillen, fullen, AS. fyllan, fr. full full; akin to D. vullen, G. füllen, Icel. fylla, Sw. fylla, Dan. fylde, Goth. fulljan. See Full, a.] 1. To make full; to supply with as much as can be held or contained; to put or pour into, till no more can be received; to occupy the whole capacity of.
Fill Fill (?), v. i. 1. To become full; to have the whole capacity occupied; to have an abundant supply; to be satiated; as, corn fills well in a warm season; the sail fills with the wind.
Fill Fill, n. [AS. fyllo. See Fill, v. t.] 1. A full supply, as much as supplies want; as much as gives complete satisfaction. “Ye shall eat your fill.” Lev. xxv. 19.

filled.c: Filled cheese Filled cheese. An inferior kind of cheese made from skim milk with a fatty “filling,” such as oleomargarine or lard, to replace the fat removed in the cream.

filler.c: Filler Fill"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, fills; something used for filling.
Filler Fill"er, n. [From 1st Fill.] A thill horse. [Prov. Eng.]

fillet.c: Fillet Fil"let (?), n. [OE. filet, felet, fr. OF. filet thread, fillet of meat, dim. of fil a thread, fr. L. filum. See Fille a row.] 1. A little band, especially one intended to encircle the hair of the head.
Fillet Fil"let, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filleted; p. pr. & vb. n. Filleting.] To bind, furnish, or adorn with a fillet.

filleting.c: Filleting Fil"let*ing, n. 1. (Arch.) The protecting of a joint, as between roof and parapet wall, with mortar, or cement, where flashing is employed in better work.

fillibeg.c: Fillibeg Fil"li*beg (?), n. A kilt. See Filibeg.

filling.c: Filling Fill"ing (?), n. 1. That which is used to fill a cavity or any empty space, or to supply a deficiency; as, filling for a cavity in a tooth, a depression in a roadbed, the space between exterior and interior walls of masonry, the pores of open-grained wood, the space between the outer and inner planks of a vessel, etc.

fillip.c: Fillip Fil"lip (fĭl"lĭp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filliped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Filliping.] [For filp, flip. Cf. Flippant.] 1. To strike with the nail of the finger, first placed against the ball of the thumb, and forced from that position with a sudden spring; to snap with the finger. “You fillip me o' the head.” Shak.
Fillip Fil"lip, n. 1. A jerk of the finger forced suddenly from the thumb; a smart blow.

fillister.c: Fillister Fil"lis*ter (?), n. 1. The rabbet on the outer edge of a sash bar to hold the glass and the putty. Knight.

filly.c: Filly Fil"ly (?), n.; pl. Fillies (#). [Cf. Icel. fylia, fr. foli foal. See Foal.] 1. (Zool.) A female foal or colt; a young mare. Cf. Colt, Foal.

film.c: Film Film (?), n. [AS. film skin, fr. fell skin; akin to fylmen membrane, OFries. filmene skin. See Fell skin.] 1. A thin skin; a pellicle; a membranous covering, causing opacity.
Film Film, v. t. 1. To cover with a thin skin or pellicle.

filminess.c: Filminess Film"i*ness (?), n. State of being filmy.

filmy.c: Filmy Film"y (?), a. Composed of film or films.

filoplumaceous.c: Filoplumaceous Fil`o*plu*ma"ceous (?), a. (Zool.) Having the structure of a filoplume.

filoplume.c: Filoplume Fil"o*plume (?), n. [L. filum a thread? pluma a soft feather.] (Zool.) A hairlike feather; a father with a slender scape and without a web in most or all of its length.

filose.c: Filose Fi"lose` (?), a. [L. filum a thread.] Terminating in a threadlike process.

filoselle.c: Filoselle Fil`o*selle" (?), n. [F., floss silk.] A kind of silk thread less glossy than floss, and spun from coarser material. It is much used in embroidery instead of floss.

fils.c: Fils ‖Fils (?), n. [F., fr. L. filius. See Filial.] Son; -- sometimes used after a French proper name to distinguish a son from his father, as, Alexandre Dumas, fils.

filter.c: Filter Fil"ter (?), n. [F. filtre, the same word as feutre felt, LL. filtrum, feltrum, felt, fulled wool, this being used for straining liquors. See Feuter.] Any porous substance, as cloth, paper, sand, or charcoal, through which water or other liquid may passed to cleanse it from the solid or impure matter held in suspension; a chamber or device containing such substance; a strainer; also, a similar device for purifying air.

Filter Fil"ter, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filtered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Filtering] [Cf. F. filter. See Filter, n., and cf. Filtrate.] To purify or defecate, as water or other liquid, by causing it to pass through a filter.
Filter Fil"ter, v. i. To pass through a filter; to percolate.

filth.c: Filth Filth (fĭlth), n. [OE. filthe, fulðe, AS. fȳlð, fr. fūl foul; akin to OHG. fūlida. See Foul, and cf. File.] 1. Foul matter; anything that soils or defiles; dirt; nastiness.

filthily.c: Filthily Filth"i*ly (?), adv. In a filthy manner; foully.

filthiness.c: Filthiness Filth"i*ness, n. 1. The state of being filthy.

filthy.c: Filthy Filth"y (?), a. [Compar. Filthier (?); superl. Filthiest.] Defiled with filth, whether material or moral; nasty; dirty; polluted; foul; impure; obscene. “In the filthy-mantled pool.” Shak.

filtrate.c: Filtrate Fil"trate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Filtrated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Filtrating. (?)] [Cf. LL. filtrare. See Filter.] To filter; to defecate; as liquid, by straining or percolation. Arbuthnot.
Filtrate Fil"trate (?), n. That which has been filtered; the liquid which has passed through the filter in the process of filtration. Contrasted with retentate, the material remaining on the filter.

filtration.c: Filtration Fil*tra"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. filtration.] The act or process of filtering; the mechanical separation of a liquid from the undissolved particles floating in it.

fimble.c: Fimble hemp Fimble { Fim"ble, n., or Fim"ble hemp` (fĭm"b'l hĕmp`). }[Corrupted from female hemp.] Light summer hemp, that bears no seed.

fimbria.c: Fimbria ‖Fim"bri*a (?), n.; pl. Fimbriæ (#). [L., fringe. See Fringle.] (Anat.) (a) pl. A fringe, or fringed border. (b) A band of white matter bordering the hippocampus in the brain. -- Fim"bri*al (#), a.

fimbriate.c: Fimbriate Fim*bri*ate (?), a. [L. fimbriatus fibrous, fringed, fr. fimbria fiber, fringe. See Fringe.] Having the edge or extremity bordered by filiform processes thicker than hairs; fringed; as, the fimbriate petals of the pink; the fimbriate end of the Fallopian tube.
Fimbriate Fim"bri*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fimbriated; p. pr. & vb. n. Fimbriating.] To hem; to fringe. Fuller.

fimbriated.c: Fimbriated Fim"bri*a`ted (?), a. 1. Having a fringed border; fimbriate.

fin.c: Fin Fin (fĭn), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Finned (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Finning.] [Cf. Fin of a fish.] To carve or cut up, as a chub.
Fin Fin, n. [See Fine, n.] End; conclusion; object. [Obs.] “She knew eke the fin of his intent.” Chaucer.

Fin Fin, n.[OE. finne, fin, AS. finn; akin to D. vin, G. & Dan. finne, Sw. fena, L. pinna, penna, a wing, feather. Cf. pen a feather.] 1. (Zool.) An organ of a fish, consisting of a membrane supported by rays, or little bony or cartilaginous ossicles, and serving to balance and propel it in the water.

Fin de siecle ‖Fin` de siè"cle (?). [F.] Lit., end of the century; -- mostly used adjectively in English to signify: belonging to, or characteristic of, the close of the 19th century. At that time the phrase was also intended to imply “modern” or “up-to-date;” as, fin-de-siècle ideas.

Fin keel Fin keel. (Naut.) A projection downward from the keel of a yacht, resembling in shape the fin of a fish, though often with a cigar-shaped bulb of lead at the bottom, and generally made of metal. Its use is to ballast the boat and also to enable her to sail close to the wind and to make the least possible leeway by offering great resistance to lateral motion through the water.

finable.c: Finable Fin"a*ble (?), a. [From Fine.] Liable or subject to a fine; as, a finable person or offense. Bacon.

final.c: Final Fi"nal (fī"nail), a. [F., fr. L. finalis, fr. finis boundary, limit, end. See Finish.] 1. Pertaining to the end or conclusion; last; terminating; ultimate; as, the final day of a school term.

finale.c: Finale ‖Fi*na"le (fe*nä"la), n. [It. See Final.] Close; termination; as: (a) (Mus.) The last movement of a symphony, sonata, concerto, or any instrumental composition. (b) The last composition performed in any act of an opera. (c) The closing part, piece, or scene in any public performance or exhibition.

finalist.c: Finalist Fi"nal*ist (?), n. (Sports) Any of the players who meet in the final round of a tournament in which the losers in any round do not play again.

finality.c: Finality Fi*nal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Finalities (#). [L. finalitas the being last.] 1. The state of being final, finished, or complete; a final or conclusive arrangement; a settlement. Baxter.

finally.c: Finally Fi"nal*ly (?), adv. 1. At the end or conclusion; ultimately; lastly; as, the contest was long, but the Romans finally conquered.

finance.c: Finance Fi*nance" (?), n. [F., fr. LL. financia payment of money, money, fr. finare to pay a fine or subsidy (cf. OF. finer to finish, pay), fr. L. finis end. See Fine, n., Finish.] 1. The income of a ruler or of a state; revenue; public money; sometimes, the income of an individual; often used in the plural for funds; available money; resources.
Finance Fi*nance" (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Financed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Financing.] To conduct the finances of; to provide for, and manage, the capital for; to financier.

financial.c: Financial Fi*nan"cial (?), a. Pertaining to finance. “Our financial and commercial system.” Macaulay.

financially.c: Financially Fi*nan"cial*ly, adv. In a financial manner. Burke.

financier.c: Financier Fin`an*cier" (?; 277), n. [Cf. F. financier.] 1. One charged with the administration of finance; an officer who administers the public revenue; a treasurer. Burke.
Financier Fin`an*cier", v. i. [imp. & p. p. Financiered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Financiering.] To conduct financial operations.

finative.c: Finative Fi"na*tive (?), a. Conclusive; decisive; definitive; final. [Obs.] Greene (1593).

finback.c: Finback Fin"back` (?), n. (Zool.) Any whale of the genera Sibbaldius, Balænoptera, and allied genera, of the family Balænopteridæ, characterized by a prominent fin on the back. The common finbacks of the New England coast are Sibbaldius tectirostris and S. tuberosus.

finbat.c: Finbat kite Fin"bat kite (?). same as Eddy kite. [Eng.]

finch.c: Finch Finch (fĭnch), n.; pl. Finches (fĭnch"ĕz). [AS. finc; akin to D. vink, OHG. fincho, G. fink; cf. W. pinc a finch; also E. spink.] (Zool.) A small singing bird of many genera and species, belonging to the family Fringillidæ.

finchbacked.c: Finchbacked Finch"backed` (?), a. Streaked or spotted on the back; -- said of cattle.

find.c: Find Find (fīnd), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Found (found); p. pr. & vb. n. Finding.] [AS. findan; akin to D. vinden, OS. & OHG. findan, G. finden, Dan. finde, icel. & Sw. finna, Goth. finþan; and perh. to L. petere to seek, Gr. pi`ptein to fall, Skr. pat to fall, fly, E. petition.] 1. To meet with, or light upon, accidentally; to gain the first sight or knowledge of, as of something new, or unknown; hence, to fall in with, as a person.
Find Find (?), v. i. (Law) To determine an issue of fact, and to declare such a determination to a court; as, the jury find for the plaintiff. Burrill.
Find Find, n. Anything found; a discovery of anything valuable; especially, a deposit, discovered by archæologists, of objects of prehistoric or unknown origin.

findable.c: Findable Find"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being found; discoverable. Fuller.

finder.c: Finder Find"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, finds; specifically (Astron.), a small telescope of low power and large field of view, attached to a larger telescope, for the purpose of finding an object more readily, called also a finder telescope or finder scope.

findfault.c: Findfault Find"fault` (?), n. A censurer or caviler. [Obs.]

findfaulting.c: Findfaulting Find"fault`ing, a. Apt to censure or cavil; faultfinding; captious. [Obs.] Whitlock.

finding.c: Finding Find"ing, n. 1. That which is found, come upon, or provided; esp. (pl.), that which a journeyman artisan finds or provides for himself; as tools, trimmings, etc.

findy.c: findy fin"dy (fĭn"dy̆), a. [AS. finding heavy; cf. Dan. fyndig strong, energetical, fynd strength, energy, emphasis.] Full; heavy; firm; solid; substantial. [Obs.]

fine.c: fine fine (fīn), a. [Compar. finer (fīn"ẽr); superl. finest.] [F. fin, LL. finus fine, pure, fr. L. finire to finish; cf. finitus, p. p., finished, completed (hence the sense accomplished, perfect.) See Finish, and cf. Finite.] 1. Finished; brought to perfection; refined; hence, free from impurity; excellent; superior; elegant; worthy of admiration; accomplished; beautiful.
Fine Fine, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fined (fīnd); p. pr. & vb. n. Fining.] [From Fine, a.] 1. To make fine; to refine; to purify, to clarify; as, to fine gold.

Fine Fine (fīn), n. [OE. fin, L. finis end, also in LL., a final agreement or concord between the lord and his vassal; a sum of money paid at the end, so as to make an end of a transaction, suit, or prosecution; mulct; penalty; cf. OF. fin end, settlement, F. fin end. See Finish, and cf. Finance.] 1. End; conclusion; termination; extinction. [Obs.] “To see their fatal fine.” Spenser.

Fine Fine, v. t. [From Fine, n.] To impose a pecuniary penalty upon for an offense or breach of law; to set a fine on by judgment of a court; to punish by fine; to mulct; as, the trespassers were fined ten dollars.
Fine Fine, v. i. To pay a fine. See Fine, n., 3 (b). [R.]
Fine Fine, v. t. & i. [OF. finer, F. finir. See Finish, v. t.] To finish; to cease; or to cause to cease. [Obs.]
Fine Fine (fīn), adv. 1. Finely; well; elegantly; fully; delicately; mincingly. [Obs., Dial., or Colloq.]
Fine Fine (fīn), v. i. To become fine (in any one of various senses); as, the ale will fine; the weather fined.

finedraw.c: Finedraw Fine"draw` (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Finedrawn (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Finedrawing.] To sew up, so nicely that the seam is not perceived; to renter. Marryat.

finedrawn.c: Finedrawn Fine"drawn` (?), a. Drawn out with too much subtilty; overnice; as, finedrawn speculations.

fineer.c: Fineer Fi*neer" (?), v. i. To run in debt by getting goods made up in a way unsuitable for the use of others, and then threatening not to take them except on credit. [R.] Goldsmith.

fineless.c: Fineless Fine"less (?), a. [Fine end + -less.] Endless; boundless. [Obs.] Shak.

finely.c: Finely Fine"ly, adv. In a fine or finished manner.

fineness.c: Fineness Fine"ness, n. [From Fine, a.] 1. The quality or condition of being fine.

finer.c: Finer Fin"er (?), n. One who fines or purifies.

finespun.c: Finespun Fine"spun` (?), a. Spun so as to be fine; drawn to a fine thread; attenuated; hence, unsubstantial; visionary; as, finespun theories.

finesse.c: Finesse Fi`nesse" (? or?), n. [F., fr. fin fine. See Fine, a.] 1. Subtilty of contrivance to gain a point; artifice; stratagem.
Finesse Fi*nesse" (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Finessed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Finessing.] 1. To use artifice or stratagem. Goldsmith.

finestill.c: Finestill Fine"still` (?), v. t. To distill, as spirit from molasses or some saccharine preparation.

finfish.c: Finfish Fin"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A finback whale. (b) (pl.) True fish, as distinguished from shellfish.

finfoot.c: Finfoot Fin"foot` (?), n. (Zool.) A South American bird (Heliornis fulica) allied to the grebes. The name is also applied to several related species of the genus Podica.

finfooted.c: Fin-footed Fin"-foot`ed, a. (Zool.) (a) Having palmate feet. (b) Having lobate toes, as the coot and grebe.

finger.c: Finger Fin"ger (fĭṉ"gẽr), n. [AS. finger; akin to D. vinger, OS. & OHG. fingar, G. finger, Icel. fingr, Sw. & Dan. finger, Goth. figgrs; of unknown origin; perh. akin to E. fang.] 1. One of the five terminating members of the hand; a digit; esp., one of the four extremities of the hand, other than the thumb.
Finger Fin"ger (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fingered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fingering.] 1. To touch with the fingers; to handle; to meddle with.
Finger Fin"ger, v. i. (Mus.) To use the fingers in playing on an instrument. Busby.

fingerer.c: Fingerer Fin"ger*er (?), n. One who fingers; a pilferer.

fingering.c: Fingering Fin"ger*ing, n. 1. The act or process of handling or touching with the fingers.

fingerling.c: Fingerling Fin"ger*ling (?), n. [Finger + -ling.] (Zool.) A young salmon. See Parr.

finglefangle.c: Fingle-fangle Fin"gle-fan`gle (?), n. [From fangle.] A trifle. [Low] Hudibras.

fingrigo.c: Fingrigo ‖Fin"gri*go (?), n.; pl. Fingrigos (#). [So called in Jamaica.] (Bot.) A prickly, climbing shrub of the genus Pisonia. The fruit is a kind of berry.

finial.c: Finial Fin"i*al (?), n. [L. finire to finish, end. See Finish.] (Arch.) The knot or bunch of foliage, or foliated ornament, that forms the upper extremity of a pinnacle in Gothic architecture; sometimes, the pinnacle itself.

finical.c: Finical Fin"i*cal (?), a. [From Fine, a.] Affectedly fine; overnice; unduly particular; fastidious. “Finical taste.” Wordsworth.

finicality.c: Finicality Fin`i*cal"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being finical; finicalness.

finicky.c: Finicky Finicking { Fin"ick*ing (?), Fin"ick*y, a. } Finical; unduly particular; excessively demanding over minor details. [Colloq.]

finific.c: Finific Fi*nif"ic (? or?), n. [L. finis end + facere to make.] A limiting element or quality. [R.]

finify.c: Finify Fin"i*fy (? or?), v. t. [Fine, a. + -fy.] To make fine; to dress finically. [Obs.]

finikin.c: Finikin Fin"i*kin (?), a. [Fine, a. + -kin.] Precise in trifles; idly busy. [Colloq.] Smart.

fining.c: Fining Fin"ing (?), n. 1. The act of imposing a fin?.

finis.c: Finis ‖Fi"nis (?), n. [L.] An end; conclusion. It is often placed at the end of a book.

finish.c: Finish Fin"ish (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Finished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Finishing.] [F. finir (with a stem finiss- in several forms, whence E. -ish: see -ish.),fr. L. finire to limit, finish, end, fr. finis boundary, limit, end; perh. for fidnis, and akin findere to cleave, E. fissure.] 1. To arrive at the end of; to bring to an end; to put an end to; to make an end of; to terminate.
Finish Fin"ish, v. i. 1. To come to an end; to terminate.
Finish Fin"ish, n. 1. That which finishes, puts an end to? or perfects.

finished.c: Finished Fin"ished (?), a. Polished to the highest degree of excellence; complete; perfect; as, a finished poem; a finished education.

finisher.c: Finisher Fin"ish*er (?), n. 1. One who finishes, puts an end to, completes, or perfects; esp. used in the trades, as in hatting, weaving, etc., for the workman who gives a finishing touch to the work, or any part of it, and brings it to perfection.

finishing.c: Finishing Fin"ish*ing, n. The act or process of completing or perfecting; the final work upon or ornamentation of a thing.
Finishing Fin"ish*ing, a. Tending to complete or to render fit for the market or for use.

finite.c: Finite Fi"nite (?), a. [L. finitus, p. p. of finire. See Finish, and cf. Fine, a.] Having a limit; limited in quantity, degree, or capacity; bounded; -- opposed to infinite; as, finite number; finite existence; a finite being; a finite mind; finite duration.

finiteless.c: Finiteless Fi"nite*less, a. Infinite. [Obs.] Sir T. browne.

finitely.c: Finitely Fi"nite*ly, adv. In a finite manner or degree.

finiteness.c: Finiteness Fi"nite*ness, n. The state of being finite.

finitude.c: Finitude Fin"i*tude (?), n. [L. finire. See Finish.] Limitation. Cheyne.

finjan.c: Finjan Fin*jan" (?), n. [Also fingan, findjan, fingian, etc.] [Ar. finjān.] In the Levant, a small coffee cup without a handle, such as is held in a cup or stand called a zarf.

finlander.c: Finlander Fin"land*er (?), n. A native or inhabitant of Finland.

finlet.c: Finlet Fin"let (?), n. [Fin + -let.] A little fin; one of the parts of a divided fin.

finn.c: Finn Finn (?), a. A native of Finland; one of the Finn? in the ethnological sense. See Finns.

finnan.c: Finnan haddie Fin"nan had"die (fĭn"nain hăd"dĭ). [See Haddock.] Haddock cured in peat smoke, originally at Findon (pron. fĭn"ain), Scotland. The name is also applied to other kinds of smoked haddock. [Written also finnan haddock.]

finned.c: Finned Finned (?), a. Having a fin, or fins, or anything resembling a fin. Mortimer.

finnic.c: Finnic Finn"ic (?), a. Of or pertaining to the Finns.

finnikin.c: Finnikin Fin"ni*kin (?), n. (Zool.) A variety of pigeon, with a crest somewhat resembling the mane of a horse. [Written also finikin.]

finnish.c: Finnish Finn"ish (?), a. Of or pertaining to Finland, to the Finns, or to their language. -- n. A Northern Turanian group of languages; the language of the Finns.

finns.c: Finns Finns (?), n. pl.; sing. Finn. (Ethnol.) (a) Natives of Finland; Finlanders. (b) A branch of the Mongolian race, inhabiting Northern and Eastern Europe, including the Magyars, Bulgarians, Permians, Lapps, and Finlanders. [Written also Fins.]

finny.c: Finny Fin"ny (?), a. 1. (Zool.) Having, or abounding in, fins, as fishes; pertaining to fishes.

finochio.c: Finochio ‖Fi*no"chi*o (?; 277), n. [It. finocchio fennel, LL. fenuclum. See Fennel.] (Bot.) An umbelliferous plant (Fœniculum dulce) having a somewhat tuberous stem; sweet fennel. The blanched stems are used in France and Italy as a culinary vegetable.

finos.c: Finos ‖Fi"nos (?), n. pl. [Sp., pl., fr. fino fine.] Second best wool from Merino sheep. Gardner.

finpike.c: Finpike Fin"pike` (?), n. (Zool.) The bichir. See Crossopterygii.

finsen.c: Finsen light Fin"sen light (?). [After Prof. Niels R. Finsen (b. 1860), Danish physician.] (Med.) Highly actinic light, derived from sunlight or from some form of electric lamp, used in the treatment of lupus and other cutaneous affections.

fint.c: Fint Fint (?), 3d pers. sing. pr. of Find, for findeth. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fintoed.c: Fin-toed Fin"-toed` (?), a. (Zool.) Having toes connected by a membrane; palmiped; palmated; also, lobate.

fiord.c: Fiord ‖Fiord (fy?rd; i or y consonant, § 272), n. [Dan. & Norw. fiord. See Frith.] A narrow inlet of the sea, penetrating between high banks or rocks, as on the coasts of Norway and Alaska. [Written also fjord.]

fiorin.c: Fiorin Fi"o*rin (?), n. [Cf. Ir. fiothran a sort of grass.] (Bot.) A species of creeping bent grass (Agrostis alba); -- called also fiorin grass.

fiorite.c: Fiorite Fi"o*rite (?), n. (Min.) A variety of opal occuring in the cavities of volcanic tufa, in smooth and shining globular and botryoidal masses, having a pearly luster; -- so called from Fiora, in Ischia.

fioriture.c: Fioriture ‖Fio`ri*tu"re (?), n. pl. [It., pl. of fioritura a flowering.] (Mus.) Little flowers of ornament introduced into a melody by a singer or player.

fippenny.c: Fippenny bit Fip"pen*ny bit` (? or?). [Corruption of five penny bit.] The Spanish half real, or one sixteenth of a dollar, -- so called in Pennsylvania and the adjacent States. [Obs.]

fipple.c: Fipple Fip"ple (fẽr), n. [perh. fr. L. fibula a clasp, a pin; cf. Prov. E. fible a stick used to stir pottage.] A stopper, as in a wind instrument of music. [Obs.] Bacon.

fir.c: Fir Fir (fẽr), n. [Dan. fyr, fyrr; akin to Sw. furu, Icel. fura, AS. furh in furhwudu fir wood, G. föhre, OHG. forha pine, vereheih a sort of oak, L. quercus oak.] (Bot.) A genus (Abies) of coniferous trees, often of large size and elegant shape, some of them valued for their timber and others for their resin. The species are distinguished as the balsam fir, the silver fir, the red fir, etc. The Scotch fir is a Pinus.
Fir tree Fir" tree` (fẽr" trē`). See Fir.

fire.c: Fire Fire (fīr), n. [OE. fir, fyr, fur AS. fȳr; akin to D. vuur, OS. & OHG. fiur, G. feuer, Icel. fȳri, fūrr, Gr. py^r, and perh. to L. purus pure, E. pure Cf. Empyrean, Pyre.] 1. The evolution of light and heat in the combustion of bodies; combustion; state of ignition.
Fire Fire (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fired (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fring.] 1. To set on fire; to kindle; as, to fire a house or chimney; to fire a pile.
Fire Fire, v. i. 1. To take fire; to be kindled; to kindle.

Fire beetle Fire" bee`tle (?). (Zool.) A very brilliantly luminous beetle (Pyrophorus noctilucus), one of the elaters, found in Central and South America; -- called also cucujo. The name is also applied to other species. See Firefly.

firearm.c: Firearm Fire"arm` (fīr"ärm`), n. A gun, pistol, or any weapon from which a shot is discharged by the force of an explosive substance, as gunpowder.

fireback.c: Fireback Fire"back` (fīr"băk`), n. (Zool.) One of several species of pheasants of the genus Euplocamus, having the lower back a bright, fiery red. They inhabit Southern Asia and the East Indies.

fireball.c: Fireball Fire"ball` (?), n. 1. (Mil.) A ball filled with powder or other combustibles, intended to be thrown among enemies, and to injure by explosion; also, to set fire to their works and light them up, so that movements may be seen.

fireboard.c: Fireboard Fire"board` (?), n. A chimney board or screen to close a fireplace when not in use.

firebote.c: Firebote Fire"bote` (?), n. (O. Eng. Law) An allowance of fuel. See Bote.

firebrand.c: Firebrand Fire"brand` (?), n. 1. A piece of burning wood. L'Estrange.

firecracker.c: firecracker fire"crack`er (?), n. A small explosive device consisting of a paper or cardboard cylinder having only sufficient explosive mixture to make a loud bang, ignited by a short fuse, and used mostly as an entertainment or in celebrations. Same as Cracker., n., 3.

firecrest.c: Firecrest Fire"crest` (?), n. (Zool.) A small European kinglet (Regulus ignicapillus), having a bright red crest; -- called also fire-crested wren.

firedog.c: Firedog Fire"dog` (?), n. A support for wood in a fireplace; an andiron.

firedrake.c: Firedrake Fire"drake` (fīr"drāk`), n. [AS. fȳrdraca; fȳr fire + draca a dragon. See Fire, and Drake a dragon.] [Obs.] 1. A fiery dragon. Beau. & Fl.

firefanged.c: Fire-fanged Fire"-fanged` (?), a. [Fire + fanged seized.] Injured as by fire; burned; -- said of manure which has lost its goodness and acquired an ashy hue in consequence of heat generated by decomposition.

firefish.c: Firefish Fire"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) A singular marine fish of the genus Pterois, family Scorpænidæ, of several species, inhabiting the Indo-Pacific region. They are usually red, and have very large spinose pectoral and dorsal fins.

fireflaire.c: Fireflaire Fire"flaire` (?), n. [Fire + Prov. E. flaire a ray.] (Zool.) A European sting ray of the genus Trygon (T. pastinaca); -- called also fireflare and fiery flaw.

fireflame.c: Fireflame Fire"flame` (?), n. (Zool.) The European band fish (Cepola rubescens).

firefly.c: Firefly Fire"fly` (?), n.; pl. Fireflies (?). (Zool.) Any luminous winged insect, esp. luminous beetles of the family Lampyridæ.

firelock.c: Firelock Fire"lock`, n. An old form of gunlock, as the flintlock, which ignites the priming by a spark; perhaps originally, a matchlock. Hence, a gun having such a lock.

fireman.c: Fireman Fire"man (?), n.; pl. Firemen (-men). 1. A man whose business is to extinguish fires in towns; a member of a fire company.

firenew.c: Fire-new Fire"-new` (?), a. Fresh from the forge; bright; quite new; brand-new. Charles reade.

fireplace.c: Fireplace Fire"place` (?), n. The part a chimney appropriated to the fire; a hearth; -- usually an open recess in a wall, in which a fire may be built.

fireproof.c: Fireproof Fire"proof` (?), a. Proof against fire; incombustible.

fireproofing.c: Fireproofing Fire"proof`ing (?), n. The act or process of rendering anything incombustible; also, the materials used in the process.

firer.c: Firer Fir"er (?), n. One who fires or sets fire to anything; an incendiary. [R.] R. Carew.

fireroom.c: Fireroom Fire"room`, n. Same as Stokehold, below.
