fireset.c: Fire-set Fire"-set` (?), n. A set of fire irons, including, commonly, tongs, shovel, and poker.

fireside.c: Fireside Fire"side` (?), n. A place near the fire or hearth; home; domestic life or retirement.

firestone.c: Firestone Fire"stone` (?; 110), n. [AS. fȳrstān flint; fȳr fire + stān stone.] 1. Iron pyrites, formerly used for striking fire; also, a flint.

firetail.c: Firetail Fire"tail` (?), n. (Zool.) The European redstart; -- called also fireflirt. [prov. Eng.]

firewarden.c: Firewarden Fire"ward`en (?), n. An officer who has authority to direct in the extinguishing of fires, or to order what precautions shall be taken against fires; -- called also fireward.

fireweed.c: Fireweed Fire"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) (a) An American plant (Erechthites hiercifolia), very troublesome in spots where brushwood has been burned. (b) The great willow-herb (Epilobium spicatum).

firework.c: firework fire"work` (fīr"wûrk`), n. 1. A device for producing a striking display of light, or a figure or figures in plain or colored fire, by the combustion of materials that burn in some peculiar manner, as gunpowder, sulphur, metallic filings, and various salts; also called a pyrotechnic device. The most common feature of fireworks is a paper or pasteboard tube filled with the combustible material. A number of these tubes or cases are often combined so as to make, when kindled, a great variety of figures in fire, often variously colored. The skyrocket is a common form of firework. The art of designing fireworks for purposes of entertainment is called pyrotechnics. The name firework is also given to various combustible preparations used in war.

fireworm.c: Fireworm Fire"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) The larva of a small tortricid moth which eats the leaves of the cranberry, so that the vines look as if burned; -- called also cranberry worm.

firing.c: Firing Fir"ing, n. 1. The act of discharging firearms.
Firing pin Fir"ing pin`. In the breech mechanism of a firearm, the pin which strikes the head of the cartridge and explodes it.

firk.c: Firk Firk (?), v. t. [Cf. OE. ferken to proceed, hasten, AS. fercian to bring, assist; perh. akin to faran to go, E. fare.] To beat; to strike; to chastise. [Obs.]
Firk Firk, v. i. To fly out; to turn out; to go off. [Obs.]
Firk Firk, n. A freak; trick; quirk. [Obs.] Ford.

firkin.c: Firkin Fir"kin (?), n. [From AS. feówer four (or an allied word, perh. Dutch or Danish) + -kin. See Four.] 1. A varying measure of capacity, usually being the fourth part of a barrel; specifically, a measure equal to nine imperial gallons. [Eng.]

firlot.c: Firlot Fir"lot (?), n. [Scot., the fourth part of a boll of grain, from a word equiv. to E. four + lot part, portion. See Firkin.] A dry measure formerly used in Scotland; the fourth part of a boll of grain or meal. The Linlithgow wheat firlot was to the imperial bushel as 998 to 1000; the barley firlot as 1456 to 1000. Brande & C.

firm.c: Firm Firm (?), a. [Compar. Firmer (?); superl. Firmest.] [OE. ferme, F. ferme, fr.L. firmus; cf. Skr. dharman support, law, order, dh? to hold fast, carry. Cf. Farm, Throne.] 1. Fixed; hence, closely compressed; compact; substantial; hard; solid; -- applied to the matter of bodies; as, firm flesh; firm muscles, firm wood.

Firm Firm, n. [It. firma the (firm, sure, or confirming) signature or subscription, or Pg. firma signature, firm, cf. Sp. firma signature; all fr. L. firmus, adj., firm. See Firm, a.] The name, title, or style, under which a company transacts business; a partnership of two or more persons; a commercial house; as, the firm of Hope & Co.
Firm Firm, v. t. [OE. fermen to make firm, F. fermer, fr. L. firmare to make firm. See Firm, a.] 1. To fix; to settle; to confirm; to establish. [Obs.]

firmament.c: Firmament Fir"ma*ment (?), n. [L. firmamentum, fr. firmare to make firm: cf. F. firmament. See Firm, v. & a.] 1. Fixed foundation; established basis. [Obs.]

firmamental.c: Firmamental Fir`ma*men"tal (?), a. Pertaining to the firmament; celestial; being of the upper regions. Dryden.

firman.c: Firman Fir"man (? or?), n.; pl. Firmans (#) or (#). [Pers. fermān.] In Turkey and some other Oriental countries, a decree or mandate issued by the sovereign; a royal order or grant; -- generally given for special objects, as to a traveler to insure him protection and assistance. [Written also firmaun.]

firmerchisel.c: Firmer-chisel Firm"er-chis"el (?), n. A chisel, thin in proportion to its width. It has a tang to enter the handle instead of a socket for receiving it. Knight.

firmitude.c: Firmitude Firm"i*tude (?), n. [L. firmitudo. See Firm.] Strength; stability. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.

firmity.c: Firmity Firm"i*ty (?), n. [L. firmitas.] Strength; firmness; stability. [Obs.] Chillingworth.

firmly.c: Firmly Firm"ly, adv. In a firm manner.

firmness.c: Firmness Firm"ness, n. The state or quality of being firm.

firms.c: Firms Firms (?), n. pl. [From Firm, a.] (Arch.) The principal rafters of a roof, especially a pair of rafters taken together. [Obs.]

firry.c: Firry Fir"ry (?), a. Made of fir; abounding in firs.

first.c: First First (fẽrst), a. [OE. first, furst, AS. fyrst; akin to Icel. fyrstr, Sw. & Dan. förste, OHG. furist, G. fürst prince; a superlatiye form of E. for, fore. See For, Fore, and cf. Formeer, Foremost.] 1. Preceding all others of a series or kind; the ordinal of one; earliest; as, the first day of a month; the first year of a reign.
First First (fẽrst), adv. Before any other person or thing in time, space, rank, etc.; -- much used in composition with adjectives and participles.
First First, n. (Mus.) The upper part of a duet, trio, etc., either vocal or instrumental; -- so called because it generally expresses the air, and has a preëminence in the combined effect.

firstborn.c: Firstborn First"born` (fẽrst"bôrn`), a. First brought forth; first in the order of birth; eldest; hence, most excellent; most distinguished or exalted; as, the firstborn child.

firstclass.c: first-class first"-class` (fẽrst"klăs`), a. Of the best class; of the highest rank; in the first division; of the best quality; first-rate; as, a first-class telescope.

firsthand.c: First-hand First"-hand` (?), a. Obtained directly from the first or original source; hence, without the intervention of an agent; -- of information; as, a firsthand report; firsthand information; firsthand knowledge.

firstling.c: Firstling First"ling (fẽrst"lĭng), n. [First + -ling.] 1. The first produce or offspring; -- said of animals, especially domestic animals; as, the firstlings of his flock. Milton.

firstly.c: Firstly First"ly, adv. In the first place; before anything else; -- sometimes improperly used for first.

firstrate.c: First-rate First"-rate` (fẽrst"rāt`), a. Of the highest excellence; preëminent in quality, size, or estimation.
First-rate First"-rate`, n. (Naut.) A war vessel of the highest grade or the most powerful class.

firth.c: Firth Firth (fẽrth), n. [Scot. See Frith.] (Geog.) An arm of the sea; a frith.

fisc.c: Fisc Fisc (fĭsk), n. [F. fisc, fr. L. fiscus basket, money basket, treasury; prob. akin to fascis bundle. See Fasces.] A public or state treasury. Burke.

fiscal.c: Fiscal Fis"cal (fĭs"kail), a. [F. fiscal, L. fiscalis, fr. fiscus. See Fisc.] Pertaining to the public treasury or revenue.
Fiscal Fis"cal, n. 1. The income of a prince or a state; revenue; exchequer. [Obs.] Bacon.

fisetic.c: Fisetic Fi*set"ic (?), a. (Chem.) Pertaining to fustet or fisetin.

fisetin.c: Fisetin Fis"e*tin (?), n. [G. fisettholz a species of fustic.] (Chem.) A yellow crystalline substance extracted from fustet, and regarded as its essential coloring principle; -- called also fisetic acid.

fish.c: Fish Fish (fĭsh), n. [F. fiche peg, mark, fr. fisher to fix.] A counter, used in various games.

Fish Fish, n.; pl. Fishes (fĭsh"ĕz), or collectively, Fish. [OE. fisch, fisc, fis, AS. fisc; akin to D. visch, OS. & OHG. fisk, G. fisch, Icel. fiskr, Sw. & Dan. fisk, Goth. fisks, L. piscis, Ir. iasg. Cf. Piscatorial. In some cases, such as fish joint, fish plate, this word has prob. been confused with fish, fr. F. fichea peg.] 1. A name loosely applied in popular usage to many animals of diverse characteristics, living in the water.
Fish Fish (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fishing.] 1. To attempt to catch fish; to be employed in taking fish, by any means, as by angling or drawing a net.
Fish Fish, v. t. [OE. fischen, fisken, fissen, AS. fiscian; akin to G. fischen, OHG. fisc?n, Goth. fisk?n. See Fish the animal.] 1. To catch; to draw out or up; as, to fish up an anchor.

fishbellied.c: Fish-bellied Fish"-bel`lied (?), a. Bellying or swelling out on the under side; as, a fish-bellied rail. Knight.

fisher.c: Fisher Fish"er (?), n. [AS. fiscere.] 1. One who fishes.

fisherman.c: Fisherman Fish"er*man (?), n.; pl. Fishermen (?). 1. One whose occupation is to catch fish.

fishery.c: Fishery Fish"er*y (?), n.; pl. Fisheries (?). 1. The business or practice of catching fish; fishing. Addison.

fishful.c: Fishful Fish"ful (?), a. Abounding with fish. [R.] “My fishful pond.” R. Carew.

fishgig.c: Fishgig Fish"gig` (?), n. A spear with barbed prongs used for harpooning fish. Knight.

fishhawk.c: Fishhawk Fish"hawk` (?), n. (Zool.) The osprey (Pandion haliaëtus), found both in Europe and America; -- so called because it plunges into the water and seizes fishes in its talons. Called also fishing eagle, and bald buzzard.

fishhook.c: Fishhook Fish"hook` (?), n. 1. A hook for catching fish.

fishify.c: Fishify Fish"i*fy (?), v. t. To change to fish. [R.] Shak.

fishiness.c: Fishiness Fish"i*ness, n. The state or quality of being fishy or fishlike. Pennant.

fishing.c: Fishing Fish"ing, n. 1. The act, practice, or art of one who fishes.
Fishing Fish"ing, a. [From Fishing, n.] Pertaining to fishing; used in fishery; engaged in fishing; as, fishing boat; fishing tackle; fishing village.

fishlike.c: Fishlike Fish"like (?), a. Like fish; suggestive of fish; having some of the qualities of fish.

fishmonger.c: Fishmonger Fish"mon`ger (?), n. A dealer in fish.

fishskin.c: Fishskin Fish"skin` (?), n. 1. The skin of a fish (dog fish, shark, etc.)

fishtackle.c: Fish-tackle Fish"-tac`kle (?), n. A tackle or purchase used to raise the flukes of the anchor up to the gunwale. The block used is called the fish-block.

fishtail.c: Fish-tail Fish"-tail` (?), a. Like the of a fish; acting, or producing something, like the tail of a fish.

fishwoman.c: Fishwoman Fish"wom`an (?), n.; pl. Fishwomen (?). A woman who retails fish; a female fishmonger.

fishy.c: Fishy Fish"y (?), a. 1. Consisting of fish; fishlike; having the qualities or taste of fish; abounding in fish. Pope.

fisk.c: Fisk Fisk (?), v. i. [Cf. Sw. fjeska to bustle about.] To run about; to frisk; to whisk. [Obs.]

fissigemmation.c: Fissigemmation Fis`si*gem*ma"tion (?), n. [L. fissus (p. p. of findere to split) + E. gemmation.] (Biol.) A process of reproduction intermediate between fission and gemmation.

fissile.c: Fissile Fis"sile (?), a. [L. fissilis, fr. fissus, p. p. of findere to split. See Fissure.] 1. Capable of being split, cleft, or divided in the direction of the grain, like wood, or along natural planes of cleavage, like crystals.

fissilingual.c: Fissilingual Fis`si*lin"gual (?), a. [L. fissus (p. p. of findere to split) + E. lingual.] (Zool.) Having the tongue forked.

fissilinguia.c: Fissilinguia ‖Fis`si*lin"gui*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. fissus (p. p. o f findere to split) + lingua tongue.] (Zool.) A group of Lacertilia having the tongue forked, including the common lizards. [Written also Fissilingues.]

fissility.c: Fissility Fis*sil"i*ty (?), n. Quality of being fissile.

fission.c: Fission Fis"sion (?), n. [L. fissio. See Fissure.] 1. A cleaving, splitting, or breaking up into parts.

fissipalmate.c: Fissipalmate Fis`si*pal"mate (?), a. [L. fissus (p. p. of findere to split) + palma palm.] (Zool.) Semipalmate and loboped, as a grebe's foot. See Illust. under Aves.

fissipara.c: Fissipara ‖Fis*sip"a*ra (?), n. pl. [NL. See Fissiparous.] (Zool.) Animals which reproduce by fission.

fissiparism.c: Fissiparism Fis*sip"a*rism (?), n. [See Fissiparous.] (Biol.) Reproduction by spontaneous fission.

fissiparity.c: Fissiparity Fis`si*par"i*ty (?), n. (Biol.) Quality of being fissiparous; fissiparism.

fissiparous.c: Fissiparous Fis*sip"a*rous (?), a. [L. fissus (p. p. of findere to split) + parere to bring forth: cf. F. fissipare.] (Biol.) Reproducing by spontaneous fission. See Fission. -- Fis*sip"a*rous*ly, adv.

fissipation.c: Fissipation Fis`si*pa"tion (?), n. (Biol.) Reproduction by fission; fissiparism.

fissipedal.c: Fissipedal Fissiped { Fis"si*ped (?), Fis*sip"e*dal (?) }, a. [Cf. F. fissipède.] (Zool.) Having the toes separated to the base. [See Aves.]

fissiped.c: Fissiped Fis"si*ped, n. (Zool.) One of the Fissipedia.

fissipedia.c: Fissipedia ‖Fis`si*pe"di*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. fissus (p. p. of findere to cleave) + pes, pedis, a foot.] (Zool.) A division of the Carnivora, including the dogs, cats, and bears, in which the feet are not webbed; -- opposed to Pinnipedia.

fissirostral.c: Fissirostral Fis`si*ros"tral (?), a. [Cf. F. fissirostre.] (Zool.) Having the bill cleft beyond the horny part, as in the case of swallows and goatsuckers.

fissirostres.c: Fissirostres ‖Fis`si*ros"tres (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. fissus (p. p. of findere to cleave) + rostrum beak.] (Zool.) A group of birds having the bill deeply cleft.

fissural.c: Fissural Fis"sur*al (?), a. Pertaining to a fissure or fissures; as, the fissural pattern of a brain.

fissuration.c: Fissuration Fis`su*ra"tion (?), n. (Anat.) The act of dividing or opening; the state of being fissured.

fissure.c: Fissure Fis"sure (?), n. [L. fissura, fr. findere, fissum, to cleave, split; akin to E. bite: cf. F. fissure.] A narrow opening, made by the parting of any substance; a cleft; as, the fissure of a rock.
Fissure Fis"sure (?), v. t. To cleave; to divide; to crack or fracture.

fissurella.c: Fissurella ‖Fis`su*rel"la (?), n. [NL., dim. of L. fissura a fissure.] (Zool.) A genus of marine gastropod mollusks, having a conical or limpetlike shell, with an opening at the apex; -- called also keyhole limpet.

fist.c: Fist Fist (fĭst), n. [OE. fist, fust, AS. fȳst; akin to D. vuist, OHG. fūst, G. faust, and prob. to L. pugnus, Gr. pygmh` fist, py`x with the fist. Cf. Pugnacious, Pigmy.] 1. The hand with the fingers doubled into the palm; the closed hand, especially as clinched tightly for the purpose of striking a blow.
Fist Fist, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Fisting.] 1. To strike with the fist. Dryden.

fistic.c: Fistic Fist"ic (?), a. [From Fist.] Pertaining to boxing, or to encounters with the fists; puglistic; as, fistic exploits; fistic heroes. [Colloq.]

fisticuff.c: Fisticuff Fist"i*cuff (?), n. A cuff or blow with the fist or hand; (pl.) a fight with the fists; boxing. Swift.

fistinut.c: Fistinut Fis"ti*nut (?), n. [Cf. Fr. fistinq, fistuq. See Pistachio.] A pistachio nut. [Obs.] Johnson.

fistuca.c: Fistuca ‖Fis*tu"ca (?), n. [L.] An instrument used by the ancients in driving piles.

fistula.c: Fistula ‖Fis"tu*la (?; 135), n.; pl. Fistulæ (#). [L.] 1. A reed; a pipe.

fistular.c: Fistular Fis"tu*lar (?), a. [L. fistularis: cf. F. fistulaire.] Hollow and cylindrical, like a pipe or reed. Johnson.

fistularia.c: Fistularia ‖Fis`tu*la"ri*a (?), n. [NL., fr. L. fistula pipe.] (Zool.) A genus of fishes, having the head prolonged into a tube, with the mouth at the extremity.

fistularioid.c: Fistularioid Fis`tu*la"ri*oid (?), a. [Fistularia + -oid.] (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the genus Fistularia.

fistulate.c: Fistulate Fis"tu*late (?; 135), v. t. & i. [Cf. L. fistulatus furnished with pipes.] To make hollow or become hollow like a fistula, or pipe. [Obs.] “A fistulated ulcer.” Fuller.

fistuliform.c: Fistuliform Fis"tu*li*form (? or?), a. [Fistula + -form.] Of a fistular form; tubular; pipe-shaped.

fistulose.c: Fistulose Fis"tu*lose` (?; 135), a. [L. fistulosus.] Formed like a fistula; hollow; reedlike. Craig.

fistulous.c: Fistulous Fis"tu*lous (?), a. [Cf. F. fistuleux.] 1. Having the form or nature of a fistula; as, a fistulous ulcer.

fit.c: Fit Fit (fĭt), imp. & p. p. of Fight. [Obs. or Colloq.]
Fit Fit, n. [AS. fitt a song.] In Old English, a song; a strain; a canto or portion of a ballad; a passus. [Written also fitte, fytte, etc.]

Fit Fit, a. [Compar. Fitter (fĭt"tẽr); superl. Fittest (fĭt"tĕst).] [OE. fit, fyt; cf. E. feat neat, elegant, well made, or icel. fitja to web, knit, OD. vitten to suit, square, Goth. fētjan to adorn. √77.] 1. Adapted to an end, object, or design; suitable by nature or by art; suited by character, qualities, circumstances, education, etc.; qualified; competent; worthy.

Fit Fit (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fitted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fitting (?).] 1. To make fit or suitable; to adapt to the purpose intended; to qualify; to put into a condition of readiness or preparation.
Fit Fit (?), v. i. 1. To be proper or becoming.
Fit Fit, n. 1. The quality of being fit; adjustment; adaptedness; as of dress to the person of the wearer.
Fit Fit, n. [AS. fit strife, fight; of uncertain origin. √ 77.] 1. A stroke or blow. [Obs. or R.]

fitch.c: Fitch Fitch (?; 224), n.; pl. Fitches (#). [See Vetch.] 1. (Bot.) A vetch. [Obs.]
Fitch Fitch, n. [Contr. of fitched.] (Zool.) The European polecat; also, its fur.

fitche.c: fitche Fitch"é (?), a. [Cf. F. fiché, lit. p. p. of ficher to fasten, OF. fichier to pierce. Cf. 1st Fish.] (Her.) Sharpened to a point; pointed.

fitchew.c: Fitchew Fitchet { Fitch"et (?), Fitch"ew (?) }, n. [Cf. OF. fisseau, fissel, OD. fisse, visse, vitsche, D. vies nasty, loathsome, E. fizz.] (Zool.) The European polecat (Putorius fœtidus). See Polecat.

fitchy.c: Fitchy Fitch"y (?), a. Having fitches or vetches.

fitful.c: Fitful Fit"ful (?), a. [From 7th Fit.] Full of fits; irregularly variable; impulsive and unstable.

fithul.c: Fithul Fithel { Fith"el (?), Fith"ul (?) }, n. [OE. See Fiddle.] A fiddle. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fitly.c: Fitly Fit"ly (?), adv. In a fit manner; suitably; properly; conveniently; as, a maxim fitly applied.

fitment.c: Fitment Fit"ment (?), n. The act of fitting; that which is proper or becoming; equipment. [Obs.] Shak.

fitness.c: Fitness Fit"ness, n. The state or quality of being fit; as, the fitness of measures or laws; a person's fitness for office.

fittedness.c: Fittedness Fit"ted*ness (?), n. The state or quality of being fitted; adaptation. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

fitter.c: Fitter Fit"ter (?), n. 1. One who fits or makes to fit; esp.: (a) One who tries on, and adjusts, articles of dress. (b) One who fits or adjusts the different parts of machinery to each other.
Fitter Fit"ter, n. A little piece; a flitter; a flinder. [Obs.]

fitting.c: Fitting Fit"ting (?), n. Anything used in fitting up; especially (pl.), necessary fixtures or apparatus; as, the fittings of a church or study; gas fittings.
Fitting Fit"ting, a. Fit; appropriate; suitable; proper. -- Fit"ting*ly, adv. -- Fit"ting*ness, n. Jer. Taylor.

fitweed.c: Fitweed Fit"weed` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant (Eryngium fœtidum) supposed to be a remedy for fits.

fitz.c: Fitz Fitz (?), n. [OF. fils, filz, fiz, son, F. fils, L. filius. See Filial.] A son; -- used in compound names, to indicate paternity, esp. of the illegitimate sons of kings and princes of the blood; as, Fitzroy, the son of the king; Fitzclarence, the son of the duke of Clarence.

five.c: Five Five (fīv), a. [OE. fif, five, AS. fīf, fīfe; akin to D. vijf, OS. fīf, OHG. finf, funf, G. fünf, Icel. fimm, Sw. & Sw. Dan. fem, Goth. fimf, Lith. penki, W. pump, OIr. cóic, L. quinque, Gr. pe`nte, Æol. pe`mpe, Skr. pañcan. √303. Cf. Fifth, Cinque, Pentagon, Punch the drink, Quinary.] Four and one added; one more than four.
Five Five (fīv), n. 1. The number next greater than four, and less than six; five units or objects.

fivefold.c: Fivefold Five"fold` (fīv"-fōld`), a. & adv. In fives; consisting of five in one; five repeated; quintuple.

fiveleaved.c: Five-leaved Five-leafed { Five"-leafed` (?), Five"-leaved` (?) }, a. (Bot.) Having five leaflets, as the Virginia creeper.

fiveling.c: Fiveling Five"ling (?), n. (Min.) A compound or twin crystal consisting of five individuals.

fives.c: Fives Fives (fīvz), n. pl. A kind of play with a ball against a wall, resembling tennis; -- so named because three fives, or fifteen, are counted to the game. Smart.
Fives Fives, n. [See Vives.] A disease of the glands under the ear in horses; the vives. Shak.

fivetwenties.c: Five-twenties Five`-twen"ties (?), n. pl. Five-twenty bonds of the United States (bearing six per cent interest), issued in 1862, '64, and '65, redeemable after five and payable in twenty years.

fix.c: Fix Fix (fĭks), a. [OE., fr. L. fixus, p. p. of figere to fix; cf. F. fixe.] Fixed; solidified. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Fix Fix, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fixed (fĭkst); p. pr. & vb. n. Fixing.] [Cf. F. fixer.] 1. To make firm, stable, or fast; to set or place permanently; to fasten immovably; to establish; to implant; to secure; to make definite.
Fix Fix, v. i. 1. To become fixed; to settle or remain permanently; to cease from wandering; to rest.
Fix Fix, n. 1. A position of difficulty or embarassment; predicament; dilemma. [Colloq.]

fixable.c: Fixable Fix"a*ble (-ȧ*b'l), a. Capable of being fixed.

fixation.c: Fixation Fix*a"tion (fĭks*ā"shŭn), n. [Cf. F. fixation.] 1. The act of fixing, or the state of being fixed.

fixative.c: Fixative Fix"a*tive (?), n. That which serves to set or fix colors or drawings, as a mordant.

fixed.c: Fixed Fixed (fĭkst), a. 1. Securely placed or fastened; settled; established; firm; imovable; unalterable.

fixedly.c: Fixedly Fix"ed*ly (fĭks"ĕd*ly̆), adv. In a fixed, stable, or constant manner.

fixedness.c: Fixedness Fix"ed*ness, n. 1. The state or quality of being fixed; stability; steadfastness.

fixing.c: Fixing Fix"ing (fĭks"ĭng), n. 1. The act or process of making fixed.

fixity.c: Fixity Fix"i*ty (-ĭ*ty̆), n. [Cf. F. fixité.] 1. Fixedness; as, fixity of tenure; also, that which is fixed.

fixture.c: Fixture Fix"ture (fĭks"tur; 135), n. [Cf. Fixure.] 1. That which is fixed or attached to something as a permanent appendage; as, the fixtures of a pump; the fixtures of a farm or of a dwelling, that is, the articles which a tenant may not take away.

fixure.c: Fixure Fix"ure (-ur), n. [L. fixura a fastening, fr. figere to fix. See Fix, and cf. Fixture.] Fixed position; stable condition; firmness. [Obs.] Shak.

fizgig.c: fizgig fiz"gig`, n. [Fizz + gig whirling thing.] A firework, made of damp powder, which makes a fizzing or hissing noise when it explodes.
fizgig fiz"gig`, n. [See Gig a flirt.] A gadding, flirting girl. Gosson.

fizz.c: fizz fizz (fĭz), v. i. [imp. & p. p. fizzed (fĭzd); p. pr. & vb. n. fizzing.] [Cf. Icel. fīsa to break wind, Dan. fise to foist, fizzle, OSw. fisa, G. fisten, feisten. Cf. Foist.] To make a hissing sound, such as that of a burning fuse or a bubbling carbonated beverage.
Fizz Fizz, n. A hissing sound; as, the fizz of a fly.

fizzle.c: fizzle fiz"zle (fĭz"z'l), v. i. [imp. & p. p. fizzled (fĭz"z'ld); p. pr. & vb. n. fizzling (fĭz"zlĭng).] [See Fizz.] 1. To make a hissing sound.
fizzle fiz"zle, n. A failure or abortive effort; a fiasco. [Colloq.]

flabbergast.c: Flabbergast Flab"ber*gast (flăb"bẽr*găst), v. t. [Cf. Flap, and Aghast.] To astonish; to strike with wonder, esp. by extraordinary statements. [Jocular] Beaconsfield.

flabbergastation.c: Flabbergastation Flab`ber*gas*ta"tion (flăb`bẽr*găs*tā"shŭn), n. The state of being flabbergasted. [Jocular] London Punch.

flabbily.c: Flabbily Flab"bi*ly (flăb"bĭ*ly̆), adv. In a flabby manner.

flabbiness.c: Flabbiness Flab"bi*ness, n. Quality or state of being flabby.

flabby.c: flabby flab"by (flăb"by̆), a. [See Flap.] Yielding to the touch, and easily moved or shaken; hanging loose by its own weight; wanting firmness; flaccid; as, flabby flesh.

flabel.c: Flabel Fla"bel (?), n. [L. flabellum a fan, dim. of flabrum a breeze, fr. flare to blow.] A fan. [Obs.] Huloet.

flabellate.c: Flabellate Fla*bel"late (?), a. [L. flabellatus, p. p. of flabellare to fan, fr. flabellum. See Flabbel.] (Bot.) Flabelliform.

flabellation.c: Flabellation Flab`el*la"tion (?), n. The act of keeping fractured limbs cool by the use of a fan or some other contrivance. Dunglison.

flabelliform.c: Flabelliform Fla*bel"li*form (?), a. [L. flabellum a fan + -form: cf. F. flabeliforme.] Having the form of a fan; fan-shaped; flabellate.

flabellinerved.c: Flabellinerved Fla*bel"li*nerved` (?), a. [L. flabellum a fan + E. nerve.] (Bot.) Having many nerves diverging radiately from the base; -- said of a leaf.

flabellum.c: Flabellum ‖Fla*bel"lum (?), n. [L. See Flabel.] (Eccl.) A fan; especially, the fan carried before the pope on state occasions, made in ostrich and peacock feathers. Shipley.

flabile.c: Flabile Flab"ile (?), a. [L. flabilis.] Liable to be blown about. Bailey.

flaccid.c: flaccid flac"cid (flăk"sĭd or flăs"sĭd), a. [L. flaccidus, fr. flaccus flabby: cf. OF. flaccide.] Yielding to pressure for want of firmness and stiffness; soft and weak; limber; lax; drooping; flabby; as, a flaccid muscle; flaccid flesh.

flaccidity.c: Flaccidity Flac*cid"i*ty (flăk*sĭd"ĭ*ty̆ or flăs*sĭd"ĭ*ty̆), n. [Cf. F. flaccidité.] The state of being flaccid.

flacherie.c: Flacherie ‖Flache`rie" (flȧsh`rē"), n. [F.] A bacterial disease of silkworms, supposed to be due to eating contaminated mulberry leaves.

flacker.c: Flacker Flack"er (?), v. i. [OE. flakeren, fr. flacken to move quickly to and fro; cf. icel. flakka to rove about, AS. flacor fluttering, flying, G. flackern to flare, flicker.] To flutter, as a bird. [Prov. Eng.] Grose.

flacket.c: Flacket Flack"et (?), n. [OF. flasquet little flask, dim. of flasque a flask.] A barrel-shaped bottle; a flagon.

flacon.c: Flacon ‖Fla"con (flȧ"kôn), n. [F. See Flagon.] A small glass bottle with a stopper; as, a flacon for perfume. “Two glass flacons for the ink.” Longfellow.

flag.c: Flag Flag (flăg), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flagged (flăgd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flagging (flăg"gĭng).] [Cf. Icel. flaka to droop, hang loosely. Cf. Flacker, Flag an ensign.] 1. To hang loose without stiffness; to bend down, as flexible bodies; to be loose, yielding, limp.
Flag Flag (flăg), v. t. 1. To let droop; to suffer to fall, or let fall, into feebleness; as, to flag the wings. prior.
Flag Flag, n. [Cf. LG. & G. flagge, Sw. flagg, Dan. flag, D. vlag. See Flag to hang loose.] 1. That which flags or hangs down loosely.
Flag Flag, v. t. [From Flag an ensign.] 1. To signal to with a flag or by waving the hand; as, to flag a train; also used with down; as, to flag down a cab.
Flag Flag, n. [From Flag to hang loose, to bend down.] (Bot.) An aquatic plant, with long, ensiform leaves, belonging to either of the genera Iris and Acorus.
Flag Flag, v. t. To furnish or deck out with flags.
Flag Flag, n. [Icel. flaga, cf. Icel. flag spot where a turf has been cut out, and E. flake layer, scale. Cf. Floe.] 1. A flat stone used for paving. Woodward.
Flag Flag, v. t. To lay with flags of flat stones.

flagellant.c: Flagellant Flag"el*lant (?), n. [L. flagellans, p. p. of flagellare: cf.F. flagellant. See Flagellate.] (Eccl. Hist.) One of a fanatical sect which flourished in Europe in the 13th and 14th centuries, and maintained that flagellation was of equal virtue with baptism and the sacrament; -- called also disciplinant.

flagellata.c: Flagellata ‖Flag`el*la"ta (?), n. pl. [NL., fr.L. flagellatus, p. p. See Flagellate, v. t.] (Zool.) An order of Infusoria, having one or two long, whiplike cilia, at the anterior end. It includes monads. See Infusoria, and Monad.

flagellate.c: Flagellate Flag"el*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flagellated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flagellating (?).] [L. flagellatus, p. p. of flagellare to scoure, fr. flagellum whip, dim. of flagrum whip, scoure; cf. fligere to strike. Cf. Flall.] To whip; to scourge; to flog.

flagellation.c: Flagellation Flag`el*la"tion (?), n. [L. flagellatio: cf. F. flagellation.] A beating or flogging; a whipping; a scourging. Garth.

flagellator.c: Flagellator Flag"el*la`tor (?), n. One who practices flagellation; one who whips or scourges.

flagelliform.c: Flagelliform Fla*gel"li*form (?), a. [L. flagellum a whip + -form.] Shaped like a whiplash; long, slender, round, flexible, and (comming) tapering.

flagellum.c: Flagellum ‖Fla*gel"lum (?), n.; pl. E. Flagellums (#), L. Flagella (#). [L., a whip. See Flagellate, v. t.] 1. (Bot.) A young, flexible shoot of a plant; esp., the long trailing branch of a vine, or a slender branch in certain mosses.

flageolet.c: Flageolet Flag"eo*let` (?), n. [F. flageolet, dim. of OF. flaj?l (as if fr. a LL. flautio;us), of flaüte, flahute, F. fl?te. See Flute.] (Mus.) A small wooden pipe, having six or more holes, and a mouthpiece inserted at one end. It produces a shrill sound, softer than of the piccolo flute, and is said to have superseded the old recorder.

flagginess.c: Flagginess Flag"gi*ness (?), n. The condition of being flaggy; laxity; limberness. Johnson.

flagging.c: Flagging Flag"ging (?), n. A pavement or sidewalk of flagstones; flagstones, collectively.
Flagging Flag"ging, a. Growing languid, weak, or spiritless; weakening; delaying. -- Flag"ging*ly, adv.

flaggy.c: Flaggy Flag"gy (?), a. 1. Weak; flexible; limber. “Flaggy wings.” Spenser.
Flaggy Flag"gy, a. [From 5th Flag.] Abounding with the plant called flag; as, a flaggy marsh.

flagitate.c: Flagitate Flag"i*tate (?), v. t. [L. flagitatus, p. p. of flagitare to demand. See Flagitious.] To importune; to demand fiercely or with passion. [Archaic] Carcyle.

flagitation.c: Flagitation Flag`i*ta"tion (?), n. [L. flagitatio.] Importunity; urgent demand. [Archaic] Carlyle.

flagitious.c: Flagitious Fla*gi"tious (?), a. [L. flagitiosus, fr. flagitium a shameful or disgraceful act, orig., a burning desire, heat of passion, from flagitare to demand hotly, fiercely; cf. flagrare to burn, E. flagrant.] 1. Disgracefully or shamefully criminal; grossly wicked; scandalous; shameful; -- said of acts, crimes, etc.

flagman.c: Flagman Flag"man (?), n.; pl. Flagmen (?). One who makes signals with a flag.

flagon.c: Flagon Flag"on (?), n. [F. flacon, for flascon, fr. OF. flasche, from LL. flasco. See Flask.] A vessel with a narrow mouth, used for holding and conveying liquors. It is generally larger than a bottle, and of leather or stoneware rather than of glass.

flagrancy.c: Flagrancy Fla"gran*cy (?), n.; pl. Flagrancies (#). [L. flagrantia a burning. See Flagrant.] 1. A burning; great heat; inflammation. [Obs.]

flagrant.c: Flagrant Fla"grant (?), a. [L. flagrans, -antis, p. pr. of flagrate to burn, akin to Gr.?: cf. F. flagrant. Cf. Flame, Phlox.] 1. Flaming; inflamed; glowing; burning; ardent.

flagrantly.c: Flagrantly Fla"grant*ly, adv. In a flagrant manner.

flagrate.c: Flagrate Fla"grate (?), v. t. [L. flagrare, flagratum, v.i. & t., to burn.] To burn. [Obs.] Greenhill.

flagship.c: Flagship Flag"ship` (?), n. (Naut.) The vessel which carries the commanding officer of a fleet or squadron and flies his distinctive flag or pennant.

flagstaff.c: Flagstaff Flag"staff` (?), n.; pl. -staves (?) or -staffs (?). A staff{4} on which a flag is hoisted.

flagstone.c: Flagstone Flag"stone` (?), n. A flat stone used in paving, or any rock which will split into such stones. See Flag, a stone.

flagworm.c: Flagworm Flag"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) A worm or grub found among flags and sedge.

flail.c: Flail Flail (?), n. [L. flagellum whip, scourge, in LL., a threshing flail: cf. OF. flael, flaiel, F. fléau. See Flagellum.] 1. An instrument for threshing or beating grain from the ear by hand, consisting of a wooden staff or handle, at the end of which a stouter and shorter pole or club, called a swipe, is so hung as to swing freely.

flaily.c: Flaily Flail"y (?), a. Acting like a flail. [Obs.] Vicars.

flain.c: Flain Flain (?), obs. p. p. of Flay. Chaucer.

flair.c: Flair Flair (flâr), n. [OE. flaireodor, fr. OF. & F. flair, fr. OF. flairier, F. flairer, to smell, LL. flagrare for L. fragrare. See Flagrant.] 1. Smell; odor. [Obs.]

flake.c: Flake Flake (flāk), n. [Cf. Icel. flaki, fleki, Dan. flage, D. vlaak.] 1. A paling; a hurdle. [prov. Eng.]

Flake Flake (flāk), n. [Cf. Icel. flakna to flake off, split, flagna to flake off, Sw. flaga flaw, flake, flake plate, Dan. flage snowflake. Cf. Flag a flat stone.] 1. A loose filmy mass or a thin chiplike layer of anything; a film; flock; lamina; layer; scale; as, a flake of snow, tallow, or fish. “Lottle flakes of scurf.” Addison.
Flake Flake (?), n. [Etym. uncertain; cf. 1st Fake.] A flat layer, or fake, of a coiled cable.
Flake Flake, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flaked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flaking.] To form into flakes. Pope.
Flake Flake, v. i. To separate in flakes; to peel or scale off.

flakiness.c: Flakiness Flak"i*ness (?), n. The state of being flaky.

flaky.c: Flaky Flak"y (?), a. 1. Consisting of flakes or of small, loose masses; lying, or cleaving off, in flakes or layers; flakelike.

flam.c: Flam Flam (flăm), n. [Cf. AS. fleám, flǣm, flight. √84. Cf. Flimflam.] A freak or whim; also, a falsehood; a lie; an illusory pretext; deception; delusion. [Obs.]
Flam Flam, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flammed; p. pr. & vb. n. Flamming.] To deceive with a falsehood. [Obs.]

flambe.c: Flambe ‖Flam`bé" (?), a. [F., p.p. of flamber to singe, pass (a thing) through flame. Cf. Flambeau.] 1. (Ceramics) Decorated by glaze splashed or irregularly spread upon the surface, or apparently applied at the top and allowed to run down the sides; -- said of pieces of Chinese porcelain.

flambeau.c: Flambeau Flam"beau (?); n.; pl. Flambeaux (#) or Flambeaus (#). [F., fr. OF. flambe flame, for flamble, from L. flammula a little flame, dim. of flamma flame. See Flame.] A flaming torch, esp. one made by combining together a number of thick wicks invested with a quick-burning substance (anciently, perhaps, wax; in modern times, pitch or the like); hence, any torch.

flamboyant.c: Flamboyant Flam*boy"ant (?), a. [F.] (Arch.) Characterized by waving or flamelike curves, as in the tracery of windows, etc.; -- said of the later (15th century) French Gothic style.

flamboyer.c: Flamboyer Flam*boy"er (?), n. [F. flamboyer to be bright.] (Bot.) A name given in the East and West Indies to certain trees with brilliant blossoms, probably species of Cæsalpinia.

flame.c: Flame Flame (flām), n. [OE. flame, flaume, flaumbe, OF. flame, flambe, F. flamme, fr. L. flamma, fr. flamma, fr. flagrare to burn. See Flagrant, and cf. Flamneau, Flamingo.] 1. A stream of burning vapor or gas, emitting light and heat; darting or streaming fire; a blaze; a fire.

Flame Flame, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flamed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flaming.] [OE. flamen, flaumben, F. flamber, OF. also, flamer. See Flame, n.] 1. To burn with a flame or blaze; to burn as gas emitted from bodies in combustion; to blaze.
Flame Flame, v. t. To kindle; to inflame; to excite.

flamecolored.c: Flame-colored Flame"-col`ored (?), a. Of the color of flame; of a bright orange yellow color. Shak.

flameless.c: Flameless Flame"less, a. Destitute of flame. Sandys.

flamen.c: Flamen Fla"men (?), n.; pl. E. Flammens (#), L. Flamines (#). [L.] (Rom. Antiq.) A priest devoted to the service of a particular god, from whom he received a distinguishing epithet. The most honored were those of Jupiter, Mars, and Quirinus, called respectively Flamen Dialis, Flamen Martialis, and Flamen Quirinalis.

flamineous.c: Flamineous Fla*min"e*ous (?), a. Pertaining to a flamen; flaminical.

flaming.c: Flaming Flam"ing (?), a. 1. Emitting flames; afire; blazing; consuming; illuminating.

flamingly.c: Flamingly Flam"ing*ly, adv. In a flaming manner.

flamingo.c: Flamingo Fla*min"go (?), n.; pl. Flamingoes (#). [Sp. flamenco, cf. Pg. flamingo, Prov. flammant, F. flamant; prop. a p. pr. meaning flaming. So called in allusion to its color. See Flame.] (Zool.) Any bird of the genus Phœnicopterus. The flamingoes have webbed feet, very long legs, and a beak bent down as if broken. Their color is usually red or pink. The American flamingo is P. ruber; the European is P. antiquorum.

flaminical.c: Flaminical Fla*min"i*cal (?), a. Pertaining to a flamen. Milton.

flammability.c: Flammability Flam`ma*bil"ity (?), n. The quality of being flammable; inflammability. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

flammation.c: Flammation Flam*ma"tion (?), n. The act of setting in a flame or blaze. [Obs.] Sir. T. Browne.

flammeous.c: Flammeous Flam"me*ous (?), a. [L. flammeus from flamma flame.] Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling, flame. [Obs.] Sir T. Browne.

flammiferous.c: Flammiferous Flam*mif"er*ous (?), a. [L. flammifer; flamma flame + ferre to bear.] Producing flame.

flammivomous.c: Flammivomous Flam*miv"o*mous (?), a. [L. flammivomus; flamma flame + vomere to vomit.] Vomiting flames, as a volcano. W. Thompson. (1745).

flammulated.c: Flammulated Flam"mu*la`ted (?), a. [L. flammula little flame, dim. fr. flamma flame.] Of a reddish color.

flamy.c: Flamy Flam"y (?), a. [From Flame.] Flaming; blazing; flamelike; flame-colored; composed of flame. Pope.

flanch.c: Flanch Flanch (?), n.; pl. Flanches (#). [Prov. E., a projection, OF. flanche flank. See Flank.] 1. A flange. [R.]. (Her.) A bearing consisting of a segment of a circle encroaching on the field from the side.

flanched.c: Flanched Flanched (?), a. (Her.) Having flanches; -- said of an escutcheon with those bearings.

flanconade.c: Flanconade Flan`co*nade" (?), n. [F.] (Fencing) A thrust in the side.

flanerie.c: Flanerie ‖flâ`ne*rie" (?), n. [F. flânerie. See Flaneur.] Lit., strolling; sauntering; hence, aimlessness; idleness; as, intellectual flânerie.

flaneur.c: flaneur ‖fla`neur" (?), n. [F., fr. flâner to stroll.] One who strolls about aimlessly; a lounger; a loafer.

flang.c: Flang Flang (?), n. A miner's two-pointed pick.

flange.c: Flange Flange (flănj), n. [Prov. E. flange to project, flanch a projection. See Flanch, Flank.] 1. An external or internal rib, or rim, for strength, as the flange of an iron beam; or for a guide, as the flange of a car wheel (see Car wheel.); or for attachment to another object, as the flange on the end of a pipe, steam cylinder, etc. Knight.
Flange Flange, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flanged (flănjd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flanging (flăn"jĭng).] (Mach.) To make a flange on; to furnish with a flange.
Flange Flange, v. i. To be bent into a flange.

flanged.c: Flanged Flanged (flănjd), a. Having a flange or flanges; as, a flanged wheel.

flank.c: Flank Flank (flăṉk), n. [F. flanc, prob. fr. L. flaccus flabby, with n inserted. Cf. Flaccid, Flanch, Flange.] 1. The fleshy or muscular part of the side of an animal, between the ribs and the hip. See Illust. of Beef.
Flank Flank (flăṉk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flanked (flăṉkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Flanking.] [Cf. F. flanquer. See Flank, n., and cf. Flanker, v. t.] 1. To stand at the flank or side of; to border upon.
Flank Flank, v. i. 1. To border; to touch. Bp. Butler.

flanker.c: Flanker Flank"er (?), n. One who, or that which, flanks, as a skirmisher or a body of troops sent out upon the flanks of an army toguard a line of march, or a fort projecting so as to command the side of an assailing body.
Flanker Flank"er, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flankered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flankering.] [See Flank, v. t.] 1. To defend by lateral fortifications. [Obs.] Sir T. Herbert.

flannel.c: Flannel Flan"nel (flăn"nĕl), n. [F. flanelle, cf. OF. flaine a pillowcase, a mattress (?); fr. W. gwlanen flannel, fr. gwlan wool; prob. akin to E. wool. Cf. Wool.] 1. A soft, nappy, woolen cloth, of loose texture. Shak.

Flannel flower Flan"nel flow`er. (Bot.) (a) The common mullein. (b) A Brazilian apocynaceous vine (Macrosiphonia longiflora) having woolly leaves. (c) An umbelliferous Australian flower (Actinotus helianthi), often erroneously thought to be composite. The involucre looks as if cut out of white flannel.

flanneled.c: Flanneled Flan"neled (?), a. Covered or wrapped in flannel.

flannen.c: Flannen Flan"nen (?), a. Made or consisting of flannel. [Obs.] “Flannen robes.” Dryden.

flap.c: Flap Flap (?), n. [OE. flappe, flap, blow, bly-flap; cf. D. flap, and E. flap, v.] Anything broad and limber that hangs loose, or that is attached by one side or end and is easily moved; as, the flap of a garment.
Flap Flap, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flapped (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flapping (?).] [Prob. of imitative origin; cf. D. flappen, E. flap, n., flop, flippant, fillip.] 1. To beat with a flap; to strike.
Flap Flap, v. i. 1. To move as do wings, or as something broad or loose; to fly with wings beating the air.

flapdragon.c: Flapdragon Flap"drag`on (?), n. 1. A game in which the players catch raisins out burning brandy, and swallow them blazing. Johnson.
Flapdragon Flap"drag`on, v. t. To swallow whole, as a flapdragon; to devour. [Obs.]

flapeared.c: Flap-eared Flap"-eared` (?), a. Having broad, loose, dependent ears. Shak.

flapjack.c: Flapjack Flap"jack` (flăp"jăk`), n. 1. A flat cake turned on the griddle while cooking; a griddlecake or pancake.

flapmouthed.c: Flap-mouthed Flap"-mouthed` (?), a. Having broad, hanging lips. [R.] Shak.

flapper.c: Flapper Flap"per (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, flaps.

flare.c: Flare Flare (flâr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flared (flârd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flaring.] [Cf. Norw. flara to blaze, flame, adorn with tinsel, dial. Sw. flasa upp, and E. flash, or flacker.] 1. To burn with an unsteady or waving flame; as, the candle flares.
Flare Flare, n. 1. An unsteady, broad, offensive light.
Flare Flare, n. Leaf of lard. “Pig's flare.” Dunglison.

flareup.c: Flare-up Flare"-up` (?), n. 1. A sudden burst of anger or passion; an angry dispute. [Colloq.]

flaring.c: Flaring Flar"ing (?), a. 1. That flares; flaming or blazing unsteadily; shining out with a dazzling light.

flaringly.c: Flaringly Flar"ing*ly, adv. In a flaring manner.

flash.c: Flash Flash (flăsh), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flashed (flăsht); p. pr. & vb. n. Flashing.] [Cf. OE. flaskien, vlaskien to pour, sprinkle, dial. Sw. flasa to blaze, E. flush, flare.] 1. To burst or break forth with a sudden and transient flood of flame and light; as, the lighting flashes vividly; the powder flashed.
Flash Flash (flăsh), v. t. 1. To send out in flashes; to cause to burst forth with sudden flame or light.
Flash Flash, n.; pl. Flashes (?). 1. A sudden burst of light; a flood of light instantaneously appearing and disappearing; a momentary blaze; as, a flash of lightning.
Flash Flash, a. 1. Showy, but counterfeit; cheap, pretentious, and vulgar; as, flash jewelry; flash finery.
Flash Flash, n. Slang or cant of thieves and prostitutes.
Flash Flash, n. [OE. flasche, flaske; cf. OF. flache, F. flaque.] 1. A pool. [Prov. Eng.] Haliwell.

Flash boiler Flash boiler. A variety of water-tube boiler, used chiefly in steam automobiles, consisting of a nest of strong tubes with very little water space, kept nearly red hot so that the water as it trickles drop by drop into the tubes is immediately flashed into steam and superheated.
Flash burner Flash burner. A gas burner with a device for lighting by an electric spark.

flashboard.c: Flashboard Flash"board` (?), n. A board placed temporarily upon a milldam, to raise the water in the pond above its usual level; a flushboard. [U.S.]

flasher.c: Flasher Flash"er (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, flashes.

flashily.c: Flashily Flash"i*ly (?), adv. In a flashy manner; with empty show.

flashiness.c: Flashiness Flash"i*ness, n. The quality of being flashy.

flashing.c: Flashing Flash"ing, n. 1. (Engineering) The creation of an artificial flood by the sudden letting in of a body of water; -- called also flushing.

flashy.c: Flashy Flash"y (?), a. 1. Dazzling for a moment; making a momentary show of brilliancy; transitorily bright.

flask.c: Flask Flask (flăsk or flȧsk), n. [AS. flasce, flaxe; akin to D. flesch, OHG. flasca, G. flasche, Icel. & Sw. flaska, Dan. flaske, OF. flasche, LL. flasca, flasco; of uncertain origin; cf. L. vasculum, dim. of vas a vessel, Gr. fla`skh, fla`skwn, fla`skion. Cf. Flagon, Flasket.] 1. A small bottle-shaped vessel for holding fluids; as, a flask of oil or wine.

flasket.c: Flasket Flask"et (?), n. [Cf. W. fflasged a vessel of straw or wickerwork, fflasg flask, basket, and E. flask.] 1. A long, shallow basket, with two handles. [Eng.]

flat.c: Flat Flat (flăt), a. [Compar. Flatter (flăt"rẽr); superl. Flattest (flăt"tĕst).] [Akin to Icel. flatr, Sw. flat, Dan. flad, OHG. flaz, and AS. flet floor, G. flötz stratum, layer.] 1. Having an even and horizontal surface, or nearly so, without prominences or depressions; level without inclination; plane.
Flat Flat (?), adv. 1. In a flat manner; directly; flatly.

Flat Flat, n. 1. A level surface, without elevation, relief, or prominences; an extended plain; specifically, in the United States, a level tract along the along the banks of a river; as, the Mohawk Flats.
Flat Flat (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flatted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flatting (?).] 1. To make flat; to flatten; to level.
Flat Flat, v. i. 1. To become flat, or flattened; to sink or fall to an even surface. Sir W. Temple.

flatbill.c: Flatbill Flat"bill` (?), n. (Zool.) Any bird of the genus Flatyrynchus. They belong to the family of flycatchers.

flatboat.c: Flatboat Flat"boat` (?), n. A boat with a flat bottom and square ends; -- used for the transportation of bulky freight, especially in shallow waters.

flatbottomed.c: flat-bottomed flat-bottom flat"-bot`tom flat"-bot`tomed (?), a. Having an even lower surface or bottom; as, a flat-bottomed boat.

flatcap.c: Flat-cap Flat"-cap` (?), n. A kind of low-crowned cap formerly worn by all classes in England, and continued in London after disuse elsewhere; -- hence, a citizen of London. Marston.

flatfish.c: Flatfish Flat"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) Any fish of the family Pleuronectidæ; esp., the winter flounder (Pleuronectes Americanus). The flatfishes have the body flattened, swim on the side, and have eyes on one side, as the flounder, turbot, and halibut. See Flounder.

flatfoot.c: flatfoot flat foot flat" foot`, flat"foot` (?). (Med.) A foot in which the arch of the instep is flattened so that the entire sole of the foot rests upon the ground; also, the deformity, usually congential, exhibited by such a foot; splayfoot.

flatfooted.c: Flat-footed Flat"-foot`ed, a. 1. Having a flat foot, with little or no arch of the instep; suffering from fallen arches. [wns=3]

flathead.c: Flathead Flat"head` (?), a. Characterized by flatness of head, especially that produced by artificial means, as a certain tribe of American Indians.
Flathead Flat"head`, n. (Ethnol.) A Chinook Indian. See Chinook, n., 1.

flatheaded.c: Flat-headed Flat"-head`ed (?), a. Having a head with a flattened top; as, a flat-headed nail.

flatiron.c: Flatiron Flat"i`ron (?), n. An iron with a flat, smooth surface for ironing clothes.

flative.c: Flative Fla"tive (?), a. [L. flare, flatum to blow.] Producing wind; flatulent. [Obs.] A. Brewer.

flatling.c: Flatling Flat"ling (?), adv. [Flat, a. + adverbial suff. -ling.] With the flat side, as of a sword; flatlong; in a prostrate position. [Obs.] Spenser.

flatlong.c: Flatlong Flat"long (?; 115), adv. With the flat side downward; not edgewise. Shak.

flatly.c: Flatly Flat"ly, adv. 1. In a flat manner; evenly; horizontally; without spirit; dully; frigidly.

flatness.c: flatness flat"ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being flat.

flatten.c: Flatten Flat"ten (flăt"t'n), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flattened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flattening.] [From Flat, a.] 1. To reduce to an even surface or one approaching evenness; to make flat; to level; to make plane.
Flatten Flat"ten, v. i. To become or grow flat, even, depressed, dull, vapid, spiritless, or depressed below pitch.

flatter.c: Flatter Flat"ter (flăt"tẽr), n. 1. One who, or that which, makes flat or flattens.

Flatter Flat"ter (flăt"tẽr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flattered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flattering.] [OE. flateren, cf. OD. flatteren; akin to G. flattern to flutter, Icel. flaðra to fawn, flatter: cf. F. flatter. Cf. Flitter, Flutter, Flattery.] 1. To treat with praise or blandishments; to gratify or attempt to gratify the self-love or vanity of, esp. by artful and interested commendation or attentions; to blandish; to cajole; to wheedle.
Flatter Flat"ter, v. i. To use flattery or insincere praise.

flattering.c: Flattering Flat"ter*ing, a. That flatters (in the various senses of the verb); as, a flattering speech.

flattery.c: Flattery Flat"ter*y (?), n.; pl. Flatteries (#). [OE. flaterie, OF. flaterie, F. flaterie, fr. flater to flatter, F. flatter; of uncertain origin. See Flatter, v. t.] The act or practice of flattering; the act of pleasing by artful commendation or compliments; adulation; false, insincere, or excessive praise.

flatting.c: Flatting Flat"ting (?), n. 1. The process or operation of making flat, as a cylinder of glass by opening it out.

flatulency.c: Flatulency Flatulence { Flat"u*lence (?), Flat"u*len*cy (?) }, n. [Cf. F. flatulence.] The state or quality of being flatulent.

flatulent.c: Flatulent Flat"u*lent (?), a. [L. flatus a blowing, flatus ventris windiness, flatulence, fr. flare to blow: cf. F. flatulent. See Blow.] 1. Affected with flatus{2} or gases generated in the alimentary canal; windy.

flatulently.c: Flatulently Flat"u*lent*ly, adv. In a flatulent manner; with flatulence.

flatuosity.c: Flatuosity Flat`u*os"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. flatuosité.] Flatulence. [Obs.] Bacon.

flatuous.c: Flatuous Flat"u*ous (?), a. [Cf. F. flatueux.] Windy; generating wind. [Obs.] Bacon.

flatus.c: Flatus ‖Fla"tus (?), n.; pl. E. Flatuses (#), L. Flatus. [L., fr. flare to blow.] 1. A breath; a puff of wind. Clarke.

flatwise.c: Flatwise Flat"wise` (?), a. or adv. With the flat side downward, or next to another object; not edgewise.

flatworm.c: Flatworm Flat"worm` (?), n. (Zool.) Any worm belonging to the Platyhelminthes; also, sometimes applied to the planarians.

flaunt.c: Flaunt Flaunt (flänt or flänt; 277), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flaunted; p. pr. & vb. n.. Flaunting.] [Cf. dial. G. flandern to flutter, wave; perh. akin to E. flatter, flutter.] To throw or spread out; to flutter; to move ostentatiously; as, a flaunting show.
Flaunt Flaunt, v. t. To display ostentatiously; to make an impudent show of. “If you've got it, flaunt it.”
Flaunt Flaunt, n. Anything displayed for show. [Obs.]

flauntingly.c: Flauntingly Flaunt"ing*ly, adv. In a flaunting way.

flautist.c: Flautist Flau"tist (?), n. [It. flauto a flute See Flute.] A player on the flute; a flutist.

flavaniline.c: Flavaniline Fla*van"i*line (? or?; 104), n. [L. flavus yellow + E. aniline.] (Chem.) A yellow, crystalline, organic dyestuff, C16H14N2, of artifical production. It is a strong base, and is a complex derivative of aniline and quinoline.

flavescent.c: Flavescent Fla*ves"cent (?), a. [L. flavescens, p. pr. of flavescere to turn yellow.] Turning yellow; yellowish.

flavicomous.c: Flavicomous Fla*vic"o*mous (?), a. [L. flavicomus; flavus yellow + coma hair.] Having yellow hair. [R.]

flavin.c: Flavin Fla"vin (?), n. [L. flavus yellow.] (Chem.) A yellow, vegetable dyestuff, resembling quercitron.

flavine.c: Flavine Fla"vine (?; 104), n. (Chem.) A yellow, crystalline, organic base, C13H12N2O, obtained artificially.

flavol.c: Flavol Fla"vol (?), n. [L. flavus yellow + -oil.] (Chem.) A yellow, crystalline substance, obtained from anthraquinone, and regarded as a hydroxyl derivative of it.

flavor.c: Flavor Fla"vor (?), n. [OF. fleur, flaur (two syllables), odor, cf. F. fleurer to emit an odor, It. flatore a bad odor, prob. fr. L. flare to bow, whence the sense of exhalation. Cf. Blow.] [Written also flavour.] 1. That quality of anything which affects the smell; odor; fragrances; as, the flavor of a rose.
Flavor Fla"vor, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flavored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flavoring.] To give flavor to; to add something (as salt or a spice) to, to give character or zest.

flavored.c: Flavored Fla"vored (?), a. Having a distinct flavor; as, high-flavored wine.

flavorless.c: flavorless fla"vor*less (?), a. Without flavor; tasteless. Opposite of flavorful.

flavorous.c: Flavorous Fla"vor*ous (?), a. Imparting flavor; pleasant to the taste or smell; sapid. Dryden.

flaw.c: Flaw Flaw (flä), n. [OE. flai, flaw flake; cf. Sw. flaga flaw, crack, breach, flake, D. vlaag gust of wind, Norw. flage, flaag, and E. flag a flat stone.] 1. A crack or breach; a gap or fissure; a defect of continuity or cohesion; as, a flaw in a knife or a vase.
Flaw Flaw, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flawed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flawing.] 1. To crack; to make flaws in.

flawless.c: Flawless Flaw"less, a. Free from flaws. Boyle.

flawn.c: Flawn Flawn (flän), n. [OF. flaon, F. flan, LL. flado, fr. OHG. flado, G. fladen, a sort of pancake; cf. Gr.? broad. See Place.] A sort of flat custard or pie. [Obs.] Tusser.

flawter.c: Flawter Flaw"ter (?), v. t. [Cf. Flay.] To scrape or pare, as a skin. [Obs.] Johnson.

flawy.c: Flawy Flaw"y (?), a. 1. Full of flaws or cracks; broken; defective; faulty. Johnson.

flax.c: Flax Flax (flăks), n. [AS. fleax; akin to D. vlas, OHG. flahs, G. flachs, and prob. to flechten to braid, plait,m twist, L. plectere to weave, plicare to fold, Gr.? to weave, plait. See Ply.] 1. (Bot.) A plant of the genus Linum, esp. the L. usitatissimum, which has a single, slender stalk, about a foot and a half high, with blue flowers. The fiber of the bark is used for making thread and cloth, called linen, cambric, lawn, lace, etc. Linseed oil is expressed from the seed.

flaxen.c: Flaxen Flax"en (?), a. Made of flax; resembling flax or its fibers; of the color of flax; of a light soft straw color; fair and flowing, like flax or tow; as, flaxen thread; flaxen hair.

flaxplant.c: Flax-plant Flax"-plant` (?), n. (Bot.) A plant in new Zealand (Phormium tenax), allied to the lilies and aloes. The leaves are two inches wide and several feet long, and furnish a fiber which is used for making ropes, mats, and coarse cloth.

flaxseed.c: Flaxseed Flax"seed` (?), n. The seed of the flax; linseed.

flaxy.c: Flaxy Flax"y (?), a. Like flax; flaxen. Sir M. Sandys.

flay.c: Flay Flay (flā), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flayed (flād); p. pr. & vb. n. Flaying.] [OE. flean, flan, AS. fleán; akin to D. vlaen, Icel. flā, Sw. flå, Dan. flaae, cf. Lith. pleszti to tear, plyszti, v.i., to burst, tear; perh. akin to E. flag a flat stone, flaw.] To skin; to strip off the skin or surface of; as, to flay an ox; to flay the green earth.

flayer.c: Flayer Flay"er (?), n. One who strips off the skin.

flea.c: Flea Flea (flē), v. t. [See Flay.] To flay. [Obs.]

Flea Flea, n. [OE. fle, flee, AS. fleá, fleáh; akin to D. vtoo, OHG. flōh, G. floh, Icel. flō, Russ. blocha; prob. from the root of E. flee. √84. See Flee.] (Zool.) An insect belonging to the genus Pulex, of the order Aphaniptera. Fleas are destitute of wings, but have the power of leaping energetically. The bite is poisonous to most persons. The human flea (Pulex irritans), abundant in Europe, is rare in America, where the dog flea (Ctenocephalides canis, formerly Pulex canis) and the smaller cat flea (Ctenocephalides felis) take its place. See Aphaniptera, and Dog flea. See Illustration in Appendix.

fleabane.c: Fleabane Flea"bane` (?), n. (Bot.) One of various plants, supposed to have efficacy in driving away fleas. They belong, for the most part, to the genera Conyza, Erigeron, and Pulicaria.

fleabeetle.c: Flea-beetle Flea"-bee`tle (?), n. (Zool.) A small beetle of the family Halticidæ, of many species. They have strong posterior legs and leap like fleas. The turnip flea-beetle (Phyllotreta vittata) and that of the grapevine (Graptodera chalybea) are common injurious species.

fleabite.c: Flea-bite Flea"-bite` (?), n. 1. The bite of a flea, or the red spot caused by the bite.

fleabitten.c: flea-bitten flea"-bit`ten (?), a. 1. Bitten by a flea; as, a flea-bitten face.

fleak.c: Fleak Fleak (flēk), n. A flake; a thread or twist. [Obs.]

fleaking.c: Fleaking Fleak"ing, n. A light covering of reeds, over which the main covering is laid, in thatching houses. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.

flealouse.c: Flea-louse Flea"-louse` (?), n. (Zool.) A jumping plant louse of the family Psyllidæ, of many species. That of the pear tree is Psylla pyri.

fleam.c: Fleam Fleam (?), n. [F. flamme, OF. flieme, fr. LL. flevotomum, phlebotomum; cf. D. vlijm. See Phlebotomy.] (Surg. & Far.) A sharp instrument used for opening veins, lancing gums, etc.; a kind of lancet.

fleamy.c: Fleamy Fleam"y (?), a. Bloody; clotted. [Obs. or Prov.]

flear.c: Flear Flear (?), v. t. & i. See Fleer.

fleawort.c: Fleawort Flea"wort` (?), n. (Bot.) An herb used in medicine (Plantago Psyllium), named from the shape of its seeds. Loudon.

fleche.c: Fleche ‖Flèche (?), n. [F. flèche, prop., an arrow.] (Fort.) A simple fieldwork, consisting of two faces forming a salient angle pointing outward and open at the gorge.

fleck.c: Fleck Fleck (?), n. A flake; also, a lock, as of wool. [Obs.] J. Martin.
Fleck Fleck (?), n. [Cf. Icel. flekkr; akin to Sw. fläck, D. vlek, G. fleck, and perh. to E. flitch.] A spot; a streak; a speckle. “A sunny fleck.” Longfellow.

Fleck Fleck, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flecked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flecking.] [Cf. Icel. flekka, Sw. fläcka, D. vlekken, vlakken, G. flecken. See Fleck, n.] To spot; to streak or stripe; to variegate; to dapple.

flecker.c: Flecker Fleck"er (?), v. t. To fleck. Johnson.

fleckless.c: Fleckless Fleck"less, a. Without spot or blame. [R.]

flection.c: Flection Flec"tion (?), n. [See Flexion.] 1. The act of bending, or state of being bent.

flectional.c: Flectional Flec"tion*al (?), a. Capable of, or pertaining to, flection or inflection.

fled.c: Fled Fled (?), imp. & p. p. of Flee.

fledge.c: Fledge Fledge (?), a. [OE. flegge, flygge; akin to D. vlug, G. flügge, flücke, OHG. flucchi, Icel. fleygr, and to E. fly. √84. See Fly, v. i.] Feathered; furnished with feathers or wings; able to fly.
Fledge Fledge, v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Fledged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fledging.] 1. To furnish with feathers; to supply with the feathers necessary for flight.

flee.c: Flee Flee (flē), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fled (flĕd); p. pr. & vb. n. Fleeing.] [OE. fleon, fleen, AS. fleón (imperf. fleáh); akin to D. vlieden, OHG. & OS. fliohan, G. fliehen, Icel. flȳja (imperf. flȳði), Dan. flye, Sw. fly (imperf. flydde), Goth. þliuhan. √84. Cf. Flight.] To run away, as from danger or evil; to avoid in an alarmed or cowardly manner; to hasten off; -- usually with from. This is sometimes omitted, making the verb transitive.

fleece.c: Fleece Fleece (flēs), n. [OE. flees, AS. fleós; akin to D. flies, vlies.] 1. The entire coat of wool that covers a sheep or other similar animal; also, the quantity shorn from a sheep, or animal, at one time.
Fleece Fleece, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fleeced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fleecing.] 1. To deprive of a fleece, or natural covering of wool.

fleeced.c: Fleeced Fleeced (?), a. 1. Furnished with a fleece; as, a sheep is well fleeced. Spenser.

fleecer.c: Fleecer Flee"cer (?), n. One who fleeces or strips unjustly, especially by trickery or fraund. Prynne.

fleecy.c: Fleecy Flee"cy (?), a. Covered with, made of, or resembling, a fleece. “Fleecy flocks.” Prior.

fleen.c: fleen fleen (flēn), n. pl. Obs. pl. of Flea. Chaucer.

fleer.c: fleer fle"er (flē"ẽr), n. One who flees. Ld. Berners.

fleer fleer (flēr), [imp. & p. p. fleered (flērd); p. pr. & vb. n. fleering.] [OE. flerien; cf. Scot. fleyr, Norw. flira to titter, giggle, laugh at nothing, MHG. vlerre, vlarre, a wide wound.] 1. To make a wry face in contempt, or to grin in scorn; to deride; to sneer; to mock; to gibe; as, to fleer and flout.
Fleer Fleer, v. t. To mock; to flout at. Beau. & Fl.
Fleer Fleer, n. 1. A word or look of derision or mockery.

fleerer.c: fleerer fleer"er (flēr"ẽr), n. One who fleers. Beau. & Fl.

fleeringly.c: fleeringly fleer"ing*ly, adv. In a fleering manner.

fleet.c: fleet fleet (flēt), v. i. [imp. & p. p. fleeted; p. pr. & vb. n. fleeting.] [OE. fleten, fleoten, to swim, AS. fleótan to swim, float; akin to D. vlieten to flow, OS. fliotan, OHG. fliozzan, G. fliessen, Icel. fljōta to float, flow, Sw. flyta, D. flyde, L. pluere to rain, Gr. plei^n to sail, swim, float, Skr. plu to swim, sail. √84. Cf. Fleet, n. & a., Float, Pluvial, Flow.] 1. To sail; to float. [Obs.]
Fleet Fleet, v. t. 1. To pass over rapidly; to skin the surface of; as, a ship that fleets the gulf. Spenser.
Fleet Fleet, a. [Compar. Fleeter (?); superl. Fleetest.] [Cf. Icel. fljōtr quick. See Fleet, v. i.] 1. Swift in motion; moving with velocity; light and quick in going from place to place; nimble.

Fleet Fleet, n. [OE. flete, fleote, AS. fleót ship, fr. fleótan to float, swim. See Fleet, v. i. and cf. Float.] A number of vessels in company, especially war vessels; also, the collective naval force of a country, etc.

Fleet Fleet, n. [AS. fleót a place where vessels float, bay, river; akin to D. vliet rill, brook, G. fliess. See Fleet, v. i.] 1. A flood; a creek or inlet; a bay or estuary; a river; -- obsolete, except as a place name, -- as Fleet Street in London.
Fleet Fleet (?), v. t. [AS. flēt cream, fr. fleótan to float. See Fleet, v. i.] To take the cream from; to skim. [Prov. Eng.] Johnson.

fleeten.c: Fleeten Fleet"en (?), n. Fleeted or skimmed milk. [Obs.]

fleetfoot.c: Fleet-foot Fleet"-foot` (?), a. Swift of foot. Shak.

fleeting.c: Fleeting Fleet"ing, a. Passing swiftly away; not durable; transient; transitory; as, the fleeting hours or moments.

fleetingly.c: Fleetingly Fleet"ing*ly, adv. In a fleeting manner; swiftly.

fleetings.c: Fleetings Fleet"ings (?), n. pl. A mixture of buttermilk and boiling whey; curds. [prov. Eng.] Wright.

fleetly.c: Fleetly Fleet"ly, adv. In a fleet manner; rapidly.

fleetness.c: Fleetness Fleet"ness, n. Swiftness; rapidity; velocity; celerity; speed; as, the fleetness of a horse or of time.

fleigh.c: Fleigh Fleigh (?), obs. imp. of Fly. Chaucer.

fleme.c: Fleme Fleme (?), v. t. [AS. flēman, flȳman.] To banish; to drive out; to expel. [Obs.] “Appetite flemeth discretion.” Chaucer.

flemer.c: Flemer Flem"er (?), n. One who, or that which, banishes or expels. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fleming.c: Fleming Flem"ing (?), n. A native or inhabitant of Flanders.

flemish.c: Flemish Flem"ish (?), a. Pertaining to Flanders, or the Flemings. -- n. The language or dialect spoken by the Flemings; also, collectively, the people of Flanders.

flench.c: Flench Flench (?), v. t. Same as Flence.

flense.c: Flense Flense (?), v. t. [Cf. Dan. flense, D. vlensen, vlenzen, Scot. flinch.] To strip the blubber or skin from, as from a whale, seal, etc.

flesh.c: Flesh Flesh (flĕsh), n. [OE. flesch, flesc, AS. flǣsc; akin to OFries. flāsk, D. vleesch, OS. flēsk, OHG. fleisc, G. fleisch, Icel. & Dan. flesk lard, bacon, pork, Sw. fläsk.] 1. The aggregate of the muscles, fat, and other tissues which cover the framework of bones in man and other animals; especially, the muscles.

Flesh Flesh, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fleshed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fleshing.] 1. To feed with flesh, as an incitement to further exertion; to initiate; -- from the practice of training hawks and dogs by feeding them with the first game they take, or other flesh. Hence, to use upon flesh (as a murderous weapon) so as to draw blood, especially for the first time.

fleshed.c: Fleshed Fleshed (?), a. 1. Corpulent; fat; having flesh.

fleshhood.c: Fleshhood Flesh"hood (?), n. The state or condition of having a form of flesh; incarnation. [R.]

fleshiness.c: Fleshiness Flesh"i*ness (?), n. The state of being fleshy; plumpness; corpulence; grossness. Milton.

fleshings.c: Fleshings Flesh"ings (?), n. pl. Flesh-colored tights, worn by actors and dancers. D. Jerrold.

fleshless.c: Fleshless Flesh"less, a. Destitute of flesh; lean. Carlyle.

fleshliness.c: Fleshliness Flesh"li*ness (?), n. The state of being fleshly; carnal passions and appetites. Spenser.

fleshling.c: Fleshling Flesh"ling (?), n. A person devoted to fleshly things. [Obs.] Spenser.

fleshly.c: Fleshly Flesh"ly (flĕsh"ly̆), a. [AS. flǣsclīc.] 1. Of or pertaining to the flesh; corporeal. “Fleshly bondage.” Denham.
Fleshly Flesh"ly, adv. In a fleshly manner; carnally; lasciviously. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fleshment.c: Fleshment Flesh"ment (?), n. The act of fleshing, or the excitement attending a successful beginning. [R.] Shak.

fleshmonger.c: Fleshmonger Flesh"mon`ger (?), n. [AS. flǣsc mangere.] One who deals in flesh; hence, a pimp; a procurer; a pander. [R.] Shak.

fleshpot.c: Fleshpot Flesh"pot` (?), n. 1. A pot or vessel in which flesh is cooked.

fleshquake.c: Fleshquake Flesh"quake` (?), n. A quaking or trembling of the flesh; a quiver. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

fleshy.c: Fleshy Flesh"y (?), a. [Compar. Fleshier (?); superl. Fleshiest (?).] 1. Full of, or composed of, flesh; plump; corpulent; fat; gross.

flet.c: Flet Flet (?), p. p. of Fleet. Skimmed. [Obs.]

fletch.c: Fletch Fletch (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fletched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fletching.] [F. flèche arrow.] To feather, as an arrow. Bp. Warburton.

fletcher.c: Fletcher Fletch"er (?), n. [OF. flechier.] One who fletches or feathers arrows; a manufacturer of bows and arrows. [Obs.] Mortimer.

flete.c: Flete Flete (?), v. i. [See Fleet, v. i.] To float; to swim. [Obs.] “Whether I sink or flete.” Chaucer.

fletiferous.c: Fletiferous Fle*tif"er*ous (?), a. [L. fletifer; fletus a weeping (from flere, fletum, to weep) + ferre to bear.] Producing tears. [Obs.] Blount.

fleurdelis.c: Fleur-de-lis ‖Fleur`-de-lis` (?), n.; pl. Fleurs-de-lis (#). [F., flower of the lily. Cf. Flower-de-luce, Lily.] 1. (Bot.) The iris. See Flower-de-luce.

fleuron.c: Fleuron ‖Fleu`ron" (?), n. [F., fr. OF. floron. Cf. Floroon.] A flower-shaped ornament, esp. one terminating an object or forming one of a series, as a knob of a cover to a dish, or a flower-shaped part in a necklace.

fleury.c: Fleury Fleur"y (?), a. [F. fleuri covered with flowers, p. p. of fleurir. See Flourish.] (Her.) Finished at the ends with fleurs-de-lis; -- said esp. of a cross so decorated.

flewed.c: Flewed Flewed (?), a. Having large flews. Shak.

flews.c: Flews Flews (?), n. pl. The pendulous or overhanging lateral parts of the upper lip of dogs, especially prominent in hounds; -- called also chaps. See Illust. of Bloodhound.

flex.c: Flex Flex (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flexed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flexing.] [L. flexus, p. p. of flectere to bend, perh. flectere and akin to falx sickle, E. falchion. Cf. Flinch.] To bend; as, to flex the arm.

flexanimous.c: Flexanimous Flex*an"i*mous (?), a. [L. flexanimus; flectere, flexum, to bend + animus mind.] Having power to change the mind. [Obs.] Howell.

flexibility.c: Flexibility Flex`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [L. flexibilitas: cf. F. flexibilite.] The state or quality of being flexible; flexibleness; pliancy; pliability; as, the flexibility of strips of hemlock, hickory, whalebone or metal, or of rays of light. Sir I. Newton.

flexible.c: Flexible Flex"i*ble (?), a. [L. flexibilis: cf. F. flexible.] 1. Capable of being flexed or bent; admitting of being turned, bowed, or twisted, without breaking; pliable; yielding to pressure; not stiff or brittle.

flexicostate.c: Flexicostate Flex`i*cos"tate (?), a. [L. flexus bent + E. costate.] (Anat.) Having bent or curved ribs.

flexile.c: Flexile Flex"ile (?), a. [L. flexilis.] Flexible; pliant; pliable; easily bent; plastic; tractable. Wordsworth.

flexion.c: Flexion Flex"ion (?), n. [L. flexio: cf. F. flexion.] 1. The act of flexing or bending; a turning.

flexor.c: Flexor Flex"or (?), n. [NL.] (Anat.) A muscle which bends or flexes any part; as, the flexors of the arm or the hand; -- opposed to extensor.

flexuous.c: Flexuous Flex"u*ous (?), a. [L. flexuosus, fr. flexus a bending, turning.] 1. Having turns, windings, or flexures.

flexural.c: Flexural Flex"u*ral (?), a. [From Flexure.] Of, pertaining to, or resulting from, flexure; of the nature of, or characterized by, flexure; as, flexural elasticity.

flexure.c: Flexure Flex"ure (?; 135), n. [L. flexura.] 1. The act of flexing or bending; a turning or curving; flexion; hence, obsequious bowing or bending.

flibbergib.c: Flibbergib Flib"ber*gib (?), n. A sycophant. [Obs. & Humorous.] “Flatterers and flibbergibs.” Latimer.

flibustier.c: Flibustier ‖Fli`bus`tier" (?), n. [F.] A buccaneer; an American pirate. See Filibuster. [Obs.]

flick.c: Flick Flick (flĭk), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flicked (flĭkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Flicking.] [Cf. Flicker.] 1. To whip lightly or with a quick jerk; to flap; as, to flick a horse; to flick the dirt from boots. Thackeray.
Flick Flick, n. A flitch; as, a flick of bacon.
Flick Flick, n. [See Flick, v. t.] 1. A light quick stroke or blow, esp. with something pliant; a flirt; also, the sound made by such a blow.

flicker.c: Flicker Flick"er (flĭk"ẽr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flickered (flĭk"ẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flickering.] [OE. flikeren, flekeren, to flutter, AS. flicerian, flicorian, cf. D. flikkeren to sparkle. √84. Cf. Flacker.] 1. To flutter; to flap the wings without flying.
Flicker Flick"er, n. 1. The act of wavering or of fluttering; fluctuation; sudden and brief increase of brightness; as, the last flicker of the dying flame.

flickeringly.c: Flickeringly Flick"ering*ly, adv. In a flickering manner.

flidge.c: Flidge Flidge, v. i. To become fledged; to fledge. [Obs.]

flier.c: Flier Fli"er (flī"ẽr), n. [Form Fly, v.; cf. Flyer] 1. One who flies or flees; a runaway; a fugitive. Shak.

flight.c: Flight Flight (flīt), n. [AS. fliht, flyht, a flying, fr. fleógan to fly; cf. flyht a fleeing, fr. fleón to flee, G. flucht a fleeing, Sw. flykt, G. flug a flying, Sw. flygt, D. vlugt a fleeing or flying, Dan. flugt. √84. See Flee, Fly.] 1. The act of flying; a passing through the air by the help of wings; volitation; mode or style of flying.

flighted.c: Flighted Flight"ed (?), a. 1. Taking flight; flying; -- used in composition. “Drowsy-flighted steeds.” Milton.

flighter.c: Flighter Flight"er (?), n. (Brewing) A horizontal vane revolving over the surface of wort in a cooler, to produce a circular current in the liquor. Knight.

flightily.c: Flightily Flight"i*ly (?), adv. In a flighty manner.

flightiness.c: Flightiness Flight"i*ness, n. The state or quality of being flighty.

flightshot.c: Flight-shot Flight"-shot` (?), n. The distance to which an arrow or flight may be shot; bowshot, -- about the fifth of a mile. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.]

flimflam.c: Flimflam Flim"flam (?), n. [Cf. Flam.] A freak; a trick; a lie. Beau. & Fl.

flimsily.c: Flimsily Flim"si*ly (?), adv. In a flimsy manner.

flimsiness.c: Flimsiness Flim"si*ness, n. The state or quality of being flimsy.

flimsy.c: Flimsy Flim"sy (?), a. [Compar. Flimsier (?); superl. Flimsiest.] [Cf. W. llymsi naked, bare, empty, sluggish, spiritless. Cf. Limsy.] Weak; feeble; limp; slight; vain; without strength or solidity; of loose and unsubstantial structure; without reason or plausibility; as, a flimsy argument, excuse, objection.
Flimsy Flim"sy, n. 1. Thin or transfer paper.

flinch.c: Flinch Flinch (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flinched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flinching.] [Prob. fr. OE. flecchen to waver, give way, F. fléchir, fr. L. flectere to bend; but prob. influenced by E. blench. Cf. Flex.] 1. To withdraw from any suffering or undertaking, from pain or danger; to fail in doing or perserving; to show signs of yielding or of suffering; to shrink; to wince; as, one of the parties flinched from the combat.
Flinch Flinch, n. The act of flinching.

flincher.c: Flincher Flinch"er (?), n. One who flinches or fails.

flinchingly.c: Flinchingly Flinch"ing*ly, adv. In a flinching manner.

flindermouse.c: Flindermouse Flin"der*mouse` (?), n.[OE. vlindre moth (cf. D. vlinder butterfly) + E. mouse. Cf. Flittermouse, Flinders.] (Zool.) A bat; a flittermouse.

flinders.c: Flinders Flin"ders (?), n. pl. [Scot. flenders, flendris; perh. akin to E. flutter; cf. D. flenters rags, broken pieces.] Small pieces or splinters; fragments.

fling.c: Fling Fling (flĭng), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flung (flŭng); p. pr. & vb. n. Flinging.] [OE. flingen, flengen, to rush, hurl; cf. Icel. flengia to whip, ride furiously, OSw. flenga to strike, Sw. flänga to romp, Dan. flenge to slash.] 1. To cast, send, to throw from the hand; to hurl; to dart; to emit with violence as if thrown from the hand; as, to fing a stone into the pond.
Fling Fling (?), v. i. 1. To throw; to wince; to flounce; as, the horse began to kick and fling.
Fling Fling, n. 1. A cast from the hand; a throw; also, a flounce; a kick; as, the fling of a horse.

flingdust.c: Flingdust Fling"dust` (?), n. One who kicks up the dust; a streetwalker; a low manner. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

flinger.c: Flinger Fling"er (?), n. One who flings; one who jeers.

flint.c: Flint Flint (?), n. [AS. flint, akin to Sw. flinta, Dan. flint; cf. OHG. flins flint, G. flinte gun (cf. E. flintlock), perh. akin to Gr.? brick. Cf. Plinth.] 1. (Min.) A massive, somewhat impure variety of quartz, in color usually of a gray to brown or nearly black, breaking with a conchoidal fracture and sharp edge. It is very hard, and strikes fire with steel.

Flint glass Flint" glass` (?). (Chem.) A soft, heavy, brilliant glass, consisting essentially of a silicate of lead and potassium. It is used for tableware, and for optical instruments, as prisms, its density giving a high degree of dispersive power; -- so called, because formerly the silica was obtained from pulverized flints. Called also crystal glass. Cf. Glass.

flintiness.c: Flintiness Flint"i*ness (?), n. The state or quality of being flinty; hardness; cruelty. Beau. & Fl.

flintlock.c: Flintlock Flint"lock` (?), n. 1. A lock for a gun or pistol, having a flint fixed in the hammer, which on striking the steel ignites the priming.

flintware.c: Flintware Flint"ware` (?), n. A superior kind of earthenware into whose composition flint enters largely. Knight.

flintwood.c: Flintwood Flint"wood` (?), n. (Bot.) An Australian name for the very hard wood of the Eucalyptus piluralis.

flinty.c: Flinty Flint"y (?), a. [Compar. Flintier (?); superl. Flintiest.] Consisting of, composed of, abounding in, or resembling, flint; as, a flinty rock; flinty ground; a flinty heart.

flip.c: Flip Flip (flĭp), n. [Cf. Prov. E. flip nimble, flippant, also, a slight blow. Cf. Flippant.] A mixture of beer, spirit, etc., stirred and heated by a hot iron.
Flip Flip, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flipped (flĭpt); p. pr. & vb. n. Flipping.] 1. To toss (an object) into the air so as make it turn over one or more times; to fillip; as, to flip up a cent.

flipe.c: Flipe Flipe (flīp), v. t. To turn inside out, or with the leg part back over the foot, as a stocking in pulling off or for putting on. [Scot.]

flipflap.c: Flip-flap Flip"-flap` (?), n. [See Flip, and Flap.] The repeated stroke of something long and loose. Johnson.
Flip-flap Flip"-flap`, adv. With repeated strokes and noise, as of something long and loose. Ash.

flippancy.c: Flippancy Flip"pan*cy (?), n.[See Flippant.] The state or quality of being flippant.

flippant.c: Flippant Flip"pant (?), a. [Prov. E. flip to move nimbly; cf. W. llipa soft, limber, pliant, or Icel. fleipa to babble, prattle. Cf. Flip, Fillip, Flap, Flipper.] 1. Of smooth, fluent, and rapid speech; speaking with ease and rapidity; having a voluble tongue; talkative.
Flippant Flip"pant, n. A flippant person. [R.] Tennyson.

flippantly.c: Flippantly Flip"pant*ly, adv. In a flippant manner.

flippantness.c: Flippantness Flip"pant*ness, n. State or quality of being flippant.

flipper.c: Flipper Flip"per (?), n. [Cf. Flip, Flippant.] 1. (Zool.) A broad flat limb used for swimming, as those of seals, sea turtles, whales, etc.

flirt.c: Flirt Flirt (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flirted; p. pr. & vb. n. Flirting.] [Cf. AS. fleard trifle, folly, fleardian to trifle.] 1. To throw with a jerk or quick effort; to fling suddenly; as, they flirt water in each other's faces; he flirted a glove, or a handkerchief.

Flirt Flirt, v. i. 1. To run and dart about; to act with giddiness, or from a desire to attract notice; especially, to play the coquette; to play at courtship; to coquet; as, they flirt with the young men.
Flirt Flirt, n. 1. A sudden jerk; a quick throw or cast; a darting motion; hence, a jeer.

flirtation.c: Flirtation Flir*ta"tion (?), n. 1. Playing at courtship; coquetry.

flirtgill.c: Flirt-gill Flirt"-gill` (?), n. A woman of light behavior; a gill-flirt. [Obs.] Shak.

flirtigig.c: Flirtigig Flirt"i*gig (?), n. A wanton, pert girl. [Obs.]

flirtingly.c: Flirtingly Flirt"ing*ly, adv. In a flirting manner.

flisk.c: Flisk Flisk (?), v. i. To frisk; to skip; to caper. [Obs. Scot.] “The flisking flies.” Gosson.
Flisk Flisk, n. A caper; a spring; a whim. [Scot.]

flit.c: Flit Flit (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flitted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flitting (?).] [OE. flitten, flutten, to carry away; cf. Icel. flytja, Sw. flytta, Dan. flytte. √84. Cf. Fleet, v. i.] 1. To move with celerity through the air; to fly away with a rapid motion; to dart along; to fleet; as, a bird flits away; a cloud flits along.
Flit Flit, a. Nimble; quick; swift. [Obs.] See Fleet.

flitch.c: Flitch Flitch (?), n.; pl. Flitches (#). [OE. flicche, flikke, AS. flicce, akin to Icel. flikki; cf. Icel. flīk flap, tatter; perh. akin to E. fleck. Cf. Flick, n.] 1. The side of a hog salted and cured; a side of bacon. Swift.
Flitch Flitch (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flitched (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flitching.] [See Flitch, n.] To cut into, or off in, flitches or strips; as, to flitch logs; to flitch bacon.

flite.c: Flite Flite (?), v. i. [AS. flītan to strive, contend, quarrel; akin to G. fleiss industry.] To scold; to quarrel. [Prov. Eng.] Grose.

flyte.c: Flyte Flite { Flite, Flyte } (?), n. [AS. flīt. See Flite.] Strife; dispute; abusive or upbraiding talk, as in fliting; wrangling. [Obs. or Scot. & Prov. Eng.]

flitter.c: Flitter Flit"ter (?), v. i. To flutter. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Flitter Flit"ter, v. t. To flutter; to move quickly; as, to flitter the cards. [R.] Lowell.
Flitter Flit"ter, n. [Cf. G. flitter spangle, tinsel, flittern to make a tremulous motion, to glitter. Cf. Flitter, v. i.] A rag; a tatter; a small piece or fragment.

flittermouse.c: Flittermouse Flit"ter*mouse` (?), n. [Flitter, v.i. + mouse; cf. G. fledermaus, OHG. fledarmūs. Cf. Flickermouse, Flindermouse.] (Zool.) A bat; -- called also flickermouse, flindermouse, and flintymouse.

flittern.c: Flittern Flit"tern (?), a. A term applied to the bark obtained from young oak trees. McElrath.

flittiness.c: Flittiness Flit"ti*ness (?), n. [From Flitty.] Unsteadiness; levity; lightness. [Obs.] Bp. Hopkins.

flitting.c: Flitting Flit"ting (?), n. 1. A flying with lightness and celerity; a fluttering.

flytting.c: Flytting Flitting { Flitt"ing, Flytt"ing } (?), n. Contention; strife; scolding; specif., a kind of metrical contest between two persons, popular in Scotland in the 16th century. [Obs. or Scot.]

flittingly.c: Flittingly Flit"ting*ly, adv. In a flitting manner.

flitty.c: Flitty Flit"ty (?), a. [From Flit.] Unstable; fluttering. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

flix.c: Flix Flix (?), n. [Cf. Flax.] Down; fur. [Obs. or Eng.] J. Dyer.
Flix Flix, n. The flux; dysentery. [Obs.] Udall.

flo.c: Flo Flo (flō), n.; pl. Flon (flōn). [AS. flā, flān.] An arrow. [Obs.] Chaucer.

float.c: Float Float (flōt), n.[OE. flote ship, boat, fleet, AS. flota ship, fr. fleótan to float; akin to D. vloot fleet, G. floss raft, Icel. floti float, raft, fleet, Sw. flotta. √ 84. See Fleet, v. i., and cf. Flotilla, Flotsam, Plover.] 1. Anything which floats or rests on the surface of a fluid, as to sustain weight, or to indicate the height of the liquid surface, or mark the place of, something.
