Specifically: (a) A mass of timber or boards fastened together, and conveyed down a stream by the current; a raft. (b) The hollow, metallic ball of a self-acting faucet, which floats upon the water in a cistern or boiler. (c) The cork or quill used in angling, to support the bait line, and indicate the bite of a fish. (d) Anything used to buoy up whatever is liable to sink; an inflated bag or pillow used by persons learning to swim; a life preserver. (e) The hollow, metallic ball which floats on the fuel in the fuel tank of a vehicle to indicate the level of the fuel surface, and thus the amount of fuel remaining. (f) A hollow elongated tank mounted under the wing of a seaplane which causes the plane to float when resting on the surface of the water.

Float Float, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Floated; p. pr. & vb. n. Floating.] [OE. flotien, flotten, AS. flotian to float, swim, fr. fleótan. See Float, n.] 1. To rest on the surface of any fluid; to swim; to be buoyed up.
Float Float, v. t. 1. To cause to float; to cause to rest or move on the surface of a fluid; as, the tide floated the ship into the harbor.

floatable.c: Floatable Float"a*ble (?), a. That may be floated.

floater.c: Floater Float"er (?), n. 1. One who floats or swims.

floating.c: Floating Float"ing, a. 1. Buoyed upon or in a fluid; a, the floating timbers of a wreck; floating motes in the air.
Floating Float"ing (?), n. 1. (Weaving) Floating threads. See Floating threads, above.

floatingly.c: Floatingly Float"ing*ly, adv. In a floating manner.

floaty.c: Floaty Float"y (?), a. Swimming on the surface; buoyant; light. Sir W. Raleigh.

flobert.c: Flobert Flo"bert (?), n. (Gun.) A small cartridge designed for target shooting; -- sometimes called ball cap.

floccillation.c: Floccillation Floc`cil*la"tion (?), n. [L. floccus a flock of wool. Cf. Flock of wool.] (Med.) A delirious picking of bedclothes by a sick person, as if to pick off flocks of wool; carphology; -- an alarming symptom in acute diseases. Dunglison.

floccose.c: Floccose Floc*cose" (?), a. [L. floccosus. Cf. 2d Flock, n.] 1. Spotted with small tufts like wool. Wright.

floccular.c: Floccular Floc"cu*lar (?), a. (Anat.) Of or pertaining to the flocculus.

flocculate.c: Flocculate Floc"cu*late (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flocculated; p. pr. & vb. n. Flocculating.] (Geol.) To aggregate into small lumps.
Flocculate Floc"cu*late (?), a. (Zool.) Furnished with tufts of curly hairs, as some insects.
Flocculate Floc"cu*late (?), v. t. To convert into floccules or flocculent aggregates; to make granular or crumbly; as, the flocculating of a soil improves its mechanical condition.

flocculation.c: Flocculation Floc`cu*la"tion (?), n. (Geol.) 1. The process by which small particles of fine soils and sediments aggregate into larger lumps.

floccule.c: Floccule Floc"cule (?), n. [See Flocculus.] 1. A detached mass of loosely fibrous structure like a shredded tuft of wool.

flocculence.c: Flocculence Floc"cu*lence (?), n. The state of being flocculent.

flocculent.c: Flocculent Floc"cu*lent (?), a. [See Flock of wool.] 1. Clothed with small flocks or flakes; woolly. Gray.

flocculus.c: Flocculus ‖Floc"cu*lus (?), n.; pl. Flocculi (#). [NL., dim. of L. floccus a lock or flock of wool.] (Anat.) A small lobe in the under surface of the cerebellum, near the middle peduncle; the subpeduncular lobe.

floccus.c: Floccus ‖Floc"cus (?), n.; pl. Flocci (#). [L., a flock of wool.] 1. (Zool.) (a) The tuft of hair terminating the tail of mammals. (b) A tuft of feathers on the head of young birds.

flock.c: Flock Flock (?), n. [AS. flocc flock, company; akin to Icel. flokkr crowd, Sw. flock, Dan. flok; prob. orig. used of flows, and akin to E. fly. See Fly.] 1. A company or collection of living creatures; -- especially applied to sheep and birds, rarely to persons or (except in the plural) to cattle and other large animals; as, a flock of ravenous fowl. Milton.
Flock Flock, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flocked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flocking.] To gather in companies or crowds.
Flock Flock, v. t. To flock to; to crowd. [Obs.]
Flock Flock, n. [OE. flokke; cf. D. vlok, G. flocke, OHG. floccho, Icel. flōki, perh. akin to E. flicker, flacker, or cf. L. floccus, F. floc.] 1. A lock of wool or hair.
Flock Flock, v. t. To coat with flock, as wall paper; to roughen the surface of (as glass) so as to give an appearance of being covered with fine flock.

flockly.c: Flockly Flock"ly, adv. In flocks; in crowds. [Obs.]

flockmel.c: Flockmel Flock"mel (?), adv. [AS. flocm?lum. See Meal part.] In a flock; in a body. [Obs.]

flocky.c: Flocky Flock"y, a. Abounding with flocks; floccose.

floe.c: Floe Floe (flō), n. [Cf. Dan. flag af iis, iisflage, Sw. flaga, flake, isflaga, isflake. See Flag a flat stone.] A low, flat mass of floating ice.

flog.c: Flog Flog (flŏg), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flogged (flŏgd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flogging (-gĭng).] [Cf. Scot. fleg blow, stroke, kick, AS. flocan to strike, or perh. fr. L. flagellare to whip. Cf. Flagellate.] To beat or strike with a rod or whip; to whip; to lash; to chastise with repeated blows.

flogging.c: Flogging Flog"ging (?), a. & n. from Flog, v. t.

flon.c: Flon Flon (?), n. pl. See Flo. [Obs.] Chaucer.

flong.c: Flong Flong (? or?), obs. imp. & p. p. of Fling.
Flong Flong (?), n. [Of the same origin as flawn, flan, a metal disk.] (Stereotyping) A compressed mass of paper sheets, forming a matrix or mold for stereotype plates.

flood.c: Flood Flood (flŭd), n. [OE. flod a flowing, stream, flood, AS. flōd; akin to D. vloed, OS. flōd, OHG. fluot, G. flut, Icel. flōð, Sw. & Dan. flod, Goth. flōdus; from the root of E. flow. √80. See Flow, v. i.] 1. A great flow of water; a body of moving water; the flowing stream, as of a river; especially, a body of water, rising, swelling, and overflowing land not usually thus covered; a deluge; a freshet; an inundation.
Flood Flood, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flooded; p. pr. & vb. n. Flooding.] 1. To overflow; to inundate; to deluge; as, the swollen river flooded the valley.

flooder.c: Flooder Flood"er (?), n. One who floods anything.

flooding.c: Flooding Flood"ing, n. The filling or covering with water or other fluid; overflow; inundation; the filling anything to excess.

flook.c: Flook Flook (flōok), n. A fluke of an anchor.

flukan.c: Flukan Flookan { Flook"an (?), Flu"kan (?) }, n. (Mining) See Flucan.

floor.c: Floor Floor (flōr), n. [AS. flōr; akin to D. vloer, G. flur field, floor, entrance hall, Icel. flōr floor of a cow stall, cf. Ir. & Gael. lar floor, ground, earth, W. llawr, perh. akin to L. planus level. Cf. Plain smooth.] 1. The bottom or lower part of any room; the part upon which we stand and upon which the movables in the room are supported.
Floor Floor, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Floored (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flooring.] 1. To cover with a floor; to furnish with a floor; as, to floor a house with pine boards.

floorer.c: Floorer Floor"er (?), n. Anything that floors or upsets a person, as a blow that knocks him down; a conclusive answer or retort; a task that exceeds one's abilities. [Colloq.]

floorheads.c: Floorheads Floor"heads`, n. pl. (Naut.) The upper extermities of the floor of a vessel.

flooring.c: Flooring Floor"ing, n. A platform; the bottom of a room; a floor; pavement. See Floor, n. Addison.

floorwalker.c: Floorwalker Floor"walk`er (?), n. One who walks about in a large retail store as an overseer and director. [U.S.]

flop.c: Flop Flop (flŏp), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flopped (flŏpt); p. pr. & vb. n. Flopping.] [A variant of flap.] 1. To clap or strike, as a bird its wings, a fish its tail, etc.; to flap.
Flop Flop (flŏp), v. i. 1. To strike about with something broad and flat, as a fish with its tail, or a bird with its wings; to rise and fall; as, the brim of a hat flops.
Flop Flop, n. Act of flopping. [Colloq.] W. H. Russell.

floppy.c: Floppy Flop"py (?), n. Having a tendency to flop or flap; as, a floppy hat brim. G. Eliot.

flora.c: Flora Flo"ra (?), n. [L., the goddess of flowers, from flos, floris, flower. See Flower.] 1. (Rom. Myth.) The goddess of flowers and spring.

floral.c: Floral Flo"ral (?), a. [L. Floralis belonging to Flora: cf. F. floral. See Flora.] 1. Pertaining to Flora, or to flowers; made of flowers; as, floral games, wreaths.

florally.c: Florally Flo"ral*ly, adv. In a floral manner.

floramour.c: Floramour Flo"ra*mour (?), n.[L. flos, floris, flower + amorlove.] The plant love-lies-bleeding. [Obs.] Prior.

floran.c: Floran Flo"ran (?), n. (Mining) Tin ore scarcely perceptible in the stone; tin ore stamped very fine. Pryce.

floreal.c: Floreal ‖Flo`réal" (?), n. [F. floréal, fr. L. flos, floris, flower.] The eight month of the French republican calendar. It began April 20, and ended May 19. See Vendémiare.

floren.c: Floren Flor"en (?), n. [LL. florenus. See Florin.] A cerain gold coin; a Florence. [Obs.] Chaucer.

florence.c: Florence Flor"ence (?), n. [From the city of Florence: cf. F. florence a kind of cloth, OF. florin.] 1. An ancient gold coin of the time of Edward III., of six shillings sterling value. Camden.

florentine.c: Florentine Flor"en*tine (? or?; 277), a. [L. Florentinus, fr. Florentia Florence: cf. F. florentin.] Belonging or relating to Florence, in Italy.
Florentine Flor"en*tine, n. 1. A native or inhabitant of Florence, a city in Italy.

florescence.c: Florescence Flo*res"cence (?), n. [See Florescent.] (Bot.) A bursting into flower; a blossoming. Martyn.

florescent.c: Florescent Flo*res"cent (?), a. [L. florescens, p. pr. of florescere begin to blossom, incho. fr. florere to blossom, fr. flos, floris, flower. See Flower.] Expanding into flowers; blossoming.

floret.c: Floret Flo"ret (?), n. [OF. florete, F. fleurette, dim. of OF. lor, F. fleur. See Flower, and cf. Floweret, 3d Ferret.] 1. (Bot.) A little flower; one of the numerous little flowers which compose the head or anthodium in such flowers as the daisy, thistle, and dandelion. Gray.

floriage.c: Floriage Flo"ri*age (?), n. [L. flos, floris, flower.] Bloom; blossom. [Obs.] J. Scott.

floriated.c: Floriated Flo"ri*a`ted (?), a. (Arch.) Having floral ornaments; as, floriated capitals of Gothic pillars.

floriation.c: Floriation Flo`ri*a"tion (?), n. 1. Ornamentation by means of flower forms, whether closely imitated or conventionalized.

floricomous.c: Floricomous Flo*ric"o*mous (?), a. [L. flos, floris, flower + coma hair.] Having the head adorned with flowers. [R.]

floricultural.c: Floricultural Flo`ri*cul"tur*al (? or?; 135), a. Pertaining to the cultivation of flowering plants.

floriculture.c: Floriculture Flo"ri*cul`ture (? or?; 135, 277), n. [L. flos, floris, flower + cultura culture.] The cultivation of flowering plants.

floriculturist.c: Floriculturist Flo`ri*cul"tur*ist (?), n. One skilled in the cultivation of flowers; a florist.

florid.c: Florid Flor"id (?), a. [L. floridus, fr. flos, floris, flower. See Flower.] 1. Covered with flowers; abounding in flowers; flowery. [R.]

florida.c: Florida bean Flor"i*da bean" (?). (Bot.) (a) The large, roundish, flattened seed of Mucuna urens. See under Bean. (b) One of the very large seeds of the Entada scandens.

florideae.c: Florideae ‖Flo*rid"e*æ (?), prop. n. pl. [NL., from L. flos, floris, a flower.] (Bot.) A subclass of algæ including all the red or purplish seaweeds; the Rhodospermeæ of many authors; -- so called from the rosy or florid color of most of the species.

floridity.c: Floridity Flo*rid"i*ty (?), n. The quality of being florid; floridness. Floyer.

floridly.c: Floridly Flor"id*ly (?), adv. In a florid manner.

floridness.c: Floridness Flor"id*ness, n. The quality of being florid. Boyle.

floriferous.c: Floriferous Flo*rif"er*ous (?), a. [L. florifer; flos, floris, flower + ferre to bear; cf. F. florifère.] Producing flowers. Blount.

florification.c: Florification Flo`ri*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. flos, floris, flower + facere to make.] The act, process, or time of flowering; florescence.

floriform.c: Floriform Flo"ri*form (? or?), a. [L. flos, floris, flower + -form: cf. F. floriforme.] Having the form of a flower; flower-shaped.

floriken.c: Floriken Flo"ri*ken (?), n. (Zool.) An Indian bustard (Otis aurita). The Bengal floriken is Sypheotides Bengalensis. [Written also florikan, florikin, florican.]

florilege.c: Florilege Flo"ri*lege (?), n. [L. florilegus flower-culling; flos, floris, flower + legere to gather: cf. F. florilège.] The act of gathering flowers.

florin.c: Florin Flor"in (?), n. [F. florin, It. florino, orig., a Florentine coin, with a lily on it, fr. flore a flower, fr. L. flos. See Flower, and cf. Floren.] A silver coin of Florence, first struck in the twelfth century, and noted for its beauty. The name is given to different coins in different countries. The florin of England, first minted in 1849, is worth two shillings, or about 48 cents; the florin of the Netherlands, about 40 cents; of Austria, about 36 cents.

florist.c: Florist Flo"rist (? or?; 277), n. [Cf. F. fleuriste, floriste, fr. F. fleur flower. See Flower.] 1. A cultivator of, or dealer in, flowers.

floroon.c: Floroon Flo*roon" (?), n. [F. fleuron. See Flower.] A border worked with flowers. Wright.

florulent.c: Florulent Flor"u*lent (?), a. [L. florulentus, fr. flos, floris, flower.] Flowery; blossoming. [Obs.] Blount.

floscularian.c: Floscularian Flos`cu*la"ri*an (?), n. [From L. flosculus a floweret.] (Zool.) One of a group of stalked rotifers, having ciliated tentacles around the lobed disk.

floscule.c: Floscule Flos*cule (?), n. [L. flosculus, dim. of flos flower: cf. F. floscule.] (Bot.) A floret.

flosculous.c: Flosculous Flos"cu*lous (?), a. (Bot.) Consisting of many gamopetalous florets.

flosferri.c: Flos-ferri ‖Flos`-fer"ri (?), n.[L., flower of iron.] (Min.) A variety of aragonite, occuring in delicate white coralloidal forms; -- common in beds of iron ore.

flosh.c: Flosh Flosh (?), n. [Cf. G. flösse a trough in which tin ore is washed.] (Metallurgy) A hopper-shaped box or?nortar in which ore is placed for the action of the stamps. Knight.

floss.c: Floss Floss (?; 195), n. [It. floscio flabby, soft, fr. L. fluxus flowing, loose, slack. See Flux, n.] 1. (Bot.) The slender styles of the pistillate flowers of maize; also called silk.
Floss Floss, n. [Cf. G. floss a float.] 1. A small stream of water. [Eng.]

flossification.c: Flossification Flos`si*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Cf. Florification.] A flowering; florification. [R.] Craig.

flossy.c: Flossy Floss"y (?; 115), a. Pertaining to, made of, or resembling, floss; hence, light; downy.

flota.c: Flota ‖Flo"ta (?), n. [Sp. See Flotilla.] A fleet; especially, a?eet of Spanish ships which formerly sailed every year from Cadiz to Vera Cruz, in Mexico, to transport to Spain the production of Spanish America.

flotage.c: Flotage Flo"tage (?), n. [OF. flotage, F. flottage, fr. flotter to float.] 1. The state of floating.

flotant.c: Flotant Flo"tant (?), a. [OF. flotant, F. flottant, p. pr. of flotter to float.] (Her.) Represented as flying or streaming in the air; as, a banner flotant.

flotation.c: Flotation Flo*ta"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. flottation a floating, flottaison water line, fr. flotter to float. See Flotilla.] 1. The act, process, or state of floating.

Flotation process Flotation process. A process of separating the substances contained in pulverized ore or the like by depositing the mixture on the surface of a flowing liquid, the substances that are quickly wet readily overcoming the surface tension of the liquid and sinking, the others flowing off in a film or slime on the surface, though, perhaps, having a greater specific gravity than those that sink.

flote.c: Flote Flote (?), v. t. To fleet; to skim. [Obs.] Tusser.
Flote Flote, n. [Cf. F. flot, L. fluctus; also cf. Float, n.] A wave. [Obs.] “The Mediterranean flote.” Shak.

flotilla.c: Flotilla Flo*til"la (?), n. [Sp. flotilla, dim. of flota fleet; akin to F. flotte, It. flotta, and F. flot wave, fr. L. fluctus, but prob. influenced by words akin to E. float. See Fluctuate, and cf. Float, n.] A little fleet, or a fleet of small vessels.

flotson.c: Flotson Flotsam { Flot"sam (?), Flot"son (?) }, n. [F. flotter to float. See FFlotilla, and cf. Jetsam.] (Law) Goods lost by shipwreck, and floating on the sea; -- in distinction from jetsam or jetson. Blackstone.

flotten.c: Flotten Flot"ten (?), p. p. of Flote, v. t. Skimmed. [Obs.]

flounce.c: Flounce Flounce (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flounced (flounst); p. pr. & vb. n. Flouncing (?).] [Cf. OSw. flunsa to immerge.] To throw the limbs and body one way and the other; to spring, turn, or twist with sudden effort or violence; to struggle, as a horse in mire; to flounder; to throw one's self with a jerk or spasm, often as in displeasure.
Flounce Flounce (?), n. The act of floucing; a sudden, jerking motion of the body.

Flounce Flounce, n. [Cf. G. flaus, flausch, a tuft of wool or hair; akin to vliess, E. fleece; or perh. corrupted fr. rounce.] An ornamental appendage to the skirt of a woman's dress, consisting of a strip gathered and sewed on by its upper edge around the skirt, and left hanging.
Flounce Flounce, v. t. To deck with a flounce or flounces; as, to flounce a petticoat or a frock.

flounder.c: Flounder Floun"der (?), n. [Cf. Sw. flundra; akin to Dan. flynder, Icel. fly?ra, G. flunder, and perh. to E. flounder, v.i.] 1. (Zool.) A flatfish of the family Pleuronectidæ, of many species.

Flounder Floun"der, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Floundered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Floundering.] [Cf. D. flodderen to flap, splash through mire, E. flounce, v.i., and flounder the fish.] To fling the limbs and body, as in making efforts to move; to struggle, as a horse in the mire, or as a fish on land; to roll, toss, and tumble; to flounce.
Flounder Floun"der, n. The act of floundering.

flour.c: Flour Flour (flour), n. [F. fleur de farine the flower (i.e., the best) of meal, cf. Sp. flor de la harina superfine flour, Icel. flür flower, flour. See Flower.] The finely ground meal of wheat, or of any other grain; especially, the finer part of meal separated by bolting; hence, the fine and soft powder of any substance; as, flour of emery; flour of mustard.
Flour Flour, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Floured (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flouring.] 1. To grind and bolt; to convert into flour; as, to flour wheat.

floured.c: Floured Floured (?), p. a. Finely granulated; -- said of quicksilver which has been granulated by agitation during the amalgamation process. Raymond.

flourish.c: Flourish Flour"ish (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flourished (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flourishing.] [OE. florisshen, flurisshen, OF. flurir, F. fleurir, fr. L. florere to bloom, fr. flos, floris, flower. See Flower, and -ish.] 1. To grow luxuriantly; to increase and enlarge, as a healthy growing plant; a thrive.
Flourish Flour"ish, v. t. 1. To adorn with flowers orbeautiful figures, either natural or artificial; to ornament with anything showy; to embellish. [Obs.] Fenton.
Flourish Flour"ish (?), n.; pl. Flourishes (?). 1. A flourishing condition; prosperity; vigor. [Archaic]

flourishingly.c: Flourishingly Flour"ish*ing*ly, adv. In a flourishing manner; ostentatiously.

floury.c: Floury Flour"y (?), a. Of or resembling flour; mealy; covered with flour. Dickens.

flout.c: Flout Flout (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flouted; p. pr. & vb. n. Flouting.] [OD. fluyten to play the flute, to jeer, D. fluiten, fr. fluit, fr. French. See Flute.] To mock or insult; to treat with contempt.
Flout Flout, v. i. To practice mocking; to behave with contempt; to sneer; to fleer; -- often with at.
Flout Flout, n. A mock; an insult.

flouter.c: Flouter Flout"er (?), n. One who flouts; a mocker.

floutingly.c: Floutingly Flout"ing*ly, adv. With flouting; insultingly; as, to treat a lover floutingly.

flow.c: Flow Flow (flō), obs. imp. sing. of Fly, v. i. Chaucer.

Flow Flow (flō), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flowed (flōd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flowing.] [AS. flōwan; akin to D. vloeijen, OHG. flawen to wash, Icel. flōa to deluge, Gr. plw`ein to float, sail, and prob. ultimately to E. float, fleet. √80. Cf. Flood.] 1. To move with a continual change of place among the particles or parts, as a fluid; to change place or circulate, as a liquid; as, rivers flow from springs and lakes; tears flow from the eyes.
Flow Flow, v. t. 1. To cover with water or other liquid; to overflow; to inundate; to flood.
Flow Flow, n. 1. A stream of water or other fluid; a current; as, a flow of water; a flow of blood.

flowage.c: Flowage Flow"age (?; 48), n. An overflowing with water; also, the water which thus overflows.

flowen.c: Flowen Flow"en (?), obs. imp. pl. of Fly, v. i. Chaucer.

flower.c: Flower Flow"er (flou"ẽr), n. [OE. flour, OF. flour, flur, flor, F. fleur, fr. L. flos, floris. Cf. Blossom, Effloresce, Floret, Florid, Florin, Flour, Flourish.] 1. In the popular sense, the bloom or blossom of a plant; the showy portion, usually of a different color, shape, and texture from the foliage.

Flower Flow"er (flou"ẽr), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flowered (flou"ẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Flowering.] [From the noun. Cf. Flourish.] 1. To blossom; to bloom; to expand the petals, as a plant; to produce flowers; as, this plant flowers in June.
Flower Flow"er, v. t. To embellish with flowers; to adorn with imitated flowers; as, flowered silk.
Flower State Flow"er State. Florida; -- a nickname, alluding to sense of L. floridus, from florida flowery. See Florid.

flowerage.c: Flowerage Flow"er*age (?; 48), n. State of flowers; flowers, collectively or in general. Tennyson.

flowerdeluce.c: Flower-de-luce Flow"er-de-luce" (?), n. [Corrupted fr. fleur-de-lis.] (Bot.) A genus of perennial herbs (Iris) with swordlike leaves and large three-petaled flowers often of very gay colors, but probably white in the plant first chosen for the royal French emblem.

flowerer.c: Flowerer Flow"er*er (?), n. A plant which flowers or blossoms.

floweret.c: Floweret Flow"er*et (?), n. A small flower; a floret. Shak.

flowerfence.c: Flower-fence Flow"er-fence` (?), n. (Bot.) A tropical leguminous bush (Poinciana pulcherrima, or Cæsalpinia, pulcherrima) with prickly branches, and showy yellow or red flowers; -- so named from its having been sometimes used for hedges in the West Indies. Baird.

flowerful.c: Flowerful Flow"er*ful (?), a. Abounding with flowers. Craig.

flowergentle.c: Flower-gentle Flow"er-gen`tle (?), n. (Bot.) A species of amaranth (Amarantus melancholicus).

floweriness.c: Floweriness Flow"er*i*ness (?), n. The state of being flowery.

flowering.c: Flowering Flow"er*ing, a. (Bot.) Having conspicuous flowers; -- used as an epithet with many names of plants; as, flowering ash; flowering dogwood; flowering almond, etc.
Flowering Flow"er*ing, n. 1. The act of blossoming, or the season when plants blossom; florification.

flowerlessness.c: Flowerlessness Flow"er*less*ness, n. State of being without flowers.

flowerpot.c: Flowerpot Flow"er*pot` (?), n. A vessel, commonly or earthenware, for earth in which plants are grown.

flowery.c: Flowery Flow"er*y (?), a. 1. Full of flowers; abounding with blossoms.

flowerykirtled.c: Flowery-kirtled Flow"er*y-kir`tled (?), a. Dressed with garlands of flowers. [Poetic & Rare] Milton.

flowing.c: Flowing Flow"ing, a. That flows or for flowing (in various sense of the verb); gliding along smoothly; copious.
Flowing Flow"ing (?), a. & n. from Flow, v. i. & t.

flowingly.c: Flowingly Flow"ing*ly, adv. In a flowing manner.

flowingness.c: Flowingness Flow"ing*ness, n. Flowing tendency or quality; fluency. [R.] W. Nichols.

flown.c: Flown Flown (?), p. p. of Fly; -- often used with the auxiliary verb to be; as, the birds are flown.

floxed.c: Floxed silk Floxed" silk` (?). See Floss silk, under Floss.

floyte.c: Floyte Floyte (?), n. & v. A variant of Flute. [Obs.]

fluate.c: Fluate Flu"ate (?), n. [Cf. F. fluate. See Fluor.] (Chem.) A fluoride. [Obs.]

fluavil.c: Fluavil Flu"a*vil (?), n. [Etymol. uncertain.] (Chem.) A hydrocarbon extracted from gutta-percha, as a yellow, resinous substance; -- called also fluanil.

flucan.c: Flucan Flu"can (?), n. (Mining) Soft clayey matter in the vein, or surrounding it. [Written also flookan, flukan, and fluccan.]

fluctiferous.c: Fluctiferous Fluc*tif"er*ous (?), a. [L. fluctus wave + -ferous.] Tending to produce waves. Blount.

fluctisonous.c: Fluctisonous Fluc*tis"o*nous (?), a. [L. fluctisonus; fluctus wave + sonus sound.] Sounding like waves.

fluctuability.c: Fluctuability Fluc`tu*a*bil"i*ty (?; 135), n. The capacity or ability to fluctuate. [R.] H. Walpole.

fluctuant.c: Fluctuant Fluc"tu*ant (?; 135), a. [L. fluctuans, p. pr. of fluctuare. See Fluctuate.] 1. Moving like a wave; wavering; (Med.) showing undulation or fluctuation; as, a fluctuant tumor.

fluctuate.c: Fluctuate Fluc"tu*ate (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fluctuated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fluctuating (?).] [L. fluctuatus, p. p. of fluctuare, to wave, fr. fluctus wave, fr. fluere, fluctum, to flow. See Fluent, and cf. Flotilla.] 1. To move as a wave; to roll hither and thither; to wave; to float backward and forward, as on waves; as, a fluctuating field of air. Blackmore.
Fluctuate Fluc"tu*ate, v. t. To cause to move as a wave; to put in motion. [R.]

fluctuation.c: Fluctuation Fluc`tu*a"tion (?), n. [L. fluctuatio; cf. F. fluctuation.] 1. A motion like that of waves; a moving in this and that direction; as, the fluctuations of the sea.

flue.c: Flue Flue (flū), n. [Cf. OF. flue a flowing, fr. fluer to flow, fr. L. fluere (cf. Fluent); a perh. a corruption of E. flute.] 1. An inclosed passage way for establishing and directing a current of air, gases, etc.; an air passage; esp.: (a) A compartment or division of a chimney for conveying flame and smoke to the outer air. (b) A passage way for conducting a current of fresh, foul, or heated air from one place to another. (c) (Steam Boiler) A pipe or passage for conveying flame and hot gases through surrounding water in a boiler; -- distinguished from a tube which holds water and is surrounded by fire. Small flues are called fire tubes or simply tubes.
Flue Flue (flū), n. [Cf. F. flou light, tender, G. flau weak, W. llwch dust. √84.] Light down, such as rises from cotton, fur, etc.; very fine lint or hair. Dickens.

Flue pipe Flue pipe. (Music) A pipe, esp. an organ pipe, whose tone is produced by the impinging of a current of air upon an edge, or lip, causing a wave motion in the air within; a mouth pipe; -- distinguished from reed pipe. Flue pipes are either open or closed (stopped at the distant end). The flute and flageolet are open pipes; a bottle acts as a closed pipe when one blows across the neck. The organ has both open and closed flue pipes, those of metal being usually round in section, and those of wood triangular or square.

fluency.c: Fluency Flu"en*cy (?), n. [L. fluentia: cf. F. fluence. See Fluent.] The quality of being fluent; smoothness; readiness of utterance; volubility.

fluent.c: Fluent Flu"ent (?), a. [L. fluens, -entis, p. pr. of fluere to flow; cf. Gr.? to boil over. Cf. Fluctuate, Flux.] 1. Flowing or capable of flowing; liquid; glodding; easily moving.
Fluent Flu"ent, n. 1. A current of water; a stream. [Obs.]

fluently.c: Fluently Flu"ent*ly, adv. In a fluent manner.

fluentness.c: Fluentness Flu"ent*ness, n. The quality of being fluent.

fluework.c: Fluework Flue"work` (?), n. (Mus.) A general name for organ stops in which the sound is caused by wind passing through a flue or fissure and striking an edge above; -- in distinction from reedwork.

fluff.c: Fluff Fluff (?), n. [Cf. 2d Flue. √84.] 1. Nap or down; flue[2]; soft, downy feathers.
Fluff Fluff (?), v. t. & i. To make or become fluffy; to move lightly like fluff. Holmes.

fluffy.c: Fluffy Fluff"y (?), a. [Compar. Fluffier (?); superl. Fluffiest.] Pertaining to, or resembling, fluff or nap; soft and downy. “The carpets were fluffy.” Thackeray.

fluegel.c: Fluegel Flugel ‖Flü"gel (?), n. [G., a wing.] (Mus.) 1. A grand piano or a harpsichord, both being wing-shaped. [archaic]

flugelman.c: Flugelman Flu"gel*man (?), n. [G. flügelman.] (Mil.) Same as Fugleman.

fluid.c: Fluid Flu"id (flū"ĭd), a. [L. fluidus, fr. fluere to flow: cf. F. fluide. See Fluent.] Having particles which easily move and change their relative position without a separation of the mass, and which easily yield to pressure; capable of flowing; liquid or gaseous.
Fluid Flu"id, n. A fluid substance; a body whose particles move easily among themselves.

fluidal.c: Fluidal Flu"id*al (?), a. Pertaining to a fluid, or to its flowing motion.

fluidity.c: Fluidity Flu*id"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. fluidité.] The quality of being fluid or capable of flowing; a liquid, aëriform, or gaseous state; -- opposed to solidity.

fluidize.c: Fluidize Flu"id*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fluidized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fluidizing.] To render fluid.

fluidness.c: Fluidness Flu"id*ness, n. The state of being fluid; fluidity.

fluidounce.c: Fluidounce Flu"id*ounce`, n. See Fluid ounce, under Fluid.

fluidrachm.c: Fluidrachm Flu"i*drachm` (?), n. See Fluid dram, under Fluid. Pharm. of the U. S.

fluke.c: Fluke Fluke (flūk or flōok), n. [Cf. AS. flōc a kind of flatfish, Icel. flōki a kind of halibut.] 1. (Zool.) The European flounder. See Flounder. [Written also fleuk, flook, and flowk.]
Fluke Fluke (flūk), n. [Cf. LG. flunk, flunka wing, the palm of an anchor; perh. akin to E. fly.] 1. The part of an anchor which fastens in the ground; a flook. See Anchor.
Fluke Fluke (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Fluked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fluking (?).] To get or score by a fluke; as, to fluke a play in billiards. [Slang]

fluky.c: Fluky Fluk"y (?), a. Formed like, or having, a fluke.

flume.c: Flume Flume (f;ūm), n. [Cf. OE. flum river, OF, flum, fr. L. flumen, fr. fluere to flow. √84. See Fluent.] A stream; especially, a passage channel, or conduit for the water that drives a mill wheel; or an artifical channel of water for hydraulic or placer mining; also, a chute for conveying logs or lumber down a declivity.

fluminous.c: Fluminous Flu"mi*nous (?), a. [L. flumen, fluminis, river.] Pertaining to rivers; abounding in streama.

flummery.c: Flummery Flum"mer*y (?), n. [W. llumru, or llumruwd, a kind of food made of oatmeal steeped in water until it has turned sour, fr. llumrig harsh, raw, crude, fr. llum sharp, severe.] 1. A light kind of food, formerly made of flour or meal; a sort of pap.

flung.c: Flung Flung (?), imp. & p. p. of Fling.

flunk.c: Flunk Flunk (flŭṉk), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flunked (flŭṉkt); p. pr. & vb. n. Flunking.] [Cf. Funk.] To fail, as on a lesson; to back out, as from an undertaking, through fear.
Flunk Flunk, v. t. 1. To fail in; to fail to pass (a test, examination, or course of study). [Colloq. U.S.]
Flunk Flunk, n. A failure or backing out; specifically (College cant), a total failure in a recitation. [U.S.]

flunky.c: Flunky Flun"ky (flŭṉ"ky̆), n.; pl. Flunkies (flŭṉ"kĭz). [Prob. fr. or akin to flank.] [Written also flunkey.] 1. A contemptuous name for a liveried servant or a footman.

flunkydom.c: Flunkydom Flun"ky*dom (?), n. The place or region of flunkies. C. Kingsley.

flunlyism.c: Flunlyism Flun"ly*ism (?), n. The quality or characteristics of a flunky; readiness to cringe to those who are superior in wealth or position; toadyism. Thackeray.

fluo.c: Fluo- Flu"o- (?). (Chem.) A combining form indicating fluorine as an ingredient; as in fluosilicate, fluobenzene.

fluoborate.c: Fluoborate Flu`o*bo"rate (?), n. [Cf. F. fluoborate.] (Chem.) A salt of fluoboric acid; a fluoboride.

fluoboric.c: Fluoboric Flu`o*bo"ric (?), a. [Fluo- boric: cf. F. fluoborique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, derived from, or consisting of, fluorine and boron.

fluocerite.c: Fluocerite Fluocerine { Flu`o*ce"rine (?), Flu`o*ce"rite (?) }, n. [Fluo- + cerium.] (Min.) A fluoride of cerium, occuring near Fahlun in Sweden. Tynosite, from Colorado, is probably the same mineral.

fluophosphate.c: Fluophosphate Flu`o*phos"phate (?), n. [Fluo- + phosphate.] (Chem.) A double salt of fluoric and phosphoric acids.

fluor.c: Fluor ‖Flu"or (?), n. [L., a flowing, fr. fluere to flow. See Fluent.] 1. A fluid state. [Obs.] Sir I. Newton.
Fluor albus ‖Flu"or albus (?). [L., white flow.] (Med.) The whites; leucorrhæa.

fluoranthene.c: Fluoranthene Flu`or*an"thene (?), n. [Fluorene + anthracene.] (Chem.) A white crystalline hydrocarbon C15H10, of a complex structure, found as one ingredient of the higher boiling portion of coal tar.

fluorated.c: Fluorated Flu"or*a`ted (?), a. (Chem.) Combined with fluorine; subjected to the action of fluoride. [R.]

fluorene.c: Fluorene Flu`or*ene (?), n. (Chem.) A colorless, crystalline hydrocarbon, C13H10 having a beautiful violet fluorescence; whence its name. It occurs in the higher boiling products of coal tar, and is obtained artificially.

fluorescein.c: fluorescein fluoresceine fluo`res"ce*in, fluo`res"ce*ine, flu`o*res"ce*ïn (?), n. (Chem.) A yellowish red, crystalline substance, C20H12O5, produced by heating together phthalic anhydride and resorcin; -- so called, from the very brilliant yellowish green fluorescence of its alkaline solutions. It has acid properties, and its salts of the alkalies are known to the trade under the name of uranin.

fluorescence.c: Fluorescence Flu`o*res"cence (?), n. [From Fluor.] (Chemistry, Optics) A luminescence emitted by certain substances due to the absorption of radiation at one wavelength, and the almost instantaneous re-emission of radiation at another, usually longer wavelength. The re-radiation stops almost as soon as the incident radiation is halted, thus distinguishing this phenomenon from phosphorescence, in which re-radiation of light may continue for some time after the incident radiation is halted.

fluorescent.c: Fluorescent Flu`o*res"cent (?), a. Having the property of fluorescence.

fluorescin.c: Fluorescin Flu`o*res"cin (?), n. (Chem.) A colorless, amorphous substance which is produced by the reduction of fluoresceïn, and from which the latter may be formed by oxidation.

fluoric.c: Fluoric Flu*or"ic (?), a. [Cf. F. fluorique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, obtained from, or containing, fluorine.

fluoride.c: Fluoride Flu"or*ide (? or?; 104), n. [Cf. F. fluoride.] (Chem.) A binary compound of fluorine with another element or radical.

fluorine.c: Fluorine Flu"or*ine (flū"ŏr*ĭn or flū"ŏr*ēn; 104), n. [NL. fluorina: cf. G. fluorin, F. fluorine. So called from its occurrence in the mineral fluorite.] (Chem.) A non-metallic, gaseous element of atomic number 9, strongly acid or negative, and associated with chlorine, bromine, and iodine, in the halogen group of which it is the first member. It always occurs combined, is very active chemically, and possesses such an avidity for most elements, and silicon especially, that it can neither be prepared nor kept in glass vessels, but may be contained in lead vessels. If set free it immediately attacks a containing glass vessel, so that it was not isolated until 1886. It is a pungent, corrosive, colorless gas. Symbol F. Atomic weight 19.00.

fluorite.c: Fluorite Flu"or*ite (?), n. (Min.) Calcium fluoride (CaF2), a mineral of many different colors, white, yellow, purple, green, red, etc., often very beautiful, crystallizing commonly in cubes with perfect octahedral cleavage; also massive. It is used as a flux. Some varieties are used for ornamental vessels. Also called fluor spar, or simply fluor.

fluoroid.c: Fluoroid Flu"or*oid (?), n. [Fluor + -oid.] (Crystallog.) A tetrahexahedron; -- so called because it is a common form of fluorite.

fluoroscope.c: Fluoroscope Flu*or"o*scope (?), n. [Fluorescence + -scope.] 1. (Phys.) An instrument for observing or exhibiting fluorescence.

fluoroscopy.c: Fluoroscopy Flu`or*os"co*py (?), n. Examination of an object, as the human body, by exposing it to the X rays and observing the shadow cast upon a fluorescent screen; cryptoscopy.

fluosilicate.c: Fluosilicate Flu`o*sil"i*cate (?), n. [Cf. F. fluosilicate.] (Chem.) A double fluoride of silicon and some other (usually basic) element or radical, regarded as a salt of fluosilicic acid; -- called also silicofluoride.

fluosilicic.c: Fluosilicic Flu`o*si*lic"ic (?), a. [Fluo- + silicic: cf. F. fluosilicique.] (Chem.) Composed of, or derived from, silicon and fluorine.

flurried.c: Flurried Flur"ried (?), a. Agitated; excited. -- Flur"ried*ly adv.

flurry.c: Flurry Flur"ry (?), n.; pl. Flurries (#). [Prov. E. flur to ruffle.] 1. A sudden and brief blast or gust; a light, temporary breeze; as, a flurry of wind.
Flurry Flur"ry, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flurried (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flurrying.] To put in a state of agitation; to excite or alarm. H. Swinburne.

flush.c: Flush Flush (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Flushed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Flushing.] [Cf. OE. fluschen to fly up, penetrate, F. fluz a flowing, E. flux, dial. Sw. flossa to blaze, and E. flash; perh. influenced by blush. √84.] 1. To flow and spread suddenly; to rush; as, blood flushes into the face.
Flush Flush, v. t. 1. To cause to be full; to flood; to overflow; to overwhelm with water; as, to flush the meadows; to flood for the purpose of cleaning; as, to flush a sewer.

Flush Flush, v. i. (Mining) (a) To operate a placer mine, where the continuous supply of water is insufficient, by holding back the water, and releasing it periodically in a flood. (b) To fill underground spaces, especially in coal mines, with material carried by water, which, after drainage, constitutes a compact mass.
Flush Flush, n. 1. A sudden flowing; a rush which fills or overflows, as of water for cleansing purposes.
Flush Flush, a. 1. Full of vigor; fresh; glowing; bright.
Flush Flush (?), adv. So as to be level or even.

flusher.c: Flusher Flush"er (?), n. 1. A workman employed in cleaning sewers by flushing them with water.

flushing.c: Flushing Flush"ing, n. 1. A heavy, coarse cloth manufactured from shoddy; -- commonly in the? [Eng.]

flushingly.c: Flushingly Flush"ing*ly, adv. In a flushing manner.

flushness.c: Flushness Flush"ness, n. The state of being flush; abundance.

fluster.c: Fluster Flus"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Flustered; p. pr. & vb. n. Flustering.] [Cf. Icel. flaustra to be flustered, flaustr a fluster.] To make hot and rosy, as with drinking; to heat; hence, to throw into agitation and confusion; to confuse; to muddle.
Fluster Flus"ter, v. i. To be in a heat or bustle; to be agitated and confused.
Fluster Flus"ter, n. Heat or glow, as from drinking; agitation mingled with confusion; disorder.

flusteration.c: Flusteration Flus`ter*a"tion (?), n. The act of flustering, or the state of being flustered; fluster. [Colloq.]

flustrate.c: Flustrate Flus"trate (?), v. t. [See Fluster, v. t.] To fluster. [Colloq.] Spectator.

flustration.c: Flustration Flus*tra"tion (?), n. The act of flustrating; confusion; flurry. [Colloq.] Richardson.

flute.c: Flute Flute (?), n. [OE. floute, floite, fr. OF. flaüte, flahute, flahuste, F. fl?te; cf. LL. flauta, D. fluit. See Flute, v. i.] 1. A musical wind instrument, consisting of a hollow cylinder or pipe, with holes along its length, stopped by the fingers or by keys which are opened by the fingers. The modern flute is closed at the upper end, and blown with the mouth at a lateral hole.
Flute Flute (flūt), n. [Cf. F. flûte a transport, D. fluit.] A kind of flyboat; a storeship.

Flute Flute (?), v. i. [OE. flouten, floiten, OF. flaüter, fleüter, flouster, F. flûter, cf. D. fluiten; ascribed to an assumed LL. flautare, flatuare, fr. L. flatus a blowing, fr. flare to blow. Cf. Flout, Flageolet, Flatulent.] To play on, or as on, a flute; to make a flutelike sound.
Flute Flute, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fluted (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fluting (?).] 1. To play, whistle, or sing with a clear, soft note, like that of a flute.
Flute a bec ‖Flûte` à bec" (?). [F.] (Mus.) A beak flute, an older form of the flute, played with a mouthpiece resembling a beak, and held like a flageolet.

fluted.c: Fluted Flut"ed (?), a. 1. Thin; fine; clear and mellow; flutelike; as, fluted notes. Busby.

flutemouth.c: Flutemouth Flute"mouth` (?), n. (Zool.) A fish of the genus Aulostoma, having a much elongated tubular snout.

fluter.c: Fluter Flut"er (?), n. 1. One who plays on the flute; a flutist or flautist.

fluting.c: Fluting Flut"ing, n. Decoration by means of flutes or channels; a flute, or flutes collectively; as, the fluting of a column or pilaster; the fluting of a lady's ruffle.

flutist.c: Flutist Flut"ist (?), n. [Cf. F. flûtiste.] A performer on the flute; a flautist. Busby.

flutter.c: Flutter Flut"ter (?), v. t. 1. To vibrate or move quickly; as, a bird flutters its wings.
Flutter Flut"ter, n. 1. The act of fluttering; quick and irregular motion; vibration; as, the flutter of a fan.

flutterer.c: Flutterer Flut"ter*er (?), n. One who, or that which, flutters.

flutteringly.c: Flutteringly Flut"ter*ing*ly, adv. In a fluttering manner.

fluty.c: Fluty Flut"y (?), a. Soft and clear in tone, like a flute.

fluvial.c: Fluvial Flu"vi*al (?), a. [L. fluvialis, from fluvius river, fr. fluere to flow: cf.F. fluvial. See Fluent.] Belonging to rivers; growing or living in streams or ponds; as, a fluvial plant.

fluvialist.c: Fluvialist Flu"vi*al*ist, n. One who exlpains geological phenomena by the action of streams. [R.]

fluviatic.c: Fluviatic Flu`vi*at"ic (?), a. [L. fluviaticus. See Fluvial.] Belonging to rivers or streams; fluviatile. Johnson.

fluviatile.c: Fluviatile Flu"vi*a*tile (?), a. [L. fluviatilis, fr. fluvius river: cf. F. fluviatile.] Belonging to rivers or streams; existing in or about rivers; produced by river action; fluvial; as, fluviatile starta, plants. Lyell.

fluviograph.c: Fluviograph Flu"vi*o*graph (?), n. [L. fluvius river + -graph.] An instrument for measuring and recording automatically the rise and fall of a river.

fluviomarine.c: Fluvio-marine Flu`vi*o-ma*rine" (?), a. [L. fluvius river + E. marine.] (Geol.) Formed by the joint action of a river and the sea, as deposits at the mouths of rivers.

fluviometer.c: Fluviometer Flu`vi*om"e*ter (?), n. [L. fluvius river + -meter.] An instrument for measuring the height of water in a river; a river gauge.

flux.c: Flux Flux (flŭks), n. [L. fluxus, fr. fluere, fluxum, to flow: cf.F. flux. See Fluent, and cf. 1st & 2d Floss, Flush, n., 6.] 1. The act of flowing; a continuous moving on or passing by, as of a flowing stream; constant succession; change.
Flux Flux, a. [L. fluxus, p. p. of fluere. See Flux, n.] Flowing; unstable; inconstant; variable.
Flux Flux, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fluxed (flŭkst); p. pr. & vb. n. Fluxing.] 1. To affect, or bring to a certain state, by flux.

fluxation.c: Fluxation Flux*a"tion (?), n. The act of fluxing.

fluxibility.c: Fluxibility Flux`i*bil"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. LL. fluxibilitas fluidity.] The quality of being fluxible. Hammond.

fluxible.c: Fluxible Flux"i*ble (?), a. [Cf.LL. fluxibilis fluid, OF. fluxible.] Capable of being melted or fused, as a mineral. Holland.

fluxile.c: Fluxile Flux"ile (?), a. [L. fluxilis, a., fluid.] Fluxible. [R.]

fluxility.c: Fluxility Flux*il"i*ty (?), n. State of being fluxible.[Obs.]

fluxion.c: Fluxion Flux"ion (?), n. [Cf. F. fluxion.] The act of flowing. Cotgrave.

fluxional.c: Fluxional Flux"ion*al (?), a. Pertaining to, or having the nature of, fluxion or fluxions; variable; inconstant.

fluxionist.c: Fluxionist Flux"ion*ist, n. One skilled in fluxions. Berkeley.

fluxive.c: Fluxive Flux"ive (?), a. Flowing; also, wanting solidity. B. Jonson.

fluxure.c: Fluxure Flux"ure (?; 138), n. [L. fluxura a flowing.] 1. The quality of being fluid. [Obs.] Fielding.

fly.c: Fly Fly (flī), v. i. [imp. Flew (flū); p. p. Flown (flōn); p. pr. & vb. n. Flying.] [OE. fleen, fleen, fleyen, flegen, AS. fleógan; akin to D. vliegen, OHG. fliogan, G. fliegen, Icel. fljūga, Sw. flyga, Dan. flyve, Goth. us-flaugjan to cause to fly away, blow about, and perh. to L. pluma feather, E. plume. √84. Cf. Fledge, Flight, Flock of animals.] 1. To move in or pass through the air with wings, as a bird.
Fly Fly, v. t. 1. To cause to fly or to float in the air, as a bird, a kite, a flag, etc.

Fly Fly, n.; pl. Flies (flīz). [OE. flie, flege, AS. flȳge, fleóge, fr. fleógan to fly; akin to D. vlieg, OHG. flioga, G. fliege, Icel. & Sw. fluga, Dan. flue. √ 84. See Fly, v. i.] 1. (Zool.) (a) Any winged insect; esp., one with transparent wings; as, the Spanish fly; firefly; gall fly; dragon fly. (b) Any dipterous insect; as, the house fly; flesh fly; black fly. See Diptera, and Illust. in Append.
Fly Fly (?), a. Knowing; wide awake; fully understanding another's meaning. [Slang] Dickens.

Fly fungus Fly amanita { Fly amanita, Fly fungus }. (Bot.) A poisonous mushroom (Amanita muscaria, syn. Agaricus muscarius), having usually a bright red or yellowish cap covered with irregular white spots. It has a distinct volva at the base, generally an upper ring on the stalk, and white spores. Called also fly agaric, deadly amanita.

flyaway.c: Flyaway Fly"a*way` (?), a. Disposed to fly away; flighty; unrestrained; light and free; -- used of both persons and things. -- n. A flyaway person or thing. “Truth is such a flyaway.” Emerson.
Flyaway grass Flyaway grass. (Bot.) The hair grass (Agrostis scabra). So called from its light panicle, which is blown to great distances by the wind.

flybane.c: Flybane Fly"bane` (?), n. (Bot.) A kind of catchfly of the genus Silene; also, a poisonous mushroom (Agaricus muscarius); fly agaric.

flybitten.c: Fly-bitten Fly"-bit`ten (?), a. Marked by, or as if by, the bite of flies. Shak.

flyblow.c: Flyblow Fly"blow` (?), v. t. To deposit eggs upon, as a flesh fly does on meat; to cause to be maggoty; hence, to taint or contaminate, as if with flyblows. Bp. Srillingfleet.
Flyblow Fly"blow`, n. (Zool.) One of the eggs or young larvæ deposited by a flesh fly, or blowfly.

flyblown.c: Flyblown Fly"blown` (?), a. Tainted or contaminated with flyblows; damaged; foul.

flyboat.c: Flyboat Fly"boat` (?), n. [Fly + boat: cf. D. vlieboot.] 1. (Naut.) A large Dutch coasting vessel.

flycase.c: Fly-case Fly"-case` (?), n. (Zool.) The covering of an insect, esp. the elytra of beetles.

flycatcher.c: Flycatcher Fly"catch`er (?), n. (Zool.) One of numerous species of birds that feed upon insects, which they take on the wing.

flycatching.c: Fly-catching Fly"-catch`ing, a. (Zool.) Having the habit of catching insects on the wing.

flyer.c: Flyer Fly"er (?), n. [See Flier.] 1. One that uses wings.

flyfish.c: Flyfish Fly"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) A California scorpænoid fish (Sebastichthys rhodochloris), having brilliant colors.
Fly-fish Fly"-fish, v. i. To angle, using flies for bait. Walton.

flying.c: Flying Fly"ing (?), a. [From Fly, v. i.] Moving in the air with, or as with, wings; moving lightly or rapidly; intended for rapid movement.
Flying boat Flying boat. A compact form of hydro-aëroplane having one central body, or hull.

Flying fish Fly"ing fish` (?). (Zool.) A fish which is able to leap from the water, and fly a considerable distance by means of its large and long pectoral fins. These fishes belong to several species of the genus Exocœtus, and are found in the warmer parts of all the oceans.

Flying squirrel Fly"ing squir"rel (? or?). (Zool.) One of a group of squirrels, of the genus Glaucomys (formerly Pteromus and Sciuropterus [1913 Webster]), especially Glaucomys volans and Glaucomys sabrinus, having parachute-like folds of skin extending from the fore to the hind legs, which enable them to make very long, gliding leaps.

flyman.c: Flyman Fly"man (?), n.; pl. Flymen (-m?n). The driver of a fly, or light public carriage.

flysch.c: Flysch Flysch (flēsh), n. [A Swiss word, fr. G. fliessen to flow, melt.] (Geol.) A name given to the series of sandstones and schists overlying the true nummulitic formation in the Alps, and included in the Eocene Tertiary.

flyspeck.c: Flyspeck Fly"speck (flī"spĕk), n. A speck or stain made by the excrement of a fly; hence, any insignificant dot.
Flyspeck Fly"speck (flī"spĕk), v. t. To soil with flyspecks.

flytrap.c: flytrap fly"trap (flī"trăp), n. 1. A trap for catching flies.

fnese.c: fnese fnese (fnēz), v. i. [AS. fnēsan, gefnēsan.] To breathe heavily; to snort. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fo.c: Fo Fo (fō), n. The Chinese name of Buddha.

foal.c: Foal Foal (fōl), n. [OE. fole, AS. fola; akin to OHG. folo, G. fohlen, Goth. fula, Icel. foli, Sw. fåle, Gr. pw^los, L. pullus a young animal. Cf. Filly, Poultry, Pullet.] (Zoö.) The young of any animal of the Horse family (Equidæ); a colt; a filly.
Foal Foal (fōl), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foaled (fōld); p. pr. & vb. n. Foaling.] To bring forth (a colt); -- said of a mare or a she ass.
Foal Foal (fōl), v. i. To bring forth young, as an animal of the horse kind.

foam.c: Foam Foam (fōm), n. [OE. fam, fom, AS. fām; akin to OHG. & G. feim.] The white substance, consisting of an aggregation of bubbles, which is formed on the surface of liquids, or in the mouth of an animal, by violent agitation or fermentation; froth; spume; scum; as, the foam of the sea.
Foam Foam (fōm), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Foamed (fōmd); p. pr. & vb. n. Foaming.] [AS. fǣman. See Foam, n.] 1. To gather foam; to froth; as, the billows foam.
Foam Foam (fōm), v. t. To cause to foam; as, to foam the goblet; also (with out), to throw out with rage or violence, as foam. “Foaming out their own shame.” Jude 13.

foamy.c: foamy foam"y (fōm"y̆), a. Covered with foam; frothy; spumy.

fob.c: Fob Fob (fŏb), n. [Cf. Prov. G. fuppe pocket.] 1. A little pocket for a watch; -- callled also a watch pocket.
Fob Fob (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fobbed (#); p. pr. & vb. n. Fobbing.] [Cf.Fop.]

focal.c: Focal Fo"cal (?), a. [Cf. F. focal. See Focus.] Belonging to,or concerning, a focus; as, a focal point.

focalization.c: Focalization Fo`cal*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of focalizing or bringing to a focus, or the state of being focalized.

focalize.c: Focalize Fo"cal*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Focalized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Focalizing (?).] To bring to a focus; to focus; to concentrate.

focillate.c: Focillate Foc"il*late (?), v. t. [L. focilatus, p. p. of focillare.] To nourish. [Obs.] Blount.

focimeter.c: Focimeter Fo*cim"e*ter (?), n. [Focus + -meter.] (Photog.) An assisting instrument for focusing an object in or before a camera. Knight.

focus.c: Focus Fo"cus (fō"kŭs), n.; pl. E. Focuses (fō"kŭs*ĕz), L. Foci (fō"sī). [L. focus hearth, fireplace; perh. akin to E. bake. Cf. Curfew, Fuel, Fusil the firearm.] 1. (Opt.) A point in which the rays of light meet, after being reflected or refracted, and at which the image is formed; as, the focus of a lens or mirror.
Focus Fo"cus (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Focused (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Focusing.] To bring to a focus; to focalize; as, to focus a camera. R. Hunt.

fodder.c: Fodder Fod"der (fŏd"dẽr), n. [See 1st Fother.] A weight by which lead and some other metals were formerly sold, in England, varying from 19½ to 24 cwt.; a fother. [Obs.]

Fodder Fod"der (fŏd"dẽr), n. [AS. fōdder, fōddor, fodder (also sheath case), fr. fōda food; akin to D. voeder, OHG. fuotar, G. futter, Icel. fōðr, Sw. & Dan. foder. √75. See Food and cf. Forage, Fur.] That which is fed out to cattle horses, and sheep, as hay, cornstalks, vegetables, etc.
Fodder Fod"der (fŏd"dẽr), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foddered (fŏd"dẽrd); p. pr. & vb. n. Foddering.] To feed, as cattle, with dry food or cut grass, etc.; to furnish with hay, straw, oats, etc.

fodderer.c: Fodderer Fod"der*er (?), n. One who fodders cattle.

fodient.c: Fodient Fo"di*ent (?), a. [L. fodiens, p. pr. of fodere to dig.] Fitted for, or pertaining to, digging.
Fodient Fo"di*ent (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Fodientia.

fodientia.c: Fodientia Fo`di*en"ti*a (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. fodiens p. pr., digging.] (Zool.) A group of African edentates including the aard-vark.

foe.c: Foe Foe (fō), n. [OE. fo, fa, AS. fāh hostile; prob. akin to E. fiend. √81. See Fiend, and cf. Feud a quarrel.]
Foe Foe (?), v. t. To treat as an enemy. [Obs.] Spenser.

foehn.c: Foehn ‖Foehn (?), n. [G. dial. (Swiss), fr. L. Favonius west wind. Cf. Favonian.] (Meteor.) (a) A warm dry wind that often blows in the northern valleys of the Alps, due to the indraught of a storm center passing over Central Europe. The wind, heated by compression in its descent from the mountains, reaches the base, particularly in winter, dry and warm. (b) Any similar wind, as the chinook, in other parts of the world.

foeman.c: Foeman Foe"man (fō"main), n.; pl. Foemen (-mein). [AS. fāhman.] An enemy in war.

foetus.c: foetus foetus foetus, Fœ"tus (?), n. Same as Fetus.

fog.c: Fog Fog (fŏg), n. [Cf. Scot. fog, fouge, moss, foggage rank grass, LL. fogagium, W. ffwg dry grass.] (Agric.) (a) A second growth of grass; aftergrass. (b) Dead or decaying grass remaining on land through the winter; -- called also foggage. [Prov.Eng.] Halliwell.
Fog Fog (fŏg), v. t. (Agric.) To pasture cattle on the fog, or aftergrass, of; to eat off the fog from.
Fog Fog (fŏg), v. i. [Etymol. uncertain.] To practice in a small or mean way; to pettifog. [Obs.]

Fog Fog (fŏg), n. [Dan. sneefog snow falling thick, drift of snow, driving snow, cf. Icel. fok spray, snowdrift, fjūk snowstorm, fjūka to drift.] 1. Watery vapor condensed in the lower part of the atmosphere and disturbing its transparency. It differs from cloud only in being near the ground, and from mist in not approaching so nearly to fine rain. See Cloud.
Fog Fog (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fogged (#); p. pr. & vb. n. Fogging (#).] 1. To envelop, as with fog; to befog; to overcast; to darken; to obscure.
Fog Fog (?), v. i. (Photog.) To show indistinctly or become indistinct, as the picture on a negative sometimes does in the process of development.
Fog belt Fog belt. A region of the ocean where fogs are of marked frequency, as near the coast of Newfoundland.

fogbow.c: Fogbow Fog"bow` (?), n. A nebulous arch, or bow, of white or yellowish light sometimes seen in fog, etc.

foge.c: Foge Foge (?), n. The Cornish name for a forge used for smelting tin. Raymond

fogger.c: Fogger Fog"ger (?), n. One who fogs; a pettifogger. [Obs.]

foggily.c: Foggily Fog"gi*ly (?), adv. In a foggy manner; obscurely. Johnson.

fogginess.c: Fogginess Fog"gi*ness (?), n. The state of being foggy. Johnson.

foggy.c: Foggy Fog"gy (?), a. [Compar. Foggier (?); superl. Foggiest.] [From 4th Fog.] 1. Filled or abounding with fog, or watery exhalations; misty; as, a foggy atmosphere; a foggy morning. Shak.

fogless.c: Fogless Fog"less (?), a. Without fog; clear. Kane.

fogy.c: Fogy Fo"gy (?), n.; pl. Fogies (?). 1. A dull old fellow; a person behind the times, over-conservative, or slow; -- usually preceded by old; an old fogy. [Written also fogie and fogey.] [Colloq.]

fogyism.c: Fogyism Fo"gy*ism (?), n. The principles and conduct of a fogy. [Colloq.]

foh.c: Foh Foh (?), interj. [Cf. Faugh.] An exclamation of abhorrence or contempt; poh; fie. Shak.

fohist.c: Fohist Fo"hist (?), n. A Buddhist priest. See Fo.

foible.c: Foible Foi"ble (?), a. [OF. foible. See Feeble.] Weak; feeble. [Obs.] Lord Herbert.
Foible Foi"ble (?), n. 1. A moral weakness; a failing; a weak point; a frailty.

foil.c: Foil Foil (foil), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foiled (foild); p. pr. & vb. n. Foiling.] [F. fouler to tread or trample under one's feet, to press, oppress. See Full, v. t.] 1. To tread under foot; to trample.
Foil Foil, v. t. [See 6th File.] To defile; to soil. [Obs.]
Foil Foil, n. 1. Failure of success when on the point of attainment; defeat; frustration; miscarriage. Milton.

Foil Foil, n. [OE. foil leaf, OF. foil, fuil, fueil, foille, fueille, F. feuille, fr. L. folium, pl. folia; akin to Gr.?, and perh. to E. blade. Cf. Foliage, Folio.] 1. A leaf or very thin sheet of metal; as, brass foil; tin foil; gold foil.

foilable.c: Foilable Foil"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being foiled.

foiler.c: Foiler Foil"er (?), n. One who foils or frustrates. Johnson.

foiling.c: Foiling Foil"ing, n. [Cf. F. foulées. See 1st Foil.] (Hunting) The track of game (as deer) in the grass.

foin.c: Foin Foin (foin), n. [F. fouine a marten.] 1. (Zool.) The beech marten (Mustela foina). See Marten.

Foin Foin, v. i. [OE. foinen, foignen; of uncertain origin; cf. dial. F. fouiner to push for eels with a spear, fr. F. fouine an eelspear, perh. fr. L. fodere to dig, thrust.] To thrust with a sword or spear; to lunge. [Obs.]
Foin Foin, v. t. To prick; to st?ng. [Obs.] Huloet.
Foin Foin, n. A pass in fencing; a lunge. [Obs.] Shak.

foinery.c: Foinery Foin"er*y (?), n. Thrusting with the foil; fencing with the point, as distinguished from broadsword play. [Obs.] Marston.

foiningly.c: Foiningly Foin"ing*ly (?), adv. With a push or thrust. [Obs.]

foison.c: Foison Foi"son (?), n. [F. foison, fr. L. fusio a pouring, effusion. See Fusion.] Rich harvest; plenty; abundance. [Archaic] Lowell.

foist.c: Foist Foist (foist), n. [OF. fuste stick, boat, fr. L. fustis cudgel. Cf. 1st Fust.] A light and fast-sailing ship. [Obs.] Beau. & Fl.

Foist Foist, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foisted; p. pr. & vb. n. Foisting.] [Cf. OD. vysten to fizzle, D. veesten, E. fizz, fitchet, bullfist.] To insert surreptitiously, wrongfully, or without warrant; to interpolate; to pass off (something spurious or counterfeit) as genuine, true, or worthy; -- usually followed by in.
Foist Foist, n. 1. A foister; a sharper. [Obs.] B. Jonson.

foister.c: Foister Foist"er (?), n. One who foists something surreptitiously; a falsifier. Mir. for Mag.

fold.c: Fold Fold (fōld), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Folded; p. pr. & vb. n. Folding.] [OE. folden, falden, AS. fealdan; akin to OHG. faltan, faldan, G. falten, Icel. falda, Dan. folde, Sw. fålla, Goth. falþan, cf. Gr. di-pla`sios twofold, Skr. puṭa a fold. Cf. Fauteuil.] 1. To lap or lay in plaits or folds; to lay one part over another part of; to double; as, to fold cloth; to fold a letter.
Fold Fold, v. i. To become folded, plaited, or doubled; to close over another of the same kind; to double together; as, the leaves of the door fold. 1 Kings vi. 34.
Fold Fold, n. [From Fold, v. In sense 2 AS. -feald, akin to fealdan to fold.] 1. A doubling,esp. of any flexible substance; a part laid over on another part; a plait; a plication.
Fold Fold, n. [OE. fald, fold, AS. fald, falod.] 1. An inclosure for sheep; a sheep pen.
Fold Fold, v. t. To confine in a fold, as sheep.
Fold Fold, v. i. To confine sheep in a fold. [R.]

foldage.c: Foldage Fold"age, (?) n. [See Fold inclosure, Faldage.] (O.Eng.Law.) See Faldage.

folder.c: Folder Fold"er (?), n. One who, or that which, folds; esp., a flat, knifelike instrument used for folding paper.

folderol.c: Folderol Fol"de*rol` (?), n. Nonsense; foolish talk. [Also spelled falderal and falderol.] [Colloq.]

folding.c: Folding Fold"ing (?), n. 1. The act of making a fold or folds; also, a fold; a doubling; a plication.

foldless.c: Foldless Fold"less, a. Having no fold. Milman.

foliaceous.c: Foliaceous Fo`li*a"ceous (?), a. [L. foliaceus, fr. folium leaf.] 1. (Bot.) Belonging to, or having the texture or nature of, a leaf; having leaves intermixed with flowers; as, a foliaceous spike.

foliage.c: Foliage Fo"li*age (?), n. [OF. foillage, fueillage, F. feuillage, fr. OF. foille, fueille, fueil, F. feulle, leaf, L. folium. See 3d Foil, and cf. Foliation, Filemot.]
Foliage Fo"li*age (?), v. t. To adorn with foliage or the imitation of foliage; to form into the representation of leaves. [R.] Drummond.

foliaged.c: Foliaged Fo"li*aged (?), a. Furnished with foliage; leaved; as, the variously foliaged mulberry.

foliar.c: Foliar Fo"li*ar (?), a. (Bot.) Consisting of, or pertaining to, leaves; as, foliar appendages.

foliate.c: Foliate Fo"li*ate (?), a. [L. foliatus leaved, leafy, fr. folium leaf. See Foliage.] (Bot.) Furnished with leaves; leafy; as, a foliate stalk.
Foliate Fo"li*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foliated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foliating (?).] 1. To beat into a leaf, or thin plate. Bacon.

foliated.c: Foliated Fo"li*a`ted (?), a. 1. Having leaves, or leaflike projections; as, a foliated shell.

foliation.c: Foliation Fo"li*a"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. foliation.] 1. The process of forming into a leaf or leaves.

foliature.c: Foliature Fo"li*a*ture (?), n. [L. foliatura foliage.] 1. Foliage; leafage. [Obs.] Shuckford.

foliferous.c: Foliferous Fo*lif"er*ous (?), a. [L. folium leaf+ -ferous: cf. F. foliifère.] Producing leaves. [Written also foliiferous.]

folio.c: Folio Fol"io (?), n.; pl. Folios (#). [Ablative of L. folium leaf. See 4th Foil.] 1. A leaf of a book or manuscript.
Folio Fol"io, v. t. To put a serial number on each folio or page of (a book); to page.
Folio Fol"io, a. Formed of sheets each folded once, making two leaves, or four pages; as, a folio volume. See Folio, n., 3.

foliolate.c: Foliolate Fo"li*o*late (?), a. Of or pertaining to leaflets; -- used in composition; as, bi-foliolate. Gray.

foliole.c: Foliole Fo"li*ole (?), n. [Dim. of L. folium leaf: cf. F. foliole.] (Bot.) One of the distinct parts of a compound leaf; a leaflet.

foliose.c: Foliose Fo`li*ose" (?), a. [L. foliosus, fr. folium leaf.] (Bot.) Having many leaves; leafy.

foliosity.c: Foliosity Fo`li*os"i*ty (?), n. The ponderousness or bulk of a folio; voluminousness. [R.] De Quincey.

folious.c: Folious Fo"li*ous (?), a. [See Foliose.] 1. Like a leaf; thin; unsubstantial. [R.] Sir T. Browne.

folium.c: Folium Fo"li*um (?), n.; pl. E. Foliums (#), L. Folia (#). [L., a leaf.] 1. A leaf, esp. a thin leaf or plate.

folks.c: Folks Folk { Folk (fōk), Folks (fōks) }, n. collect. & pl. [AS. folc; akin to D. volk, OS. & OHG. folk, G. volk, Icel. fōlk, Sw. & Dan. folk, Lith. pulkas crowd, and perh. to E. follow.] 1. (Eng. Hist.) In Anglo-Saxon times, the people of a group of townships or villages; a community; a tribe. [Obs.]

folkething.c: Folkething ‖Fol"ke*thing` (?), n. [Dan. See Folk, and Thing.] The lower house of the Danish Rigsdag, or Parliament. See Legislature, below.

folkland.c: Folkland Folk"land` (?), n. [AS. folcland.] (O.Eng. Law) Land held in villenage, being distributed among the folk, or people, at the pleasure of the lord of the manor, and resumed at his discretion. Not being held by any assurance in writing, it was opposed to bookland or charter land, which was held by deed. Mozley & W.

folk.c: Folk lore Folklore { Folk"lore` (?), n., or Folk" lore` }. Tales, legends, or superstitions long current among the people; the unwritten literature of a culture, such as stories, proverbs, riddles and songs. Trench.

folkmote.c: Folkmote Folk"mote` (?), n. [AS. folcmōt folk meeting.] An assembly of the people; esp. (Sax. Law), a general assembly of the people to consider and order matters of the commonwealth; also, a local court. [Hist.]

folkmoter.c: Folkmoter Folk"mot`er (?), n. One who takes part in a folkmote, or local court. [Obs.] Milton.

follicle.c: Follicle Fol"li*cle (?), n. [L. folliculus a small bag, husk, pod, dim of follis bellows, an inflated ball, a leathern money bag, perh. akin to E. bellows: cf. F. follicule. Cf. 2d Fool.] 1. (Bot.) A simple podlike pericarp which contains several seeds and opens along the inner or ventral suture, as in the peony, larkspur and milkweed.

follicular.c: Follicular Fol*lic"u*lar (?), a. 1. Like, pertaining to, or consisting of, a follicles or follicles.

folliculous.c: Folliculous Fol*lic"u*lous (?), a. [L. folliculosus full of husks: cf. F. folliculeux.] Having or producing follicles.

follow.c: Follow Fol"low (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Followed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Following.][OE. foluwen, folwen, folgen, AS. folgian, fylgean, fylgan; akin to D. volgen, OHG. folgēn, G. folgen, Icel. fylgja, Sw. följa, Dan. fölge, and perh. to E. folk.] 1. To go or come after; to move behind in the same path or direction; hence, to go with (a leader, guide, etc.); to accompany; to attend.
Follow Fol"low, v. i. To go or come after; -- used in the various senses of the transitive verb: To pursue; to attend; to accompany; to be a result; to imitate.
Follow Fol"low (?), n. The art or process of following; specif., in some games, as billiards, a stroke causing a ball to follow another ball after hitting it. Also used adjectively; as, follow shot.

follower.c: Follower Fol"low*er (?), n. [OE. folwere, AS. folgere.] 1. One who follows; a pursuer; an attendant; a disciple; a dependent associate; a retainer.

following.c: Following Fol"low*ing (?), n. 1. One's followers, adherents, or dependents, collectively. Macaulay.
Following Fol"low*ing, a. 1. Next after; succeeding; ensuing; as, the assembly was held on the following day.
Following edge Following edge. (Aëronautics) See Advancing-edge, above.
Following surface Following surface. (Aëronautics) See Advancing-surface, above.

folly.c: Folly Fol"ly (?), n.; pl. Follies (#). [OE. folie, foli, F. folie, fr. fol, fou, foolish, mad. See Fool.] 1. The state of being foolish; want of good sense; levity, weakness, or derangement of mind.

folwe.c: Folwe Fol"we (?), v. t. To follow. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fomalhaut.c: Fomalhaut Fo"mal*haut` (?), n. [Ar., prop., mouth of the large fish: cf. F. Fomalhaut.] (Astron.) A star of the first magnitude, in the constellation Piscis Australis, or Southern Fish.

foment.c: Foment Fo*ment" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fomented; p. pr. & vb. n. Fomenting.] [F. fomenter, fr. L. fomentare, fr. fomentum (for fovimentum) a warm application or lotion, fr. fovere to warm or keep warm; perh. akin to Gr.? to roast, and E. bake.] 1. To apply a warm lotion to; to bathe with a cloth or sponge wet with warm water or medicated liquid.

fomentation.c: Fomentation Fo`men*ta"tion (?), n. [?. fomentatio: cf. F. fomentation.] 1. (Med.) (a) The act of fomenting; the application of warm, soft, medicinal substances, as for the purpose of easing pain, by relaxing the skin, or of discussing tumors. (b) The lotion applied to a diseased part.

fomenter.c: Fomenter Fo*ment"er (?), n. One who foments; one who encourages or instigates; as, a fomenter of sedition.

fomes.c: Fomes ‖Fo"mes (fō"mēz), n.; pl. Fomites (fŏm"ĭ*tēz). [L. fomes, -itis, touch-wood, tinder.] (Med.) Any substance supposed to be capable of absorbing, retaining, and transporting contagious or infectious germs; as, woolen clothes are said to be active fomites.

fon.c: Fon Fon (fŏn), n. [Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. fāni silly, fāna to act silly, Sw. fåne fool. Cf. Fond, a.] A fool; an idiot. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fond.c: Fond Fond (?), obs. imp. of Find. Found. Chaucer.
Fond Fond, a. [Compar. Fonder (?); superl. Fondest.] [For fonned, p. p. of OE. fonnen to be foolish. See Fon.] 1. Foolish; silly; simple; weak. [Archaic]
Fond Fond, v. t. To caress; to fondle. [Obs.]
Fond Fond, v. i. To be fond; to dote. [Obs.] Shak.

Fond Fond (?), n. [F., fr. L. fundus. See Fund.] [Obs., or used as a French word] 1. Foundation; bottom; groundwork; specif.: (a) (Lace Making) The ground. (b) (Cookery) The broth or juice from braised flesh or fish, usually served as a sauce.

fondant.c: Fondant ‖Fon"dant (fŏn"daint; Fr. fôN`däN"), n. [F., lit., melting, p. pr. of fondre to melt, L. fundere. See Found to cast.] A kind of soft candy, made of a thick creamy sugar paste by boiling solutions to the point of crystallization, and usually molded; as, cherry fondant.

fonde.c: Fonde Fond"e (fŏnd"ei), v. t. & i. [AS. fandian to try.] To endeavor; to strive; to try. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fondle.c: Fondle Fon"dle (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fondled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fondling (?).] [From Fond, v.] To treat or handle with tenderness or in a loving manner; to caress; as, a nurse fondles a child.

fondler.c: Fondler Fon"dler (?), n. One who fondles. Johnson.

fondling.c: Fondling Fon"dling (?), n. [From Fondle.] The act of caressing; manifestation of tenderness.
Fondling Fond"ling (?), n. [Fond + -ling.] 1. A person or thing fondled or caressed; one treated with foolish or doting affection.

fondness.c: Fondness Fond"ness, n. 1. The quality or state of being fond; foolishness. [Obs.]

fondon.c: Fondon Fon"don (?), n. [Cf. F. fondant flux.] (Metal.) A large copper vessel used for hot amalgamation.

fondu.c: Fondu ‖Fon`du" (fŏn"dụ"), a. [F. fondu, p.p. of fondre to melt, blend. See Found to cast.] 1. Blended; gradually changing or passing into each other by subtle gradations; -- said of colors or of the surface or material on which the colors are laid.

Fondu Fondue ‖Fon`due" (?), n. [Also erroneously Fon`du".] [F. See Fondu; cf. Fondant.] 1. (Cookery) A dish made of cheese, eggs, butter, etc., often seasoned with kirsch and white wine, melted together, and usually used as a dip for pieces of bread.

fondus.c: Fondus ‖Fon`dus" (?), n. [F. fondu, prop. p. p. of fondre to melt, blend. See Found to cast.] A style of printing calico, paper hangings, etc., in which the colors are in bands and graduated into each other. Ure.

fone.c: Fone Fone (?), n.; pl. of Foe. [Obs.] Spenser.

fonge.c: Fonge Fong"e (?), v. t. [See Fang, v. t.] To take; to receive. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fonly.c: Fonly Fon"ly (?), adv. [See Fon.] Foolishly; fondly. [Obs.] Spenser.

font.c: Font Font (?), n. [F. fonte, fr. fondre to melt or cast. See Found to cast, and cf. Fount a font.] (Print.) A complete assortment of printing type of one size, including a due proportion of all the letters in the alphabet, large and small, points, accents, and whatever else is necessary for printing with that variety of types; a fount.
Font Font, n. [AS. font, fant, fr. L. fons, fontis, spring, fountain; cf. OF. font, funt, F. fonts, fonts baptismaux, pl. See Fount.] 1. A fountain; a spring; a source.

fontal.c: Fontal Font"al (?), a. Pertaining to a font, fountain, source, or origin; original; primitive. [R.]

fontanel.c: Fontanel Fon"ta*nel` (?), n. [F. fontanelle, prop., a little fountain, fr. fontaine fountain. See Fountain.] 1. (Med.) An issue or artificial ulcer for the discharge of humors from the body.[Obs.] Wiseman.

fontange.c: Fontange ‖Fon`tange" (?), n. [F., from the name of the first wearer, Mlle. de Fontanges, about 1679.] A kind of tall headdress formerly worn. Addison.

food.c: Food Food (?), n. [OE. fode, AS. fōda; akin to Icel. fæða, fæði, Sw. föda, Dan. & LG. föde, OHG. fatunga, Gr. patei^sthai to eat, and perh. to Skr. pā to protect, L. pascere to feed, pasture, pabulum food, E. pasture. √75. Cf. Feed, Fodder food, Foster to cherish.] 1. What is fed upon; that which goes to support life by being received within, and assimilated by, the organism of an animal or a plant; nutriment; aliment; especially, what is eaten by animals for nourishment.
Food Food, v. t. To supply with food. [Obs.] Baret.

foodful.c: Foodful Food"ful (?), a. Full of food; supplying food; fruitful; fertile. “The foodful earth.” Dryden.

foodless.c: Foodless Food"less, a. Without food; barren. Sandys.

fool.c: Fool Fool (?), n. [Cf. F. fouler to tread, crush. Cf. 1st Foil.] A compound of gooseberries scalded and crushed, with cream; -- commonly called gooseberry fool.

Fool Fool, n. [OE. fol, n. & adj., F. fol, fou, foolish, mad; a fool, prob. fr. L. follis a bellows, wind bag, an inflated ball; perh. akin to E. bellows. Cf. Folly, Follicle.] 1. One destitute of reason, or of the common powers of understanding; an idiot; a natural.
Fool Fool, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Fooled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fooling.] To play the fool.
Fool Fool, v. t. 1. To infatuate; to make foolish. Shak.

foolahs.c: Foolahs Foo"lahs` (?), n. pl.; sing. Foolah. (Ethnol.) Same as Fulahs.

foolborn.c: Fool-born Fool"-born` (?), a. Begotten by a fool. Shak.

foolery.c: Foolery Fool"er*y (?), n.; pl. Fooleries (?). 1. The practice of folly; the behavior of a fool; foolish behavior; absurdity.

foolfish.c: Foolfish Fool"fish` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) The orange filefish. See Filefish. (b) The winter flounder. See Flounder.

foolhappy.c: Fool-happy Fool"-hap`py (?), a. Lucky, without judgment or contrivance. [Obs.] Spenser.

foolhardihood.c: Foolhardihood Fool"har`di*hood (?), n. The state of being foolhardy; foolhardiness.

foolhardily.c: Foolhardily Fool"har`di*ly, adv. In a foolhardy manner.

foolhardiness.c: Foolhardiness Fool"har`di*ness, n. Courage without sense or judgment; foolish rashness; recklessness. Dryden.

foolhardise.c: Foolhardise Fool"har`dise (?), n. [Fool, F. fol, fou + F. hardiesse boldness.] Foolhardiness. [Obs.] Spenser.

foolhardy.c: Foolhardy Fool"har`dy (?), a. [OF. folhardi. See Fool idiot, and Hardy.] Daring without judgment; foolishly adventurous and bold. Howell.

foolify.c: Foolify Fool"i*fy (?), v. t. [Fool + -fy.] To make a fool of; to befool. [R.] Holland.

foolish.c: Foolish Fool"ish, a. 1. Marked with, or exhibiting, folly; void of understanding; weak in intellect; without judgment or discretion; silly; unwise.

foolishly.c: Foolishly Fool"ish*ly, adv. In a foolish manner.

foolishness.c: Foolishness Fool"ish*ness, n. 1. The quality of being foolish.

foollarge.c: Fool-large Fool"-large` (?), a. [OF. follarge. See Fool, and Large.] Foolishly liberal. [Obs.] Chaucer.

foollargesse.c: Fool-largesse Fool"-lar*gesse` (?), n. [See Fool-large, Largess.] Foolish expenditure; waste. [Obs.] Chaucer.

foolscap.c: Foolscap Fools"cap` (?), n. [So called from the watermark of a fool's cap and bells used by old paper makers. See Fool's cap, under Fool.] A writing paper made in sheets, ordinarily 16 x 13 inches, and folded so as to make a page 13 x 8 inches. See Paper.

foot.c: Foot Foot (fŏot), n.; pl. Feet (fēt). [OE. fot, foot, pl. fet, feet. AS. fōt, pl. fēt; akin to D. voet, OHG. fuoz, G. fuss, Icel. fōtr, Sw. fot, Dan. fod, Goth. fōtus, L. pes, Gr. poy`s, Skr. pād, Icel. fet step, pace measure of a foot, feta to step, find one's way. √77, 250. Cf. Antipodes, Cap-a-pie, Expedient, Fet to fetch, Fetlock, Fetter, Pawn a piece in chess, Pedal.] 1. (Anat.) The terminal part of the leg of man or an animal; esp., the part below the ankle or wrist; that part of an animal upon which it rests when standing, or moves. See Manus, and Pes.
Foot Foot (fŏot), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Footed; p. pr. & vb. n. Footing.] 1. To tread to measure or music; to dance; to trip; to skip. Dryden.
Foot Foot, v. t. 1. To kick with the foot; to spurn. Shak.
Foot candle Foot candle. (Photom.) The amount of illumination produced by a standard candle at a distance of one foot.
Foot Guards Foot" Guards` (?), pl. Infantry soldiers belonging to select regiments called the Guards. [Eng.]
Foot pound Foot" pound` (?). (Mech.) A unit of energy, or work, being equal to the work done in raising one pound avoirdupois against the force of gravity through a vertical distance of one foot.
Foot poundal Foot" pound`al (?). (Mech.) A unit of energy or work, equal to the work done in moving a body through one foot against the force of one poundal.
Foot ton Foot ton. (Mech.) A unit of energy or work, being equal to the work done in raising one ton against the force of gravity through the height of one foot.
Foot valve Foot valve. (Mech.) A suction valve or check valve at the lower end of a pipe; esp., such a valve in a steam-engine condenser opening to the air pump.

football.c: football foot"ball` (?), n. An inflated ball to be kicked in sport, usually made in India rubber, or a bladder incased in Leather. Waller.

footband.c: Footband Foot"band` (?), n. A band of foot soldiers. [Obs.]

footbath.c: Footbath Foot"bath` (?), n. A bath for the feet; also, a vessel used in bathing the feet.

footboard.c: Footboard Foot"board` (?), n. 1. A board or narrow platfrom upon which one may stand or brace his feet; as: (a) The platform for the engineer and fireman of a locomotive. (b) The foot-rest of a coachman's box.

footboy.c: Footboy Foot"boy` (?), n. A page; an attendant in livery; a lackey. Shak.

footbreadth.c: Footbreadth Foot"breadth` (?), n. The breadth of a foot; -- used as a measure. Longfellow.

footbridge.c: Footbridge Foot"bridge` (?), n. A narrow bridge for foot passengers only.

footcloth.c: Footcloth Foot"cloth` (?), n. Formerly, a housing or caparison for a horse. Sir W. Scott.

footed.c: Footed Foot"ed, a. 1. Having a foot or feet; shaped in the foot; as, a footed candlestick. “Footed like a goat.” Grew.

footfall.c: Footfall Foot"fall` (?), n. A setting down of the foot; a footstep; the sound of a footstep. Shak.

footfight.c: Footfight Foot"fight` (?), n. A conflict by persons on foot; -- distinguished from a fight on horseback. Sir P. Sidney.

footglove.c: Footglove Foot"glove` (?), n. A kind of stocking. [Obs.]

foothalt.c: Foothalt Foot"halt` (?), n. A disease affecting the feet of sheep.

foothill.c: Foothill Foot"hill` (?), n. A low hill at the foot of higher hills or mountains.

foothold.c: Foothold Foot"hold` (?), n. A holding with the feet; firm standing; that on which one may tread or rest securely; footing. L'Estrange.

foothot.c: Foothot Foot"hot` (?), adv. Hastily; immediately; instantly; on the spot; hotfoot. Gower.

footing.c: Footing Foot"ing, n. 1. Ground for the foot; place for the foot to rest on; firm foundation to stand on.

footlicker.c: Footlicker Foot"lick`er (?), n. A sycophant; a fawner; a toady. Cf. Bootlick. Shak.

footlight.c: Footlight Foot"light` (?), n. One of a row of lights in the front of the stage in a theater, etc., and on a level therewith.

footman.c: Footman Foot"man (?), n.; pl. Footmen (?). 1. A soldier who marches and fights on foot; a foot soldier.

footmanship.c: Footmanship Foot"man*ship, n. Art or skill of a footman.

footmark.c: Footmark Foot"mark` (?), n. A footprint; a track or vestige. Coleridge.

footnote.c: Footnote Foot"note` (?), n. A note of reference or comment at the foot{4} of a page.

footpace.c: Footpace Foot"pace` (?), n. 1. A walking pace or step.

footpad.c: Footpad Foot"pad` (?), n. A highwayman or robber on foot.

footpath.c: Footpath Foot"path` (?), n.; pl. Footpaths (?). A narrow path or way for pedestrains only; a footway.

footprint.c: Footprint Foot"print` (?), n. The impression of the foot; a trace or footmark; as, “Footprints of the Creator.”

footrope.c: Footrope Foot"rope` (?), n. (Aut.) (a) The rope rigged below a yard, upon which men stand when reefing or furling; -- formerly called a horse. (b) That part of the boltrope to which the lower edge of a sail is sewed.

foots.c: Foots Foots (?), n. pl. The settlings of oil, molasses, etc., at the bottom of a barrel or hogshead. Simmonds.

footsore.c: foot-sore footsore foot"sore, foot"-sore` (?), a. Having sore or tender feet, as by reason of much walking; as, foot-sore cattle.

footstalk.c: Footstalk Foot"stalk` (?), n. 1. (Bot.) The stalk of a leaf or of flower; a petiole, pedicel, or reduncle.

footstall.c: Footstall Foot"stall` (?), n. [Cf. Pedestal.] 1. The stirrup of a woman's saddle.

footstep.c: Footstep Foot"step` (?), n. 1. The mark or impression of the foot; a track; hence, visible sign of a course pursued; token; mark; as, the footsteps of divine wisdom.

footstone.c: Footstone Foot"stone` (?; 110), n. The stone at the foot of a grave; -- opposed to headstone.

footstool.c: Footstool Foot"stool` (?), n. A low stool to support the feet of one when sitting.

footway.c: Footway Foot"way` (?), n. A passage for pedestrians only.

footworn.c: Footworn Foot"worn` (?), a. Worn by, or weared in, the feet; as, a footworn path; a footworn traveler.

footy.c: Footy Foot"y (?), a. 1. Having foots, or settlings; as, footy oil, molasses, etc. [Eng.]

foozle.c: Foozle Foo"zle (?), v. t. & i. [imp. & p. p. Foozled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foozling (?).] [Cf. G. fuseln to work badly or slowly.] To bungle; to manage awkwardly; to treat or play unskillfully; as, to foozle a stroke in golf.
Foozle Foo"zle, n. 1. A stupid fellow; a fogy. [Colloq.]

fop.c: Fop Fop (?), n. [OE. foppe, fop, fool; cf. E. fob to cheat, G. foppen to make a fool of one, jeer, D. foppen.] One whose ambition it is to gain admiration by showy dress; a coxcomb; an inferior dandy.

fopdoodle.c: Fop-doodle Fop"-doo`dle (?), n. A stupid or insignificant fellow; a fool; a simpleton. [R.] Hudibras.

fopling.c: Fopling Fop"ling (?), n. A petty fop. Landor.
