foppery.c: Foppery Fop"per*y (?), n.; pl. Fopperies (#). [From Fop.] 1. The behavior, dress, or other indication of a fop; coxcombry; affectation of show; showy folly.

foppish.c: Foppish Fop"pish (?), a. Foplike; characteristic of a top in dress or manners; making an ostentatious display of gay clothing; affected in manners.

for.c: For- For- (?). [AS. for-; akin to D. & G. ver-, OHG. fir-, Icel. for-, Goth. fra-, cf. Skr. parā- away, Gr.? beside, and E. far, adj. Cf. Fret to rub.] A prefix to verbs, having usually the force of a negative or privative. It often implies also loss, detriment, or destruction, and sometimes it is intensive, meaning utterly, quite thoroughly, as in forbathe.

For For (?), prep. [AS. for, fore; akin to OS. for, fora, furi, D. voor, OHG. fora, G. vor, OHG. furi, G. für, Icel. fyrir, Sw. för, Dan. for, adv. för, Goth. faúr, faúra, L. pro, Gr.?, Skr. pra-. √ 202. Cf. Fore, First, Foremost, Forth, Pro-.] In the most general sense, indicating that in consideration of, in view of, or with reference to, which anything is done or takes place.
For For (?), conj. 1. Because; by reason that; for that; indicating, in Old English, the reason of anything.
For For, n. One who takes, or that which is said on, the affrimative side; that which is said in favor of some one or something; -- the antithesis of against, and commonly used in connection with it.

forage.c: Forage For"age (?; 48), n. [OF. fourage, F. fourrage, fr. forre, fuerre, fodder, straw, F. feurre, fr. LL. foderum, fodrum, of German or Scand, origin; cf. OHG. fuotar, G. futter. See Fodder food, and cf. Foray.] 1. The act of foraging; search for provisions, etc.

Forage For"age, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Foraged; p. pr. & vb. n. Foraging (?).] To wander or rove in search of food; to collect food, esp. forage, for horses and cattle by feeding on or stripping the country; to ravage; to feed on spoil.
Forage For"age (?), v. t. To strip of provisions; to supply with forage; as, to forage steeds. Pope.

foralite.c: Foralite For"a*lite (?), n. [L. forare to bore + -lite.] (Geol.) A tubelike marking, occuring in sandstone and other strata.

foramen.c: Foramen ‖Fo*ra"men (?), n.; pl. L. Foramina (#), E. Foramines (#). [L., fr. forare to bore, pierce.] A small opening, perforation, or orifice; a fenestra.

foraminated.c: Foraminated Fo*ram"i*na`ted (?), a. [L. foraminatus.] Having small opening, or foramina.

foraminifer.c: Foraminifer For`a*min"i*fer (?), n. (Zool.) One of the Foraminifera.

foraminifera.c: Foraminifera ‖Fo*ram`i*nif"e*ra (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. foramen, -aminis, a foramen + ferre to bear.] (Zool.) An extensive order of rhizopods which generally have a chambered calcareous shell formed by several united zooids. Many of them have perforated walls, whence the name. Some species are covered with sand. See Rhizophoda.

foraminiferous.c: Foraminiferous Fo*ram`i*nif"er*ous (?), a. 1. Having small openings, or foramina.

foraminous.c: Foraminous Fo*ram"i*nous (?), a. [L. foraminosus.] Having foramina; full of holes; porous. Bacon.

forasmuch.c: Forasmuch For`as*much" (?), conj. In consideration that; seeing that; since; because that; -- followed by as. See under For, prep.

foray.c: Foray For"ay (fŏr"a or fo*rā"; 277), n. [Another form of forahe. Cf. Forray.] A sudden or irregular incursion in border warfare; hence, any irregular incursion for war or spoils; a raid. Spenser.
Foray For"ay, v. t. To pillage; to ravage.

forayer.c: Forayer For"ay*er (? or?), n. One who makes or joins in a foray.

forbear.c: Forbear For*bear" (fŏr*bâr"), n. [See Fore, and Bear to produce.] An ancestor; a forefather; -- usually in the plural. [Scot.] [Also spelled forebear.] “Your forbears of old.” Sir W. Scott.

Forbear For*bear" (fŏr*bâr"), v. i. [imp. Forbore (?) (Forbare (?), [Obs.]); p. p. Forborne (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forbearing.] [OE. forberen, AS. forberan; pref. for- + beran to bear. See Bear to support.] 1. To refrain from proceeding; to pause; to delay.
Forbear For*bear", v. t. 1. To keep away from; to avoid; to abstain from; to give up; as, to forbear the use of a word of doubtful propriety.

forbearance.c: Forbearance For*bear"ance (?), n. The act of forbearing or waiting; the exercise of patience.

forbearer.c: Forbearer For*bear"er (?), n. One who forbears. Tusser.

forbearing.c: Forbearing For*bear"ing, a. Disposed or accustomed to forbear; patient; long-suffering. -- For*bear"ing*ly, adv.

forbid.c: Forbid For*bid" (fŏr*bĭd"), v. t. [imp. Forbade (fŏr*băd"); p. p. Forbidden (fŏr*bĭd"d'n) (Forbid, [Obs.]); p. pr. & vb. n. Forbidding (fŏr*bĭd"dĭng).] [OE. forbeden, AS. forbeódan; pref. for- + beódan to bid; akin to D. verbieden, G. verbieten, Icel. fyrirbjōða, forboða, Sw. förbjuda, Dan. forbyde. See Bid, v. t.] 1. To command against, or contrary to; to prohibit; to interdict.
Forbid For*bid" (?), v. i. To utter a prohibition; to prevent; to hinder. “I did not or forbid.” Milton.

forbiddance.c: Forbiddance For*bid"dance (?), n. The act of forbidding; prohibition; command or edict against a thing. [Obs.]

forbiddenly.c: Forbiddenly For*bid"den*ly, adv. In a forbidden or unlawful manner. Shak.

forbidder.c: Forbidder For*bid"der (?), n. One who forbids. Milton.

forbidding.c: Forbidding For*bid"ding (?), a. Repelling approach; repulsive; raising abhorrence, aversion, or dislike; disagreeable; prohibiting or interdicting; as, a forbidding aspect; a forbidding formality; a forbidding air.

forboden.c: Forboden For*bo"den (?), obs. p. p. of Forbid. Chaucer.

forbruise.c: Forbruise For*bruise" (?), v. t. To bruise sorely or exceedingly. [Obs.]

forby.c: Forby For*by" (?), adv. & prep. [See Foreby.] Near; hard by; along; past. [Obs.]

forcarve.c: Forcarve For*carve" (?), v. t. To cut completely; to cut off. [Obs.] Chaucer.

force.c: Force Force (?), v. t. [See Farce to stuff.] To stuff; to lard; to farce. [R.]
Force Force, n. [Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. fors, foss, Dan. fos.] A waterfall; a cascade. [Prov. Eng.]

Force Force, n. [F. force, LL. forcia, fortia, fr. L. fortis strong. See Fort, n.] 1. Capacity of exercising an influence or producing an effect; strength or energy of body or mind; active power; vigor; might; often, an unusual degree of strength or energy; especially, power to persuade, or convince, or impose obligation; pertinency; validity; special signification; as, the force of an appeal, an argument, a contract, or a term.

Force Force (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forced (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forcing (?).] [OF. forcier, F. forcer, fr. LL. forciare, fortiare. See Force, n.] 1. To constrain to do or to forbear, by the exertion of a power not resistible; to compel by physical, moral, or intellectual means; to coerce; as, masters force slaves to labor.
Force Force, v. i. [Obs. in all the senses.] 1. To use violence; to make violent effort; to strive; to endeavor.

Force pump Force" pump` (?). (Mach.) (a) A pump having a solid piston, or plunger, for drawing and forcing a liquid, as water, through the valves; in distinction from a pump having a bucket, or valved piston. (b) A pump adapted for delivering water at a considerable height above the pump, or under a considerable pressure; in distinction from one which lifts the water only to the top of the pump or delivers it through a spout. See Illust. of Plunger pump, under Plunger.

forced.c: Forced Forced (?), a. Done or produced with force or great labor, or by extraordinary exertion; hurried; strained; produced by unnatural effort or pressure; as, a forced style; a forced laugh.

forceful.c: Forceful Force"ful (?), a. Full of or processing force; exerting force; mighty. -- Force"ful*ly, adv.

forceless.c: Forceless Force"less, a. Having little or no force; feeble.

forcemeat.c: Forcemeat Force"meat` (?), n. [Corrupt. for farce-meat, fr. F. farce stuffing. See Farce, n.] (Cookery) Meat chopped fine and highly seasoned, either served up alone, or used as a stuffing. [Written also forced meat.]

forcement.c: Forcement Force"ment (?), n. The act of forcing; compulsion. [Obs.]

forceps.c: Forceps For"ceps (?), n. [L. forceps, -cipis, from the root of formus Hot + capere to take; akin to E. heave. Cf. Furnace.] 1. A pair of pinchers, or tongs; an instrument for grasping, holding firmly, or exerting traction upon, bodies which it would be inconvenient or impracticable to seize with the fingers, especially one for delicate operations, as those of watchmakers, surgeons, accoucheurs, dentists, etc.

forcer.c: Forcer For"cer (?), n. 1. One who, or that which, forces or drives.

forcible.c: Forcible For"ci*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. forcible forcible, forceable that may be forced.] 1. Possessing force; characterized by force, efficiency, or energy; powerful; efficacious; impressive; influential.

forciblefeeble.c: Forcible-feeble For"ci*ble-fee`ble (?), a. [From Feeble, a character in the Second Part of Shakespeare's “King Henry IV.,” to whom Falstaff derisively applies the epithet “forcible.”] Seemingly vigorous, but really weak or insipid.

forcibleness.c: Forcibleness For"ci*ble*ness, n. The quality of being forcible.

forcibly.c: Forcibly For"ci*bly, adv. In a forcible manner.

forcing.c: Forcing For"cing (?), n. 1. The accomplishing of any purpose violently, precipitately, prematurely, or with unusual expedition.

forcipal.c: Forcipal For"ci*pal (?), a. Forked or branched like a pair of forceps; constructed so as to open and shut like a pair of forceps. Sir T. Browne.

forcipated.c: Forcipated Forcipate { For"ci*pate (?), For"ci*pa`ted (?) }, a. Like a pair of forceps; as, a forcipated mouth.

forcipation.c: Forcipation For`ci*pa"tion (?), n. Torture by pinching with forceps or pinchers. Bacon.

forcite.c: Forcite For"cite (?), n. [From 3d Force, n.] (Chem.) A gelatin dynamite in which the dope is composed largely of sodium nitrate.

forcut.c: Forcut For*cut" (?), v. t. To cut completely; to cut off. [Obs.] Chaucer.

ford.c: Ford Ford (fōrd), n. [AS. ford; akin to G. furt, Icel. fjörðr bay, and to E. fare. √78. See Fare, v. i., and cf. Frith arm of the sea.] 1. A place in a river, or other water, where it may be passed by man or beast on foot, by wading.
Ford Ford, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forded; p. pr. & vb. n. Fording.] To pass or cross, as a river or other water, by wading; to wade through.

fordable.c: Fordable Ford"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being forded. -- Ford"a*ble*ness, n.

fordo.c: Fordo For*do" (?), v. t. [OE. fordon, AS. ford?n; pref. for- + d?n to do. See For-, and Do, v. i.] 1. To destroy; to undo; to ruin. [Obs.]

fordone.c: Fordone For*done" (?), a. [See Fordo.] Undone; ruined. [Obs.] Spenser.

fordrive.c: Fordrive For*drive" (?), v. t. To drive about; to drive here and there. [Obs.] Rom. of R.

fordrunken.c: Fordrunken For*drunk"en (?), a. Utterly drunk; very drunk. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fordry.c: Fordry For*dry" (?), a. Entirely dry; withered. [Obs.] “A tree fordry.” Chaucer.

fordwine.c: Fordwine For*dwine" (fŏr*dwīn"), v. i. To dwindle away; to disappear. [Obs.] Rom of R.

fore.c: Fore Fore (fōr), n. [AS. fōr, fr. faran to go. See Fare, v. i.] Journey; way; method of proceeding. [Obs.] “Follow him and his fore.” Chaucer.
Fore Fore, adv. [AS. fore, adv. & prep., another form of for. See For, and cf. Former, Foremost.] 1. In the part that precedes or goes first; -- opposed to aft, after, back, behind, etc.

Fore Fore (fōr), a. [See Fore, adv.] Advanced, as compared with something else; toward the front; being or coming first, in time, place, order, or importance; preceding; anterior; antecedent; earlier; forward; -- opposed to back or behind; as, the fore part of a garment; the fore part of the day; the fore and of a wagon.
Fore Fore, n. The front; hence, that which is in front; the future.
Fore Fore, prep. Before; -- sometimes written 'fore as if a contraction of afore or before. [Obs.]
Fore tooth Fore" tooth` (?), pl. Fore teeth (?). (Anat.) One of the teeth in the forepart of the mouth; an incisor.

foreadmonish.c: Foreadmonish Fore`ad*mon"ish (?), v. t. To admonish beforehand, or before the act or event. Bp. Hall.

foreadvise.c: Foreadvise Fore`ad*vise" (?), v. t. To advise or counsel before the time of action, or before the event. Shak.

foreallege.c: Foreallege Fore`al*lege" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forealleged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forealleging (?).] To allege or cite before. Fotherby.

foreappoint.c: Foreappoint Fore`ap*point" (?), v. t. To set, order, or appoint, beforehand. Sherwood.

foreappointment.c: Foreappointment Fore`ap*point"ment (?), n. Previous appointment; preordinantion. Sherwood.

forearm.c: Forearm Fore*arm" (?), v. t. To arm or prepare for attack or resistance before the time of need. South.
Forearm Fore"arm` (?), n. (Anat.) That part of the arm or fore limb between the elbow and wrist; the antibrachium.

forebeam.c: Forebeam Fore"beam` (?), n. The breast beam of a loom.

forebear.c: Forebear Fore*bear" (?), n. An ancestor. See Forbear.

forebode.c: Forebode Fore*bode" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foreboded; p. pr. & vb. n. Foreboding.] [AS. forebodian; fore + bodian to announce. See Bode v. t.] 1. To foretell.
Forebode Fore*bode", v. i. To foretell; to presage; to augur.

forebodement.c: Forebodement Fore*bode"ment (?), n. The act of foreboding; the thing foreboded.

foreboding.c: Foreboding Fore*bod"ing, n. Presage of coming ill; expectation of misfortune.

forebodingly.c: Forebodingly Fore*bod"ing*ly, adv. In a foreboding manner.

forebrace.c: Forebrace Fore"brace` (?), n. (Naut.) A rope applied to the fore yardarm, to change the position of the foresail.

forebrain.c: Forebrain Fore"brain` (?), n. (Anat.) The anterior of the three principal divisions of the brain, including the prosencephalon and thalamencephalon. Sometimes restricted to the prosencephalon only. See Brain.

foreby.c: Foreby Fore*by" (?), prep. [Fore + by.] Near; hard by; along; past. See Forby. Spenser.

forecast.c: Forecast Fore*cast" (?), v. t. 1. To plan beforehand; to scheme; to project.
Forecast Fore*cast", v. i. To contrive or plan beforehand.
Forecast Fore"cast (?), n. Previous contrivance or determination; predetermination.

forecaster.c: Forecaster Fore*cast"er (?), n. One who forecast. Johnson.

forecastle.c: Forecastle Fore"cas`tle (?; sailors say?), n. (Naut.) (a) A short upper deck forward, formerly raised like a castle, to command an enemy's decks. (b) That part of the upper deck of a vessel forward of the foremast, or of the after part of the fore channels. (c) In merchant vessels, the forward part of the vessel, under the deck, where the sailors live.

forecited.c: Forecited Fore"cit`ed (?), a. Cited or quoted before or above. Arbuthnot.

foreclose.c: Foreclose Fore*close" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foreclosed (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foreclosing (?).] [F. forclos, p. p. of forclore to exclude; OF. fors, F. hors, except, outside (fr. L. foris outside) + F. clore to close. See Foreign, and Close, v. t.] To shut up or out; to preclude; to stop; to prevent; to bar; to exclude.

foreclosure.c: Foreclosure Fore*clo"sure (?; 135), n. The act or process of foreclosing; a proceeding which bars or extinguishes a mortgager's right of redeeming a mortgaged estate.

foreconceive.c: Foreconceive Fore`con*ceive" (?), v. t. To preconceive; to imagine beforehand. [Obs.] Bacon.

foredate.c: Foredate Fore*date" (?), v. t. To date before the true time; to antedate.

foredeck.c: Foredeck Fore"deck` (?), n. (Naut.) The fore part of a deck, or of a ship.

foredeem.c: Foredeem Fore*deem" (?), v. t. To recognize or judge in advance; to forebode. [Obs.] Udall.
Foredeem Fore*deem", v. i. [Cf. Foredoom.] To know or discover beforehand; to foretell. [Obs.]

foredesign.c: Foredesign Fore`de*sign" (? or?), v. t. To plan beforehand; to intend previously. Cheyne.

foredetermine.c: Foredetermine Fore`de*ter"mine (?), v. t. To determine or decree beforehand. Bp. Hopkins.

foredispose.c: Foredispose Fore`dis*pose" (?), v. t. To bestow beforehand. [R.]

foredoom.c: Foredoom Fore*doom" (?), v. t. [Cf. Foredeem.] To doom beforehand; to predestinate.
Foredoom Fore"doom` (?), n. Doom or sentence decreed in advance. “A dread foredoom ringing in the ears of the guilty adult.” Southey.

forefather.c: Forefather Fore"fa`ther (?; 277), n. One who precedes another in the line of genealogy in any degree, but usually in a remote degree; an ancestor.

forefeel.c: Forefeel Fore*feel" (?), v. t. To feel beforehand; to have a presentiment of. [Obs.]

forefend.c: Forefend Fore*fend" (?), v. t. [OE. forfenden; pref. for- + fenden to fend. See Fend, v. t.] To hinder; to fend off; to avert; to prevent the approach of; to forbid or prohibit. See Forfend.

forefinger.c: Forefinger Fore"fin`ger (?), n. The finger next to the thumb; the index finger.

foreflow.c: Foreflow Fore*flow" (?), v. t. To flow before. [Obs.]

forefoot.c: Forefoot Fore"foot` (?), n. 1. One of the anterior feet of a quadruped or multiped; -- usually written fore foot.

forefront.c: Forefront Fore"front` (?), n. Foremost part or place.

foregame.c: Foregame Fore"game` (?), n. A first game; first plan. [Obs.] Whitlock.

foreganger.c: Foreganger Fore"gang`er (?), n. [Prop., a goer before cf. G. voregänger. See Fore, and Gang.] (Naut.) A short rope grafted on a harpoon, to which a longer line may be attached. Totten.

foregather.c: Foregather Fore*gath"er (?), v. i. Same as Forgather.

foregift.c: Foregift Fore"gift` (?), n. (Law) A premium paid by a lessee when taking his lease.

foregleam.c: Foregleam Fore"gleam` (?), n. An antecedent or premonitory gleam; a dawning light.

forego.c: Forego Fore*go" (?), v. t. [imp. Forewent 2; p. p. Foregone (?; 115); p. pr. & vb. n. Foregoing.] [See Forgo.] 1. To quit; to relinquish; to leave.
Forego Fore*go", v. t. [AS. foregān; fore + gān to go; akin to G. vorgehen to go before, precede. See Go, v. i.] To go before; to precede; -- used especially in the present and past participles.

foregoer.c: Foregoer Fore*go"er (?), n. 1. One who goes before another; a predecessor; hence, an ancestor; a progenitor.
Foregoer Fore*go"er, n. [Etymologically forgoer.] One who forbears to enjoy.

foreground.c: Foreground Fore"ground` (?), n. On a painting, and sometimes in a bas-relief, mosaic picture, or the like, that part of the scene represented, which is nearest to the spectator, and therefore occupies the lowest part of the work of art itself. Cf. Distance, n., 6.

foregut.c: Foregut Fore"gut` (?), n. (Anat.) The anterior part of the alimentary canal, from the mouth to the intestine, or to the entrance of the bile duct.

forehand.c: Forehand Fore"hand` (?), n. 1. All that part of a horse which is before the rider. Johnson.

forehanded.c: Forehanded Fore"hand`ed, a. 1. Early; timely; seasonable. “Forehanded care.” Jer. Taylor.

forehead.c: Forehead Fore"head (?; 277), n. 1. The front of that part of the head which incloses the brain; that part of the face above the eyes; the brow.

forehear.c: Forehear Fore*hear" (?), v. i. & t. To hear beforehand.

forehearth.c: Forehearth Fore"hearth` (?), n. (Metal.) The forward extension of the hearth of a blast furnace under the tymp.

forehew.c: Forehew Fore*hew" (?), v. t. To hew or cut in front. [Obs.] Sackville.

forehold.c: Forehold Fore"hold` (?), n. (Naut.) The forward part of the hold of a ship.

foreholding.c: Foreholding Fore*hold"ing (?), n. Ominous foreboding; superstitious prognostication. [Obs.] L'Estrange.

forehook.c: Forehook Fore"hook` (?), n. (Naut.) A piece of timber placed across the stem, to unite the bows and strengthen the fore part of the ship; a breast hook.

foreign.c: Foreign For"eign (?), a. [OE. forein, F. forain, LL. foraneus, fr. L. foras, foris, out of doors, abroad, without; akin to fores doors, and E. door. See Door, and cf. Foreclose, Forfeit, Forest, Forum.] 1. Outside; extraneous; separated; alien; as, a foreign country; a foreign government. “Foreign worlds.” Milton.

foreigner.c: Foreigner For"eign*er (?), n. A person belonging to or owning allegiance to a foreign country; one not native in the country or jurisdiction under consideration, or not naturalized there; an alien; a stranger.

foreignism.c: Foreignism For"eign*ism (?), n. Anything peculiar to a foreign language or people; a foreign idiom or custom.

foreignness.c: Foreignness For"eign*ness, n. The quality of being foreign; remoteness; want of relation or appropriateness.

forejudge.c: Forejudge Fore*judge" (?), v. t. [Fore + judge.] To judge beforehand, or before hearing the facts and proof; to prejudge.

Forejudge Fore*judge", v. t. [For forjudge, fr. F. forjuger; OF. fors outside, except + F. juger to judge.] (O. Eng. Law) To expel from court for some offense or misconduct, as an attorney or officer; to deprive or put out of a thing by the judgment of a court. Burrill.

forejudger.c: Forejudger Fore*judg"er (?), n. (Eng. Law) A judgment by which one is deprived or put out of a right or thing in question.

foreknow.c: Foreknow Fore*know" (?), v. t. [imp. Foreknew (?); p. p. Foreknown (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foreknowing.] To have previous knowledge of; to know beforehand.

foreknowable.c: Foreknowable Fore*know"a*ble (?), a. That may be foreknown. Dr. H. More.

foreknowledge.c: Foreknowledge Fore*knowl"edge (?), n. Knowledge of a thing before it happens, or of whatever is to happen; prescience.

forel.c: Forel For"el (?), n. [OE. forelcase, sheath, OF. forel, fourel, F. fourreau, LL. forellus, fr. OF. forre, fuerre, sheath, case, of German origin; cf. OHG. fuotar, akin to Goth. fōdr; prob. not the same word as E. fodder food. Cf. Fur, Fodder food.] A kind of parchment for book covers. See Forrill.
Forel For"el, v. t. To bind with a forel. [R.] Fuller.

foreland.c: Foreland Fore"land` (?), n. 1. A promontory or cape; a headland; as, the North and South Foreland in Kent, England.

forelay.c: Forelay Fore*lay" (?), v. t. 1. To lay down beforehand.

foreleader.c: Foreleader Fore*lead"er (?), n. One who leads others by his example; a guide.

forelet.c: Forelet Fore*let" (?), v. t. See Forlet. [Obs.] Holland.

forelie.c: Forelie Fore*lie" (?), v. i. To lie in front of. [Obs.]

forelift.c: Forelift Fore*lift" (?), v. t. To lift up in front. [Obs.]

forelock.c: Forelock Fore"lock` (?), n. 1. The lock of hair that grows from the forepart of the head.

forelook.c: Forelook Fore*look" (?), v. i. To look beforehand or forward. [Obs.] Spenser.

foreman.c: Foreman Fore"man (?), n.; pl. Foremen (?). The first or chief man; as: (a) The chief man of a jury, who acts as their speaker. (b) The chief of a set of hands employed in a shop, or on works of any kind, who superintends the rest; an overseer.

foremast.c: Foremast Fore"mast` (?), n. (Naut.) The mast nearest the bow.

foremeant.c: Foremeant Fore*meant" (?), a. Intended beforehand; premeditated. [Obs.] Spenser.

forementioned.c: Forementioned Fore"men`tioned (?), a. Mentioned before; already cited; aforementioned. Addison.

foremilk.c: Foremilk Fore"milk` (?), n. (Physiol.) The milk secreted just before, or directly after, the birth of a child or of the young of an animal; colostrum.

foremost.c: Foremost Fore"most` (?), a. [OE. formest first, AS. formest, fyrmest, superl. of forma first, which is a superl. fr. fore fore; cf. Goth. frumist, fruma, first. See Fore, adv., and cf. First, Former, Frame, v. t., Prime, a.] First in time or place; most advanced; chief in rank or dignity; as, the foremost troops of an army.

foremostly.c: Foremostly Fore"most`ly, adv. In the foremost place or order; among the foremost. J. Webster.

forename.c: Forename Fore"name` (?), n. A name that precedes the family name or surname; a first name. Selden.
Forename Fore"name`, v. t. To name or mention before. Shak.

forendihaz.c: Forendihaz ‖Fö"ren*di*ház` (?), n. [Hung., lit., House of Lords.] (Hungary) See Legislature.

forenenst.c: Forenenst Fore*nenst" (?), prep. [See Fore, and Anent.] Over against; opposite to. [Now dialectic]

forenight.c: Fore-night Fore"-night` (?), n. The evening between twilight and bedtime. [Scot.]

forenoon.c: Forenoon Fore"noon" (?), n. The early part of the day, from morning to meridian, or noon.

forenotice.c: Forenotice Fore"no`tice (?), n. Notice or information of an event before it happens; forewarning. [R.] Rymer.

forensic.c: Forensic Fo*ren"sic (?), a. [L. forensis, fr. forum a public place, market place. See Forum.] Belonging to courts of judicature or to public discussion and debate; used in legal proceedings, or in public discussions; argumentative; rhetorical; as, forensic eloquence or disputes.
Forensic Fo*ren"sic, n. (Amer. Colleges) An exercise in debate; a forensic contest; an argumentative thesis.

foreordain.c: Foreordain Fore`or*dain" (?), v. t. To ordain or appoint beforehand; to preordain; to predestinate; to predetermine. Hooker.

foreordination.c: Foreordination Fore*or`di*na"tion (?), n. Previous ordination or appointment; predetermination; predestination.

forepart.c: Forepart Fore part { Fore" part` (fōr"pärt), or Fore"part` }, n. The part most advanced, or first in time or in place; the beginning.

forepossessed.c: Forepossessed Fore`pos*sessed" (fōr`pŏz*zĕst" or fōr`pŏs*sĕst"), a. 1. Holding or held formerly in possession. [Obs.]

foreprize.c: Foreprize Fore*prize" (?), v. t. To prize or rate beforehand. [Obs.] Hooker.

forepromised.c: Forepromised Fore`prom"ised (?), a. Promised beforehand; preëngaged. Bp. Hall.

forequoted.c: Forequoted Fore"quot`ed (?), a. Cited before; quoted in a foregoing part of the treatise or essay.

forerank.c: Forerank Fore"rank` (?), n. The first rank; the front.

forereach.c: Forereach Fore*reach" (?), v. t. (Naut.) To advance or gain upon; -- said of a vessel that gains upon another when sailing closehauled.
Forereach Fore*reach", v. i. (Naut.) To shoot ahead, especially when going in stays. R. H. Dana, Jr.

foreread.c: Foreread Fore*read" (?), v. t. To tell beforehand; to signify by tokens; to predestine. [Obs.] Spenser.

forerecited.c: Forerecited Fore`re*cit"ed (?), a. Named or recited before. “The forerecited practices.” Shak.

foreremembered.c: Foreremembered Fore`re*mem"bered (?), a. Called to mind previously. Bp. Montagu.

foreright.c: Foreright Fore"right` (?), a. Ready; directly forward; going before. [Obs.] “A foreright wind.” Chapman.

forerun.c: Forerun Fore*run" (?), v. t. 1. To turn before; to precede; to be in advance of (something following).

forerunner.c: Forerunner Fore*run"ner (?), n. 1. A messenger sent before to give notice of the approach of others; a harbinger; a sign foreshowing something; a prognostic; as, the forerunner of a fever.

foresail.c: Foresail Fore"sail` (?), n. (Naut.) (a) The sail bent to the foreyard of a square-rigged vessel, being the lowest sail on the foremast. (b) The gaff sail set on the foremast of a schooner. (c) The fore staysail of a sloop, being the triangular sail next forward of the mast.

foresay.c: Foresay Fore*say" (?), v. t. [AS. foresecgan; fore + secgan to say. See Say, v. t.] To foretell. [Obs.]

foresee.c: Foresee Fore*see" (?), v. t. [AS. foreseón; fore + seón to see. See See, v. t.] 1. To see beforehand; to have prescience of; to foreknow.
Foresee Fore*see", v. i. To have or exercise foresight. [Obs.]

foreseen.c: Foreseen Fore*seen" (?), conj., or (strictly) p. p. Provided; in case that; on condition that. [Obs.]

foreseer.c: Foreseer Fore*se"er (?), n. One who foresees or foreknows.

foreseize.c: Foreseize Fore*seize" (?), v. t. To seize beforehand.

foreshadow.c: Foreshadow Fore*shad"ow (?), v. t. To shadow or typi?y beforehand; to prefigure. Dryden.

foreship.c: Foreship Fore"ship` (?), n. The fore part of a ship. [Obs.]

foreshorten.c: Foreshorten Fore*short"en (?), v. t. 1. (Fine Art) To represent on a plane surface, as if extended in a direction toward the spectator or nearly so; to shorten by drawing in perspective.

foreshortening.c: Foreshortening Fore*short"en*ing, n. (Fine Arts) Representation in a foreshortened mode or way.

foreshot.c: Foreshot Fore"shot` (?), n. In distillation of low wines, the first portion of spirit that comes over, being a fluid abounding in fusel oil. Knight.

foreshow.c: Foreshow Fore*show" (?), v. t. [AS. foresceáwian to foresee, provide; fore + sceáwian to see. See Show, v. t.] To show or exhibit beforehand; to give foreknowledge of; to prognosticate; to foretell.

foreside.c: Foreside Fore"side (?), n. 1. The front side; the front; esp., a stretch of country fronting the sea.

foresight.c: Foresight Fore"sight` (?), n. 1. The act or the power of foreseeing; prescience; foreknowledge. Milton.

foresighted.c: Foresighted Fore"sight`ed (?), a. Sagacious; prudent; provident for the future. Bartram.

foresignify.c: Foresignify Fore*sig"ni*fy (?), v. t. To signify beforehand; to foreshow; to typify. Milton.

foreskin.c: Foreskin Fore"skin (?), n. (Anat.) The fold of skin which covers the glans of the penis; the prepuce.

foreskirt.c: Foreskirt Fore"skirt` (?), n. The front skirt of a garment, in distinction from the train.

foresleeve.c: Foresleeve Fore"sleeve` (?), n. The sleeve below the elbow.

foreslow.c: Foreslow Fore*slow" (?), v. t. [See Forslow.] To make slow; to hinder; to obstruct. [Obs.] See Forslow, v. t.
Foreslow Fore*slow", v. i. To loiter. Same as Forslow. [Obs.]

forespeak.c: Forespeak Fore*speak", v. t. To foretell; to predict. [Obs.]

forespeaking.c: Forespeaking Fore"speak`ing, n. A prediction; also, a preface. [Obs.] Camden. Huloet.

forespent.c: Forespent Fore*spent" (?), a. [Fore + spent.] Already spent; gone by; past. [Obs.] Shak.

forespurrer.c: Forespurrer Fore*spur"rer (?), n. One who rides before; a harbinger. [Obs.] Shak.

forest.c: Forest For"est (?), n. [OF. forest, F. forêt, LL. forestis, also, forestus, forestum, foresta, prop., open ground reserved for the chase, fr. L. foris, foras, out of doors, abroad. See Foreign.] 1. An extensive wood; a large tract of land covered with trees; in the United States, a wood of native growth, or a tract of woodland which has never been cultivated.
Forest For"est, a. Of or pertaining to a forest; sylvan.
Forest For"est, v. t. To cover with trees or wood.

forestaff.c: Forestaff Fore"staff` (?), n. (Naut.) An instrument formerly used at sea for taking the altitudes of heavenly bodies, now superseded by the sextant; -- called also cross-staff. Brande & C.

forestage.c: Forestage For"est*age (?), n. [Cf. F. forestage.] (O. Eng. Law) (a) A duty or tribute payable to the king's foresters. (b) A service paid by foresters to the king.

forestal.c: Forestal For"est*al (?), a. Of or pertaining to forests; as, forestal rights.

forestall.c: Forestall Fore*stall" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forestalled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forestalling.] [OE. forstallen to stop, to obstruct; to stop (goods) on the way to the market by buying them beforehand, from forstal obstruction, AS. forsteal, foresteall, prop., a placing one's self before another. See Fore, and Stall.] 1. To take beforehand, or in advance; to anticipate.

forestaller.c: Forestaller Fore*stall"er (?), n. One who forestalls; esp., one who forestalls the market. Locke.

forestay.c: Forestay Fore"stay` (?), n. (Naut.) A large, strong rope, reaching from the foremast head to the bowsprit, to support the mast. See Illust. under Ship.

forester.c: Forester For"est*er (?), n. [F. forestier, LL. forestarius.] 1. One who has charge of the growing timber on an estate; an officer appointed to watch a forest and preserve the game.

forestick.c: Forestick Fore"stick` (?), n. Front stick of a hearth fire.

forestry.c: Forestry For"est*ry (?), n. [Cf. OF. foresterie.] The art of forming or of cultivating forests; the management of growing timber.

foreswart.c: Foreswart Foreswart { Fore"swart` (?), Fore"swart` (?), } a. [Obs.] See Forswat.

foretaste.c: Foretaste Fore"taste` (?), n. A taste beforehand; enjoyment in advance; anticipation.
Foretaste Fore*taste" (?), v. t. 1. To taste before full possession; to have previous enjoyment or experience of; to anticipate.

foretaster.c: Foretaster Fore"tast`er (? or?), n. One who tastes beforehand, or before another.

foreteach.c: Foreteach Fore*teach" (?), v. t. To teach beforehand. [Obs.]

foretell.c: Foretell Fore*tell" (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foretold (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foretelling.] To predict; to tell before occurence; to prophesy; to foreshow.
Foretell Fore*tell", v. i. To utter predictions. Acts iii. 24.

foreteller.c: Foreteller Fore*tell"er (?), n. One who predicts. Boyle.

forethink.c: Forethink Fore*think" (?), v. t. 1. To think beforehand; to anticipate in the mind; to prognosticate. [Obs.]
Forethink Fore*think", v. i. To contrive beforehand. [Obs.]

forethought.c: Forethought Fore"thought` (?), a. Thought of, or planned, beforehand; aforethought; prepense; hence, deliberate. “Forethought malice.” Bacon.
Forethought Fore"thought`, n. A thinking or planning beforehand; prescience; premeditation; forecast; provident care.

foretime.c: Foretime Fore"time` (?), n. The past; the time before the present. “A very dim foretime.” J. C. Shairp.

foretoken.c: Foretoken Fore"to`ken (?), n. [AS. foretācen. See Token.] Prognostic; previous omen. Sir P. Sidney.
Foretoken Fore*to"ken (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Foretokened (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foretokening (?).] [AS. foretācnian; fore + tācnian.] To foreshow; to presignify; to prognosticate.

foretold.c: Foretold Fore*told" (?), imp. & p. p. of Foretell.

foretop.c: Foretop Fore"top` (?), n. 1. The hair on the forepart of the head; esp., a tuft or lock of hair which hangs over the forehead, as of a horse.

foretopgallant.c: Fore-topgallant Fore`-top*gal"lant (? or?), a. (Naut.) Designating the mast, sail, yard, etc., above the topmast; as, the fore-topgallant sail. See Sail.

foretopmast.c: Fore-topmast Fore`-top"mast (?), n. (Naut.) The mast erected at the head of the foremast, and at the head of which stands the fore-topgallant mast; the mast next above the foremast. See Ship.

foretopsail.c: Fore-topsail Fore`-top"sail (? or?), n. (Naut.) the topsail on a foremast. See Sail.

forever.c: Forever For*ev"er (fŏr*ĕv"ẽr), adv. [For, prep. + ever.] 1. Through eternity; through endless ages; eternally.

forevouched.c: Forevouched Fore*vouched" (fōr*voucht"), a. Formerly vouched or avowed; affirmed in advance. [R.] Shak.

foreward.c: Foreward Fore"ward` (fōr"wärd`), n. The van; the front. [Obs.]

forewarn.c: Forewarn Fore*warn" (fōr*wärn"), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forewarned (fōr*wärnd"); p. pr. & vb. n. Forewarning.] To warn beforehand; to give previous warning, admonition, information, or notice to; to caution in advance.

forewaste.c: Forewaste Fore*waste" (?), v. t. See Forewaste. Gascoigne.

forewend.c: Forewend Fore*wend" (?), v. t. [Fore + wend.] To go before. [Obs.] Spenser.

forewish.c: Forewish Fore*wish" (?), v. t. To wish beforehand.

forewit.c: Forewit Fore"wit` (?), n. 1. A leader, or would-be leader, in matters of knowledge or taste. [Obs.]

forewite.c: Forewite Fore*wite" (?), v. t. [pres. indic. sing., 1st & 3d pers. Forewot (?), 2d person Forewost (?), pl. Forewiten (?); imp. sing. Forewiste (?), pl. Forewisten (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forewiting (?).] [AS. forewitan. See Wit to know.] To foreknow. [Obs.] [Written also forwete.] Chaucer.

forewoman.c: Forewoman Fore"wom`an (?), n.; pl. Forewomen (?). A woman who is chief; a woman who has charge of the work or workers in a shop or other place; a head woman. Tatler. W. Besant.

foreworn.c: Foreworn Fore*worn" (?), a. [See Forworn.] Worn out; wasted; used up. [Archaic]

forewot.c: Forewot Fore*wot" (?), pres. indic., 1st & 3d pers. sing. of Forewite. [Obs.] Chaucer.

foreyard.c: Foreyard Fore"yard` (?), n. (Naut.) The lowermost yard on the foremast.

forfeit.c: Forfeit For"feit (?), n. [OE. forfet crime, penalty, F. forfait crime (LL. forefactum, forifactum), prop. p. p. of forfaire to forfeit, transgress, fr. LL. forifacere, prop., to act beyond; L. foris out of doors, abroad, beyond + facere to do. See Foreign, and Fact.] 1. Injury; wrong; mischief. [Obs. & R.]
Forfeit For"feit, a. [F. forfait, p. p. of forfaire. See Forfeit, n.] Lost or alienated for an offense or crime; liable to penal seizure.

Forfeit For"feit, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forfeited; p. pr. & vb. n. Forfeiting.] [OE. forfeten. See Forfeit, n.] To lose, or lose the right to, by some error, fault, offense, or crime; to render one's self by misdeed liable to be deprived of; to alienate the right to possess, by some neglect or crime; as, to forfeit an estate by treason; to forfeit reputation by a breach of promise; -- with to before the one acquiring what is forfeited.
Forfeit For"feit, v. i. 1. To be guilty of a misdeed; to be criminal; to transgress. [Obs.]
Forfeit For"feit, p. p. or a. In the condition of being forfeited; subject to alienation. Shak.

forfeitable.c: Forfeitable For"feit*a*ble (?), a. Liable to be forfeited; subject to forfeiture.

forfeiter.c: Forfeiter For"feit*er (?), n. One who incurs a penalty of forfeiture.

forfeiture.c: Forfeiture For"fei*ture (?; 135), n. [F. forfeiture, LL. forisfactura.] 1. The act of forfeiting; the loss of some right, privilege, estate, honor, office, or effects, by an offense, crime, breach of condition, or other act.

forfend.c: Forfend For*fend" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + fend. See Forewend.] To prohibit; to forbid; to avert. [Archaic]

forfered.c: Forfered For*fer"ed (fŏr*fēr"ĕd), p. p. & a. [See For-, and Fear.] Excessively alarmed; in great fear. [Obs.] “Forfered of his death.” Chaucer.

forfete.c: Forfete For"fete (?), v. i. [See Forfeit.] To incur a penalty; to transgress. [Obs.]

forfex.c: Forfex ‖For"fex (?), n. [L.] A pair of shears. Pope.

forficate.c: Forficate For"fi*cate (?), a. [L. forfex, forficis, shears.] (Zool.) Deeply forked, as the tail of certain birds.

forficula.c: Forficula ‖For*fic"u*la (?), n. [L., small shears, scissors, dim. of forfex shears.] (Zool.) A genus of insects including the earwigs. See Earwig, 1.

forgather.c: Forgather For*gath"er (?), v. i. To convene; to gossip; to meet accidentally. [Scot.] Jamieson.

forge.c: Forge Forge (fōrj), n. [F. forge, fr. L. fabrica the workshop of an artisan who works in hard materials, fr. faber artisan, smith, as adj., skillful, ingenious; cf. Gr.? soft, tender. Cf. Fabric.] 1. A place or establishment where iron or other metals are wrought by heating and hammering; especially, a furnace, or a shop with its furnace, etc., where iron is heated and wrought; a smithy.

Forge Forge, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forged (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forging (?).] [F. forger, OF. forgier, fr. L. fabricare, fabricari, to form, frame, fashion, from fabrica. See Forge, n., and cf. Fabricate.] 1. To form by heating and hammering; to beat into any particular shape, as a metal.
Forge Forge, v. i. [See Forge, v. t., and for sense 2, cf. Forge compel.] 1. To commit forgery.
Forge Forge, v. t. (Naut.) To impel forward slowly; as, to forge a ship forward.

forgeman.c: Forgeman Forge"man (?), n.; pl. Forgemen (?). A skilled smith, who has a hammerer to assist him.

forger.c: Forger For"ger (?), n.[Cf. F. forgeur metal worker, L. fabricator artificer. See Forge, n. & v. t., and cf. Fabricator.] One who forges, makes, of forms; a fabricator; a falsifier.

forgery.c: Forgery For"ger*y (?), n.; pl. Forgeries (#). [Cf. F. forgerie.] 1. The act of forging metal into shape. [Obs.]

forget.c: Forget For*get" (?), v. t. [imp. Forgot (?) (Forgat (?), Obs.); p. p. Forgotten (?), Forgot; p. pr. & vb. n. Forgetting.] [OE. forgeten, foryeten, AS. forgietan, forgitan; pref. for- + gietan, gitan (only in comp.), to get; cf. D. vergeten, G. vergessen, Sw. förgäta, Dan. forgiette. See For-, and Get, v. t.] 1. To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory; to cease to have in mind; not to think of; also, to lose the power of; to cease from doing.

forgetful.c: Forgetful For*get"ful (?), a. 1. Apt to forget; easily losing remembrance; as, a forgetful man should use helps to strengthen his memory.

forgetfully.c: Forgetfully For*get"ful*ly, adv. In a forgetful manner.

forgetfulness.c: Forgetfulness For*get"ful*ness, n. 1. The quality of being forgetful; prononess to let slip from the mind.

forgetive.c: Forgetive For"ge*tive (?), a. [From Forge.] Inventive; productive; capable. [Obs.] Shak.

forgetmenot.c: Forget-me-not For*get"-me-not` (?), n. [Cf. G. vergissmeinnicht.] (Bot.) A small perennial herb, of the genus Myosotis (Myosotis scorpiodes, Myosotis palustris, Myosotis incespitosa, etc.), bearing a beautiful bright blue or white flowers, and extensively considered the emblem of fidelity.

forgettable.c: Forgettable For*get"ta*ble (?), a. Liable to be, or that may be, forgotten. Carlyle.

forgetter.c: Forgetter For*get"ter (?), n. One who forgets; a heedless person. Johnson.

forging.c: Forging For"ging (?), n. 1. The act of shaping metal by hammering or pressing.

forgivable.c: Forgivable For*giv"a*ble (?), a. Capable of being forgiven; pardonable; venial. Sherwood.

forgive.c: Forgive For*give" (?), v. t. [imp. Forgave (?); p. p. Forgiven (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forgiving] [OE. forgiven, foryiven, foryeven, AS. forgiefan, forgifan; perh. for- + giefan, gifan to give; cf. D. vergeven, G. vergeben, Icel. fyrirgefa, Sw. f?rgifva, Goth. fragiban to give, grant. See For-, and Give, v. t.] 1. To give wholly; to make over without reservation; to resign.

forgiveness.c: Forgiveness For*give"ness, n. [AS. forgifnes.] 1. The act of forgiving; the state of being forgiven; as, the forgiveness of sin or of injuries.

forgiver.c: Forgiver For*giv"er (?), n. One who forgives. Johnson.

forgiving.c: Forgiving For*giv"ing, a. Disposed to forgive; inclined to overlook offenses; mild; merciful; compassionate; placable; as, a forgiving temper.

forgo.c: Forgo For*go" (?), v. t. [imp. Forwent; p. p. Forgone; p. pr. & vb. n. Forgoing.] [OE. forgan, forgon, forgoon, AS. forgān, prop., to go past, hence, to abstain from; pref. for- + gān to go; akin to G. vergehen to pass away, to transgress. See Go, v. i.] 1. To pass by; to leave. See 1st Forego.

forgot.c: Forgot For*got" (?), imp. & p. p. of Forget.

forhall.c: Forhall For*hall" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + hale to draw.] To harass; to torment; to distress. [Obs.] Spenser.

forhend.c: Forhend For*hend" (?), v. t. To seize upon. [Obs.]

forinsecal.c: Forinsecal Fo*rin"se*cal (?), a. [L. forinsecus from without.] Foreign; alien. [Obs.] Bp. Burnet.

forisfamiliate.c: Forisfamiliate Fo`ris*fa*mil"i*ate (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forisfamiliated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forisfamiliating (?).] [LL. forisfamiliatus, p. p. of forisfamiliater to forisfamiliate; L. foris abroad, without + familia family.] (LAw) Literally, to put out of a family; hence, to portion off, so as to exclude further claim of inheritance; to emancipate (as a with his own consent) from paternal authority. Blackstone.
Forisfamiliate Fo`ris*fa*mil"i*ate, v. i. (Law) To renounce a legal title to a further share of paternal inheritance.

forisfamiliation.c: Forisfamiliation Fo`ris*fa*mil`i*a"tion (?), n. (Law) The act of forisfamiliating.

fork.c: Fork Fork (fôrk), n. [AS. forc, fr. L. furca. Cf. Fourché, Furcate.] 1. An instrument consisting of a handle with a shank terminating in two or more prongs or tines, which are usually of metal, parallel and slightly curved; -- used for piercing, holding, taking up, or pitching anything.
Fork Fork, v. i. [imp. & p. p. Forked (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forking.] 1. To shoot into blades, as corn.
Fork Fork, v. t. To raise, or pitch with a fork, as hay; to dig or turn over with a fork, as the soil.

forkbeard.c: Forkbeard Fork"beard` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) A European fish (Raniceps raninus), having a large flat head; -- also called tadpole fish, and lesser forked beard. (b) The European forked hake or hake's-dame (Phycis blennoides); -- also called great forked beard.

forked.c: Forked Forked (?), a. 1. Formed into a forklike shape; having a fork; dividing into two or more prongs or branches; furcated; bifurcated; zigzag; as, the forked lighting.

forkerve.c: Forkerve For*kerve (?), v. t. [Obs.] See Forcarve, v. t.

forkiness.c: Forkiness Fork"i*ness (?), n. The quality or state or dividing in a forklike manner.

forktail.c: Forktail Fork"tail` (?), n. (Zool.) (a) One of several Asiatic and East Indian passerine birds, belonging to Enucurus, and allied genera. The tail is deeply forked. (b) A salmon in its fourth year's growth. [Prov. Eng.]

forktailed.c: Fork-tailed Fork"-tailed` (?), a. (Zool.) Having the outer tail feathers longer than the median ones; swallow-tailed; -- said of many birds.

forky.c: Forky Fork"y (?), a. Opening into two or more parts or shoots; forked; furcated. “Forky tongues.” Pope.

forlaft.c: Forlaft For*laft" (?), obs. p. p. of Forleave. Chaucer.

forlay.c: Forlay For*lay" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + lay.] To lie in wait for; to ambush.

forleave.c: Forleave For*leave" (?), v. t. [OE. forleven; pref. for- + leven to leave.] To leave off wholly. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forlend.c: Forlend For*lend" (?), v. t. To give up wholly. [Obs.]

forlese.c: Forlese For*lese" (?), v. t. [p. p. Forlore (?), Forlorn (?).] [OE. forlesen. See Forlorn.] To lose utterly. [Obs.] haucer.

forlet.c: Forlet For*let", v. t. [OE. forleten, AS. forlǣtan; pref. for- + lǣtan to allow; akin to G. verlassen to leave. See Let to allow.] To give up; to leave; to abandon. [Obs.] “To forlet sin.” Chaucer.

forlore.c: Forlore For*lore" (?), imp. pl. & p. p. of Forlese. [Obs.]

forlorn.c: Forlorn For*lorn" (?), a. [OE., p. p. of forlesen to lose utterly, AS. forleósan (p. p. forloren); pref. for- + leósan (in comp.) to lose; cf. D. verliezen to lose, G. verlieren, Sw. förlora, Dan. forloren, Goth. fraliusan to lose. See For-, and Lorn, a., Lose, v. t.] 1. Deserted; abandoned; lost.
Forlorn For*lorn", n. 1. A lost, forsaken, or solitary person.

forlornly.c: Forlornly For*lorn"ly, adv. In a forlorn manner. Pollok.

forlornness.c: Forlornness For*lorn"ness, n. State of being forlorn. Boyle.

forlye.c: Forlye For*lye" (?), v. i. Same as Forlie. [Obs.]

form.c: -form -form (?). [See Form, n.] A suffix used to denote in the form or shape of, resembling, etc.; as, valiform; oviform.

Form Form (fōrm; in senses 8 & 9, often fōrm in England), n. [OE. & F. forme, fr. L. forma; cf. Skr. dhariman. Cf. Firm.] 1. The shape and structure of anything, as distinguished from the material of which it is composed; particular disposition or arrangement of matter, giving it individuality or distinctive character; configuration; figure; external appearance.

Form Form (fôrm), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Formed (fôrmd); p. pr. & vb. n. Forming.] [F. former, L. formare, fr. forma. See Form, n.] 1. To give form or shape to; to frame; to construct; to make; to fashion.
Form Form, v. i. 1. To take a form, definite shape, or arrangement; as, the infantry should form in column.

formal.c: Formal For"mal (fôr"mail), n. [L. formic + alcohol.] (Chem.) See Methylal.
Formal Form"al (fôrm"ail), a. [L. formalis: cf. F. formel.] 1. Belonging to the form, shape, frame, external appearance, or organization of a thing.

formaldehyde.c: Formaldehyde For*mal"de*hyde (?), n. [Formic + aldehyde.] (Chem.) A colorless, volatile liquid, H2CO, resembling acetic or ethyl aldehyde, and chemically intermediate between methyl alcohol and formic acid.

formalin.c: Formalin For"ma*lin (?), n. [Formic + aldehyde + -in.] (Chem.) An aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used as a preservative in museums and as a disinfectant.

formalism.c: Formalism Form"al*ism (fôrm"ail*ĭz'm), n. The practice or the doctrine of strict adherence to, or dependence on, external forms, esp. in matters of religion.

formalist.c: Formalist Form"al*ist, n. [Cf. F. formaliste.] One overattentive to forms, or too much confined to them; esp., one who rests in external religious forms, or observes strictly the outward forms of worship, without possessing the life and spirit of religion.

formality.c: Formality For*mal"i*ty (?), n.; pl. Formalities (#). [Cf. F. formalité.] 1. The condition or quality of being formal, strictly ceremonious, precise, etc.

formalize.c: Formalize Form"al*ize (fôrm"ail*īz), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Formalized (fôrm"ail*īzd); p. pr. & vb. n. Formalizing (fôrm"ail*ī`zĭng).] 1. To give form, or a certain form, to; to model. [R.]
Formalize Form"al*ize, v. i. To affect formality. [Obs.] ales.

formally.c: Formally Form"al*ly, adv. In a formal manner; essentially; characteristically; expressly; regularly; ceremoniously; precisely.

format.c: Format ‖For`mat" (for`mȧ" or for`mät"), n. [F. or G. Cf. Formation.] 1. (Print.) The shape and size of a book or other printed publication; hence, its external form. [wns=2]

formate.c: Formate For"mate (fôr"mat), n. [See Formic.] (Chem.) A salt of formic acid. [Written also formiate.]

formation.c: Formation For*ma"tion (fŏr*mā"shŭn), n. [L. formatio: cf. F. formation.] 1. The act of giving form or shape to anything; a forming; a shaping. Beattie.

formative.c: Formative Form"a*tive (?), a. [Cf. F. formatif.] 1. Giving form; having the power of giving form; plastic; as, the formative arts.

Formative Form"a*tive, n. (Gram.) (a) That which serves merely to give form, and is no part of the radical, as the prefix or the termination of a word. (b) A word formed in accordance with some rule or usage, as from a root.

forme.c: Forme For`mé" (?), a. (Her.) Same as Paté or Patté.
Forme For"me (?), a. [OE., fr. AS. forma. See Foremost.] First. [Obs.] “Adam our forme father.” Chaucer.

formed.c: Formed Formed (fôrmd), a. 1. (Astron.) Arranged, as stars in a constellation; as, formed stars. [R.]

formedon.c: Formedon For"me*don (fôr"me*dŏn), n. [OF., fr. Latin. So called because the plaintiff claimed “by the form of the gift,” L. per formam doni.] (O. Eng. Law) A writ of right for a tenant in tail in case of a discontinuance of the estate tail. This writ has been abolished.

formell.c: Formell For"mell (?), n. [Dim. of F. forme the female of a bird of prey.] (Zool.) The female of a hawk or falcon.

former.c: Former Form"er (?), n. 1. One who forms; a maker; a creator.
Former For"mer (?), a. [A compar. due to OE. formest. See Foremost.] 1. Preceding in order of time; antecedent; previous; prior; earlier; hence, ancient; long past.

formeret.c: Formeret ‖For`me*ret" (?), n. [F.] (Arch.) One of the half ribs against the walls in a ceiling vaulted with ribs.

formerly.c: Formerly For"mer*ly (?), adv. In time past, either in time immediately preceding or at any indefinite distance; of old; heretofore.

formful.c: Formful Form"ful (?), a. Creative; imaginative. [R.] “The formful brain.” Thomson.

formic.c: Formic For"mic (?), a. [L. formica an ant: cf. F. formique.] (Chem.) Pertaining to, or derived from, ants; as, formic acid; in an extended sense, pertaining to, or derived from, formic acid; as, formic ether.

formica.c: Formica ‖For*mi"ca (fôr*mī"kȧ), prop. n. [L., an ant.] (Zool.) A Linnæan genus of hymenopterous insects, including the common ants. See Ant.

formicaroid.c: Formicaroid For`mi*ca"roid (?), a. [NL. Formicarius, the typical genus + -oid.] (Zool.) Like or pertaining to the family Formicaridæ or ant thrushes.

formicary.c: Formicary For"mi*ca*ry (?), n. [LL. formicarium, fr. L. formica an ant.] (Zool.) The nest or dwelling of a swarm of ants; an ant-hill.

formicate.c: Formicate For"mi*cate (?), a. [L. formica an ant.] (Zool.) Resembling, or pertaining to, an ant or ants.
Formicate For"mi*cate (fôr"mĭ*kāt), v. i. [See Formication.] To creep or crawl like ants; swarm with, or as with, ants.

formication.c: Formication For`mi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. formicatio, fr. formicare to creep like an ant, to feel as if ants were crawling on one's self, fr. formica ant: cf. F. formication.] (Med.) A sensation resembling that made by the creeping of ants on the skin. Dunglison.

formicid.c: Formicid For"mi*cid (?), a. (Zool.) Pertaining to the ants. -- n. One of the family Formicidæ, or ants.

formidable.c: Formidable For"mi*da*ble (?), a. [L. formidabilis, fr. formidare to fear, dread: cf. F. formidable.] Exciting fear or apprehension; impressing dread; adapted to excite fear and deter from approach, encounter, or undertaking; alarming.

formidableness.c: Formidableness For"mi*da*ble*ness, n. The quality of being formidable, or adapted to excite dread. Boyle.

formidably.c: Formidably For"mi*da*bly, adv. In a formidable manner.

formidolose.c: Formidolose For*mid"o*lose (?), a. [L. formidolosus, fr. formido fear.] Very much afraid. [Obs.] Bailey.

forming.c: Forming Form"ing (?), n. The act or process of giving form or shape to anything; as, in shipbuilding, the exact shaping of partially shaped timbers.

formless.c: Formless Form"less, a. Shapeless; without a determinate form; wanting regularity of shape. -- Form"less*ly, adv. -- Form"less*ness, n.

formula.c: Formula For"mu*la (?), n.; pl. E. Formulas (#), L. Formulæ (#). [L., dim. of forma form, model. SeeForm, n.] 1. A prescribed or set form; an established rule; a fixed or conventional method in which anything is to be done, arranged, or said.

formularistic.c: Formularistic For`mu*la*ris"tic (?), a. Pertaining to, or exhibiting, formularization. Emerson.

formularization.c: Formularization For`mu*lar*i*za"tion (?), n. The act of formularizing; a formularized or formulated statement or exhibition. C. Kingsley.

formularize.c: Formularize For"mu*lar*ize (?), v. t. To reduce to a forula; to formulate.

formulary.c: Formulary For"mu*la*ry (?), a. [Cf. F. formulaire. See Formula.] Stated; prescribed; ritual.

Formulary For"mu*la*ry, n.; pl. Formularies (#). [Cf. F. formulaire.] 1. A book containing stated and prescribed forms, as of oaths, declarations, prayers, medical formulaæ, etc.; a book of precedents.

formulate.c: Formulate For"mu*late (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Formulated (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Formulating (?).] To reduce to, or express in, a formula; to put in a clear and definite form of statement or expression. G. P. Marsh.

formulation.c: Formulation For`mu*la"tion (?), n. The act, process, or result of formulating or reducing to a formula.

formule.c: Formule For"mule (?), n. [F.] A set or prescribed model; a formula. [Obs.] Johnson.

formulization.c: Formulization For`mu*li*za"tion (?), n. The act or process of reducing to a formula; the state of being formulized.

formulize.c: Formulize For"mu*lize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Formulized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Formulizing (?).] To reduce to a formula; to formulate. Emerson.

formyl.c: Formyl For"myl (?), n. [Formic + -yl.] (Chem.) (a) A univalent radical, H.C:O, regarded as the essential residue of formic acid and aldehyde. (b) Formerly, the radical methyl, CH3.

forncast.c: Forncast Forn*cast" (?), p. p. [OE. foren + cast. See Forecast.] Predestined. [Obs.] Chaucer.

fornical.c: Fornical For"ni*cal (?), a. Relating to a fornix.

fornicated.c: Fornicated Fornicate { For"ni*cate (?), For"ni*ca`ted (?) }, a. [L. fornicatus, fr. fornix, -icis, an arch, vault.] 1. Vaulted like an oven or furnace; arched.

fornicate.c: Fornicate For"ni*cate (?), v. i. [L. fornicatus, p. p. of fornicari to fornicate, fr. fornix, -icis, a vault, a brothel in an underground vault.] To commit fornication; to have unlawful sexual intercourse.

fornication.c: Fornication For`ni*ca"tion (?), n. [F. fornication, L. fornicatio.] 1. Unlawful sexual intercourse on the part of an unmarried person; the act of such illicit sexual intercourse between a man and a woman as does not by law amount to adultery.

fornicator.c: Fornicator For"ni*ca`tor (?), n. [F. fornicateur, OF. fornicator, from L. fornicator.] An unmarried person, male or female, who has criminal intercourse with the other sex; one guilty of fornication.

fornicatress.c: Fornicatress For"ni*ca`tress (?), n. [Cf. F. fornicatrice, L. fornicatrix.] A woman guilty of fornication. Shak.

fornix.c: Fornix ‖For"nix (?), n.; pl. Fornices (#). [L., an arch.] (Anat.) (a) An arch or fold; as, the fornix, or vault, of the cranium; the fornix, or reflection, of the conjuctiva. (b) Esp., two longitudinal bands of white nervous tissue beneath the lateral ventricles of the brain.

forpass.c: Forpass For*pass" (?), v. t. & i. To pass by or along; to pass over. [Obs.] Spenser.

forpine.c: Forpine For*pine" (?), v. t. To waste away completely by suffering or torment. [Archaic] “Pale as a forpined ghost.” Chaucer.

forray.c: Forray For"ray (? or?), v. t. [OE. forrayen. See Foray.] To foray; to ravage; to pillage.
Forray For"ray, n. The act of ravaging; a ravaging; a predatory excursion. See Foray.

forrill.c: Forrill For"rill (?), n. [See Forel.] Lambskin parchment; vellum; forel. McElrath.

forsake.c: Forsake For*sake" (?), v. t. [imp. Forsook (?); p. p. Forsaken (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forsaking.] [AS. forsacan to oppose, refuse; for- + sacan to contend, strive; akin to Goth. sakan. See For-, and Sake.] 1. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart or withdraw from; to leave; as, false friends and flatterers forsake us in adversity.

forsaker.c: Forsaker For*sak"er (?), n. One who forsakes or deserts.

forsay.c: Forsay For*say" (?), v. t. [AS. forsecgan to accuse; pref. for- + secgan to say.] To forbid; to renounce; to forsake; to deny. [Obs.] Spenser.

forshape.c: Forshape For*shape" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + shape, v.t.] To render misshapen. [Obs.] Gower.

forslack.c: Forslack For*slack" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + slack to neglect.] To neglect by idleness; to delay or to waste by sloth. [Obs.] Spenser.

forslouthe.c: Forslouthe For*slouth"e (?), v. t. [See For-, and Slouth.] To lose by sloth or negligence. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forslow.c: Forslow For*slow" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + slow.] To delay; to hinder; to neglect; to put off. [Obs.] Bacon.
Forslow For*slow", v. i. To loiter. [Obs.] [Also spelled foreslow.]Shak.

forslugge.c: Forslugge For*slug"ge (?), v. t. [See Slug to be idle.] To lsoe by idleness or slotch. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forsooth.c: Forsooth For*sooth" (?), adv. [AS. forsōð; for, prep. + sōð sooth, truth. See For, prep., and Sooth.] In truth; in fact; certainly; very well; -- formerly used as an expression of deference or respect, especially to woman; now used ironically or contemptuously.
Forsooth For*sooth", v. t. To address respectfully with the term forsooth. [Obs.]
Forsooth For*sooth", n. A person who used forsooth much; a very ceremonious and deferential person. [R.]

forspeak.c: Forspeak For*speak" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + speak.] 1. To forbid; to prohibit. Shak.

forspent.c: Forspent For*spent" (?), a. [AS. forspendan to consume; pref. for- + spendan to spend.] Wasted in strength; tired; exhausted. [Archaic]

forstall.c: Forstall For*stall" (?), v. t. To forestall. [Obs.] Spenser.

forstraught.c: Forstraught For*straught" (?), p. p. & a. [Pref. for- + straught; cf. distraught.] Distracted. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forswat.c: Forswat For*swat" (?), a. [See Sweat.] Spent with heat; covered with sweat. [Obs.] P. Sidney.

forswear.c: Forswear For*swear" (?), v. t. [imp. Forswore (?); p. p. Forsworn (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Forswearing.] [OE. forsweren, forswerien, AS. forswerian; pref. for- + swerian to swear. See For-, and Swear, v. i.] 1. To reject or renounce upon oath; hence, to renounce earnestly, determinedly, or with protestations.
Forswear For*swear", v. i. To swear falsely; to commit perjury. Shak.

forswearer.c: Forswearer For*swear"er (?), n. One who rejects of renounces upon oath; one who swears a false oath.

forswonk.c: Forswonk For*swonk" (?), a. [Pref. for- + swonk, p. p. of swinkto labor. See Swink.] Overlabored; exhausted; worn out. [Obs.] Spenser.

forswornness.c: Forswornness For*sworn"ness, n. State of being forsworn. [R.]

forsythia.c: Forsythia ‖For*syth"i*a (?), a. [NL. Named after William Forsyth, who brought in from China.] (Bot.) A shrub of the Olive family, with yellow blossoms.

fort.c: Fort Fort (?), n. [F., from fort strong, L. fortis; perh. akin to Skr. darh to fix, make firm, and to E. firm Cf. Forte, Force, Fortalice, Comfort, Effort.] (Mil.) A strong or fortified place; usually, a small fortified place, occupied only by troops, surrounded with a ditch, rampart, and parapet, or with palisades, stockades, or other means of defense; a fortification.

fortalice.c: Fortalice Fort"a*lice (?), n. [LL. fortalitia, or OF. fortelesce. See Fortress.] (Mil.) A small outwork of a fortification; a fortilage; -- called also fortelace.

forte.c: Forte Forte (fōrt), n. [IT. forte: cf. F. fort. See Fort.] 1. The strong point; that in which one excels. fōrt"ā -->
Forte ‖For"te (fôr"ta or fōr"ta), adv. [It. forte, a. & adv., fr. L. fortis strong.] (Mus.) Loudly; strongly; powerfully.

forted.c: Forted Fort"ed (?), a. Furnished with, or guarded by, forts; strengthened or defended, as by forts. [R.] Shak.

forth.c: Forth Forth (?), v.[AS. forð, fr. for akin to D. voort, G. fort √78. See Fore, For, and cf. Afford, Further, adv.] 1. Forward; onward in time, place, or order; in advance from a given point; on to end; as, from that day forth; one, two, three, and so forth.
Forth Forth, prep. Forth from; out of. [Archaic]
Forth Forth, n. [OE., a ford.? 78. See Frith.] A way; a passage or ford. [Obs.] Todd.

forthcoming.c: forthcoming forth"com`ing (fōrth"kŭm`ĭng or fōrth`kŭm"ĭng), a. 1. Ready or about to appear; making appearance.

forthgoing.c: Forthgoing Forth"go`ing (? or?), n. A going forth; an utterance. A. Chalmers.

forthink.c: Forthink For*think" (?), v. t. To repent; to regret; to be sorry for; to cause regret. [Obs.] “Let it forthink you.” Tyndale.

forthputing.c: Forthputing Forth"put`ing (? or?), a. Bold; forward; aggressive.

forthright.c: Forthright Forth"right` (? or?), adv. [Forth, adv. + right, adv.] Straight forward; in a straight direction. [Archaic] Sir P. Sidney.
Forthright Forth"right`, a. Direct; straightforward; as, a forthright man. [Archaic] Lowell.

forthward.c: Forthward Forth"ward (?), adv. [Forth, adv. + -ward.] Forward. [Obs.] Bp. Fisher.

forthwith.c: Forthwith Forth`with" (? or?; see With), adv. 1. Immediately; without delay; directly.

forthy.c: Forthy For*thy" (?), adv. [AS. forðȳ; for, prep. + ðȳ, instrumental neut. of se, seó, ðæt, pron. demonstrative and article. See The.] Therefore. [Obs.] Spenser.

fortieth.c: Fortieth For"ti*eth (?), a. [AS. feówertigo?a. See Forty.] 1. Following the thirty-ninth, or preceded by thirty-nine units, things, or parts.
Fortieth For"ti*eth, n. One of forty equal parts into which one whole is divided; the quotient of a unit divided by forty; one next in order after the thirty-ninth.

fortifiable.c: Fortifiable For"ti*fi`a*ble (?), a. [Cf. OF. fortifiable.] Capable of being fortified. Johnson.

fortification.c: Fortification For`ti*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [L. fortificatio: cf. F. fortification.] 1. The act of fortifying; the art or science of fortifying places in order to defend them against an enemy.

fortifier.c: Fortifier For"ti*fi`er (?), n. One who, or that which, fortifies, strengthens, supports, or upholds.

fortify.c: Fortify For"ti*fy (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fortified (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fortifying.] [F. fortifier, L. fortificare; fortis strong + -ficare (in comp.) to make. See Fort, and -fy.] 1. To add strength to; to strengthen; to confirm; to furnish with power to resist attack.
Fortify For"ti*fy, v. i. To raise defensive works. Milton.

fortilage.c: Fortilage For"ti*lage (?; 48), n. [Cf. Fortalice.] A little fort; a blockhouse. [Obs.] Spenser.

fortin.c: Fortin Fort"in (?), n. [F. See Fort, n.] A little fort; a fortlet. [Obs.]

fortissimo.c: Fortissimo ‖For*tis"si*mo (? or?), adv. [It., superl. of forte, adv. See Forte, adv.] (Mus.) Very loud; with the utmost strength or loudness.

fortition.c: Fortition For*ti"tion (?), n. [See Fortuitous.] Casual choice; fortuitous selection; hazard. [R.]

fortitude.c: Fortitude For"ti*tude (?), n. [L. fortitudo, fr. fortis strong. See Fort.] 1. Power to resist attack; strength; firmness. [Obs.]

fortitudinous.c: Fortitudinous For`ti*tu"di*nous (?), a. Having fortitude; courageous. [R.] Gibbon.

fortlet.c: Fortlet Fort"let (?), n. A little fort. [R.] Bailey.

fortnight.c: Fortnight Fort"night` (?; in U.S. often?; 277), n. [Contr. fr. fourteen nights, our ancestors reckoning time by nights and winters; so, also, seven nights, sennight, a week.] The space of fourteen days; two weeks.

fortnightly.c: Fortnightly Fort"night`ly (?), a. Occurring or appearing once in a fortnight; as, a fortnightly meeting of a club; a fortnightly magazine, or other publication. -- adv. Once in a fortnight; at intervals of a fortnight.

fortread.c: Fortread For*tread" (?), v. t. To tread down; to trample upon. [Obs.]

fortress.c: Fortress For"tress (?), n.; pl. Fortresses (#). [F. forteresse, OF. forteresce, fortelesce, LL. foralitia, fr. L. fortis strong. See Fort, and cf. Fortalice.] A fortified place; a large and permanent fortification, sometimes including a town; a fort; a castle; a stronghold; a place of defense or security.
Fortress For"tress, v. t. To furnish with a fortress or with fortresses; to guard; to fortify. Shak.

fortuitous.c: Fortuitous For*tu"i*tous (?), a. [L. fortuitus; akin to forte, adv., by chance, prop. abl. of fors, fortis, chance. See Fortune.] 1. Happening by chance; coming or occuring unexpectedly, or without any known cause; chance; as, the fortuitous concourse of atoms.

fortuity.c: Fortuity For*tu"i*ty (?), n. [Cf. F. fortuité.] Accident; chance; casualty. D. Forbes (1750).

fortunate.c: Fortunate For"tu*nate (?; 135), a. [L. fortunatus, p. p. of fortunare to make fortunate or prosperous, fr. fortuna. See Fortune, n.] 1. Coming by good luck or favorable chance; bringing some good thing not foreseen as certain; presaging happiness; auspicious; as, a fortunate event; a fortunate concurrence of circumstances; a fortunate investment.

fortunately.c: Fortunately For"tu*nate*ly, adv. In a fortunate manner; luckily; successfully; happily.

fortunateness.c: Fortunateness For"tu*nate*ness, n. The condition or quality of being fortunate; good luck; success; happiness.

fortune.c: Fortune For"tune (fôr"tun; 135), n. [F. fortune, L. fortuna; akin to fors, fortis, chance, prob. fr. ferre to bear, bring. See Bear to support, and cf. Fortuitous.] 1. The arrival of something in a sudden or unexpected manner; chance; accident; luck; hap; also, the personified or deified power regarded as determining human success, apportioning happiness and unhappiness, and distributing arbitrarily or fortuitously the lots of life.
Fortune For"tune, v. t. [OF. fortuner, L. fortunare. See Fortune, n.] 1. To make fortunate; to give either good or bad fortune to. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Fortune For"tune, v. i. To fall out; to happen.

fortuneless.c: Fortuneless For"tune*less, a. Luckless; also, destitute of a fortune or portion. Spenser.

fortunize.c: Fortunize For"tun*ize (?), v. t. To regulate the fortune of; to make happy. [Obs.] Spenser.

forty.c: Forty For"ty (fôr"ty̆), a. [OE. forti, fourti, fowerti, AS. feówertig; feówer four + suff. -tig ten; akin to OS. fiwartig, fiartig, D. veertig, G. vierzig, Icel. fjörutīu, Sw. fyratio, Dan. fyrretyve, Goth. fidwōr tigjus. See Four, and Ten, and cf. Fourteen.] Four times ten; thirty-nine and one more.
Forty For"ty, n.; pl. Forties (-tĭz). 1. The sum of four tens; forty units or objects.

fortyniner.c: Forty-niner For`ty-nin"er (?), n. One the miners who took part in the California gold rush in 1849; an argonaut. [Colloq., U. S.]

fortyspot.c: Forty-spot For"ty-spot` (?), n. (Zool.) The Tasmanian forty-spotted diamond bird (Pardalotus quadragintus).

forum.c: Forum Fo"rum (?), n.; pl. E. Forums (#), L. Fora (#). [L.; akin to foris, foras, out of doors. See Foreign.] 1. A market place or public place in Rome, where causes were judicially tried, and orations delivered to the people.

forwaked.c: Forwaked For*waked" (? or?), p. p. & a. Tired out with excessive waking or watching. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forwander.c: Forwander For*wan"der (?), v. i. To wander away; to go astray; to wander far and to weariness. [Obs.]

forward.c: Forward For"ward (?), n. [OE., fr. AS. foreweard; fore before + weard a ward. See Ward, n.] An agreement; a covenant; a promise. [Obs.]
Forward For"ward, a. 1. Near, or at the fore part; in advance of something else; as, the forward gun in a ship, or the forward ship in a fleet.

Forward For"ward (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Forwarded; p. pr. & vb. n. Forwarding.] 1. To help onward; to advance; to promote; to accelerate; to quicken; to hasten; as, to forward the growth of a plant; to forward one in improvement.

forwards.c: Forwards Forward { For"ward (?), For"wards (?) }, adv. [AS. forweard, foreweard; for, fore + -weardes; akin to G. vorwärts. The s is properly a genitive ending. See For, Fore, and -ward, -wards.] Toward a part or place before or in front; onward; in advance; progressively; -- opposed to backward.

forwarder.c: Forwarder For"ward*er (?), n. 1. One who forwards or promotes; a promoter. Udall.

forwarding.c: Forwarding For"ward*ing, n. 1. The act of one who forwards; the act or occupation of transmitting merchandise or other property for others.

forwardness.c: Forwardness For"ward*ness, n. The quality of being forward; cheerful readiness; promtness; as, the forwardness of Christians in propagating the gospel.

forwaste.c: Forwaste For*waste" (?), v. t. [Pref. for- + waste.] To desolate or lay waste utterly. [Obs.] Spenser.

forweary.c: Forweary For*wea"ry (?), v. t. To weary extremely; to dispirit. [Obs.] Spenser.

forweep.c: Forweep For*weep" (?), v. i. To weep much. [Obs.]

forwete.c: Forwete For*wete" (?), v. t. See Forewite. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forwhy.c: Forwhy For*why" (?), conj. [For + why, AS. hw?, instrumental case of hwā who.] Wherefore; because. [Obs.]

forwot.c: Forwot For*wot" (?), pres. indic. 1st & 3d pers. sing. of Forwete. [Obs.] Chaucer.

forwrap.c: Forwrap For*wrap" (?), v. t. To wrap up; to conceal. [Obs.]

foryelde.c: Foryelde For*yelde" (?), v. t. [AS. forgieldan.] To repay; to requite. [Obs.] Chaucer.

foryete.c: Foryete For*yete" (?), v. t. To forget. [Obs.] Chaucer.

foryetten.c: Foryetten For*yet"ten (?), obs. p. p. of Foryete. Chaucer.

forzando.c: Forzando ‖For*zan"do (?), adv. [It., prop. p. p. of forzare to force.] (Mus.) See Sforzato.

fossa.c: fossa fossae ‖fos"sa (?), n.; pl. fossæ (#). [L., a ditch. See Fosse.] (Anat.) A pit, groove, cavity, or depression, of greater or less depth; as, the temporal fossa on the side of the skull; the nasal fossæ containing the nostrils in most birds.

fossane.c: Fossane Fos"sane` (?), n. [Cf. F. fossane.] (Zool.) A species of civet (Viverra fossa) resembling the genet.

fosse.c: Fosse Fosse (?), n. [F., fr. L. fossa, fr. fodere, fossum, to dig.] 1. (Fort.) A ditch or moat.

fossette.c: Fossette ‖Fos`sette" (? or?), n. [F., dim. of fosse a fosse.] 1. A little hollow; hence, a dimple.

fosseway.c: Fosseway Fosse"way` (?), n. One of the great military roads constructed by the Romans in England and other parts of Europe; -- so called from the fosse or ditch on each side for keeping it dry.

fossick.c: Fossick Fos"sick (?), v. i. [Dial. E. fossick, fossuck, a troublesome person, fussick to potter over one's work, fussock to bustle about; of uncertain origin. Cf. Fuss.] 1. (Mining) To search for gold by picking at stone or earth or among roots in isolated spots, picking over abandoned workings, etc.; hence, to steal gold or auriferous matter from another's claim. [Australia]

fossil.c: Fossil Fos"sil (?), a. [L. fossilis, fr. fodere to dig: cf. F. fossile. See Fosse.] 1. Dug out of the earth; as, fossil coal; fossil salt.
Fossil Fos"sil, n. 1. A substance dug from the earth. [Obs.]

fossiliferous.c: Fossiliferous Fos`sil*if"er*ous (?), a. [Fossil + -ferous.] (Paleon.) Containing or composed of fossils.

fossilification.c: Fossilification Fos*sil`i*fi*ca"tion (?), n. [Fossil + L. facere to make.] The process of becoming fossil.

fossilism.c: Fossilism Fos"sil*ism (?), n. 1. The science or state of fossils. Coleridge.

fossilist.c: Fossilist Fos"sil*ist, n. One who is versed in the science of fossils; a paleontologist. Joseph Black.

fossilization.c: Fossilization Fos`sil*i*za"tion (?), n. [Cf. F. fossilisation.] The process of converting, or of being converted, into a fossil.

fossilize.c: Fossilize Fos"sil*ize (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fossilized (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fossilizing (?).] [Cf. F. fossiliser.] 1. To convert into a fossil; to petrify; as, to fossilize bones or wood.
Fossilize Fos"sil*ize, v. i. 1. To become fossil.

fossilized.c: Fossilized Fos"sil*ized (?), a. Converted into a fossil; antiquated; firmly fixed in views or opinions.

fossores.c: Fossores ‖Fos*so"res (?), n. pl. [NL., fr. L. fossor? digger, fr. fodere to dig.] (Zool.) A group of hymenopterous insects including the sand wasps. They excavate cells in earth, where they deposit their eggs, with the bodies of other insects for the food of the young when hatched. [Written also Fossoria.]

fossorial.c: Fossorial Fos*so"ri*al (?), a. [L. fossor a digger.] Fitted for digging, adapted for burrowing or digging; as, a fossorial foot; a fossorial animal.

fossorious.c: Fossorious Fos*so"ri*ous (?), a. (Zool.) Adapted for digging; -- said of the legs of certain insects.

fossulate.c: Fossulate Fos"su*late (?), a. [L. fossula little ditch, dim. of fossa. See Fosse.] Having, or surrounded by, long, narrow depressions or furrows.

foster.c: Foster Fos"ter (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fostered (?), p. pr. & vb. n. Fostering.] [OE. fostren, fr. AS. fōster, fōstor, food, nourishment, fr. fōda food. √75. See Food.] 1. To feed; to nourish; to support; to bring up.
Foster Fos"ter, v. i. To be nourished or trained up together. [Obs.] Spenser.

Foster Fos"ter, a. [AS. fōster, fōstor, nourishment. See Foster, v. t.] Relating to nourishment; affording, receiving, or sharing nourishment or nurture; -- applied to father, mother, child, brother, etc., to indicate that the person so called stands in the relation of parent, child, brother, etc., as regards sustenance and nurture, but not by tie of blood.

fosterage.c: Fosterage Fos"ter*age (?; 48), n. The care of a foster child; the charge of nursing. Sir W. Raleigh.

fosterer.c: Fosterer Fos"ter*er (?), n. One who, or that which, fosters.

fosterling.c: Fosterling Fos"ter*ling, n. [AS. fōstorling.] A foster child.

fostress.c: Fostress Fos"tress (?), n. [For fosteress.] A woman who feeds and cherishes; a nurse. B. Jonson.

fother.c: Fother Foth"er (?), n. [OE. fother, foder, AS. fō?er a cartload; akin to G. fuder a cartload, a unit of measure, OHG. fuodar, D. voeder, and perh. to E. fathom, or cf. Skr. pātrā vessel, dish. Cf. Fodder a fother.] 1. A wagonload; a load of any sort. [Obs.]

Fother Foth"er, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fothered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fothering.] [Cf. Fodder food, and G. füttern, futtern, to cover within or without, to line. √75.] To stop (a leak in a ship at sea) by drawing under its bottom a thrummed sail, so that the pressure of the water may force it into the crack. Totten.

fotive.c: Fotive Fo"tive (?), a. [L. fovere, fotum, to keep warm, to cherish.] Nourishing. [Obs.] T. Carew (1633).

fotmal.c: Fotmal Fot"mal (?), n. (Com.) Seventy pounds of lead.

foucault.c: Foucault current Fou`cault" cur`rent (?). [After J. B. L. Foucault (1819-68), French physicist.] (Elec.) An eddy current.

fougasse.c: Fougasse Fougade { ‖Fou`gade" (?), ‖Fou`gasse" (?) }, n. (Mil.) A small mine, in the form of a well sunk from the surface of the ground, charged with explosive and projectiles. It is made in a position likely to be occupied by the enemy.

fought.c: Fought Fought (?), imp. & p. p. of Fight.

foul.c: Foul Foul (foul), n. [See Fowl.] A bird. [Obs.] Chaucer.

Foul Foul (foul), a. [Compar. Fouler (-ẽr); superl. Foulest.] [OE. foul, ful, AS. fūl; akin to D. vuil, G. faul rotten, OHG. fūl, Icel. fūl foul, fetid; Dan. fuul, Sw. ful foul, Goth. fūls fetid, Lith. puti to be putrid, L. putere to stink, be putrid, pus pus, Gr. py`on pus, to cause to rot, Skr. pūy to stink. √82. Cf. Defile to foul, File to foul, Filth, Pus, Putrid.] 1. Covered with, or containing, extraneous matter which is injurious, noxious, offensive, or obstructive; filthy; dirty; not clean; polluted; nasty; defiled; as, a foul cloth; foul hands; a foul chimney; foul air; a ship's bottom is foul when overgrown with barnacles; a gun becomes foul from repeated firing; a well is foul with polluted water.
Foul Foul (?), v. t. [imp. & p. p. Fouled (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Fouling.] 1. To make filthy; to defile; to daub; to dirty; to soil; as, to foul the face or hands with mire.
Foul Foul, v. i. 1. To become clogged with burnt powder in the process of firing, as a gun.
Foul Foul, n. 1. An entanglement; a collision, as in a boat race.

foulard.c: Foulard ‖Fou`lard" (f. fōo`lȧr"; E. fōo`lärd"), n. [F.] 1. A thin, washable material of silk, or silk and cotton, usually with a printed pattern on it. It was originally imported from India, but now also made elsewhere.

foulder.c: Foulder Foul"der (?), v. i. [OE. fouldre lightning, fr. F. foudre, OF. also fouldre, fr. L. fulgur. See Fulgor.] To flash, as lightning; to lighten; to gleam; to thunder. [Obs.] “Flames of fouldering heat.” Spenser.

foully.c: Foully Foul"ly (?), v. In a foul manner; filthily; nastily; shamefully; unfairly; dishonorably.

foulmouthed.c: Foul-mouthed Foul"-mouthed` (?), a. Using language scurrilous, opprobrious, obscene, or profane; abusive; as, noisy foul-mouthed women all shouting at once.

foulness.c: Foulness Foul"ness, n. [AS. fūlnes.] The quality or condition of being foul.

foulspoken.c: Foul-spoken Foul"-spo`ken (?), a. Using profane, scurrilous, slanderous, or obscene language; same as foul-mouthed. Shak.

foumart.c: Foumart Fou"mart` (?), n. [OE. folmard, fulmard; AS. fūl foul + mearð, meard, marten: cf. F. marte, martre. See Foul, a., and Marten the quadruped.] (Zool.) The European polecat; -- called also European ferret, and fitchew. See Polecat. [Written also foulmart, foulimart, and fulimart.]

found.c: Found Found (?), imp. & p. p. of Find.

Found Found, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Founded; p. pr. & vb. n. Founding.] [F. fondre, L. fundere to found, pour.] To form by melting a metal, and pouring it into a mold; to cast. “Whereof to found their engines.” Milton.
Found Found, n. A thin, single-cut file for combmakers.

Found Found, v. t. [imp. & p. p. Founded; p. pr. & vb. n. Founding.] [F. fonder, L. fundare, fr. fundus bottom. See 1st Bottom, and cf. Founder, v. i., Fund.] 1. To lay the basis of; to set, or place, as on something solid, for support; to ground; to establish upon a basis, literal or figurative; to fix firmly.

foundation.c: Foundation Foun*da"tion (?), n. [F. fondation, L. fundatio. See Found to establish.] 1. The act of founding, fixing, establishing, or beginning to erect.

foundationer.c: Foundationer Foun*da"tion*er (?), n. One who derives support from the funds or foundation of a college or school. [Eng.]

founder.c: Founder Found"er (?), n. [Cf. OF. fondeor, F. fondateur, L. fundator.] One who founds, establishes, and erects; one who lays a foundation; an author; one from whom anything originates; one who endows.
Founder Found"er, n. [From Found to cast.] One who founds; one who casts metals in various forms; a caster; as, a founder of cannon, bells, hardware, or types.

Founder Found"er (?), v. i. [imp. & p. p. Foundered (?); p. pr. & vb. n. Foundering.] [OF. fondrer to fall in, cf. F. s'effondrer, fr. fond bottom, L. fundus. See Found to establish.] 1. (Naut.) To become filled with water, and sink, as a ship.
Founder Found"er, v. t. To cause internal inflammation and soreness in the feet or limbs of (a horse), so as to disable or lame him.

Founder Found"er, n. (Far.) (a) A lameness in the foot of a horse, occasioned by inflammation; closh. (b) An inflammatory fever of the body, or acute rheumatism; as, chest founder. See Chest ffounder. James White.
